descs.en: She saw through the guard nobody else noticed. He has spent ten years making people disappear, and now he wants to disappear with her.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
At a government reception on Battery Hill, sixty guards stand at the doors and look at the guests. One of them doesn’t. He watches a single man for forty-one minutes, and the only person in the building who notices is Serafina Song, there on a staff pass to inspect a red Lancia, in her sister’s dress and her own boots.

She walks across the ballroom and tells him he isn’t a guard. She’s right. Qin Haozhen has spent ten years making people disappear for a state that doesn’t put its name on doors, and nobody has ever looked at him before.

She finds his name with one bribed caterer. She asks him for a race, not a date. And a man who sleeps four hours a night in any bed in any country falls asleep in the passenger seat of her thirty-year-old car at three in the morning, and keeps coming back.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Serafina walked out of her engagement dinner between the soup and the fish in The Woman Who Sets the Price, and then turned up at her sister’s wedding in Milan with oil on her boots. I always wanted to know who could keep up with her.

The answer turned out to be the most forgettable man in the room. Haozhen is not a good man at the start of this book, and it doesn’t pretend he is. It’s about a man finding out he’s allowed to want something, starting with an egg sandwich, and a woman who decides every single morning whether she can live with the truth about him, and keeps deciding yes.

The racing is as real as I could make it: braking markers, tyre temperatures, driver changes, telemetry in four coloured lines. The spy work stays at the level of a story. And yes, the car really can do two hundred miles an hour. He did the brakes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a fast, funny book, but it has some hard moments:

• A state operative’s work, including abductions and killings, mostly off the page and remembered (What He Does for Work, The Target Has a Family, Chen Si Brokers a Truce)

• A man taken from his family in front of his young son (The Target Has a Family)

• Trauma, depression and silence after a mission (He Comes Home Wrong)

• A cruel parent and a family’s financial collapse (The Song Family Opposes the Match)

• Threats against family members and surveillance (A File on the Workbench)

• A car chase, gunfire, a gunshot wound and a burning car (Shoot the Tyres), and a fever (The Safe House in the Mountains)

• Wound stitching without a doctor (The First Time He Bleeds in Her Garage)

• A serious racing crash, intensive care and a long recovery from concussion (The Needle, Hospital, Night Two, She Drives Again)

• Illegal street racing throughout Volume One

chapters.title: The Guard Nobody Else Noticed
chapters.desc: Serafina is on Battery Hill to check a car for a forged plate, and she spots a guard who isn’t guarding anyone. So she walks over and tells him.
chapters.epigraph: “Everyone in that room was looking at somebody. He was the only one looking at the right person.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
The dress was Aurelia’s. So it was too short. Everything of Aurelia’s was too short on Serafina, by about a hand, and this one stopped two fingers above her boots. She’d thought about borrowing shoes as well. No. There were limits to what a person did for a Lancia.

The Residence on Battery Hill was all white columns and lawn. Four hundred guests, every name checked twice at the gate. A delegation from the capital. Consuls. The men who owned the container terminals, plus wives in silk. Serafina had been checked twice too. Her pass said VEHICLE SPECIALIST — LOT 9, and the photo on it looked like a mugshot.

The auction woman marched her across the service yard at a speed that should be illegal in heels.

“Forty minutes with the car. Don’t touch the paint. Don’t talk to the guests. Don’t—are those boots?”

“They’re clean boots.”

“Don’t let anyone see the boots!”

“I never talk to guests anyway. They talk to me. Then they want me to fix their son’s Porsche for free.”

“Forty minutes.” The auction woman didn’t laugh. Fine. Serafina wasn’t here to be liked. She was here for eight thousand euros and a very old man on Lake Como.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lot 9 sat in a glass pavilion at the end of the east terrace, lit from underneath like a ring in a shop window. A 1974 Lancia Stratos HF Stradale. Red. Low. Short as a sneeze. It had won the world rally championship three years running and still looked like something a boy drew in the back of a maths lesson.

Signor Bassi wanted it. He was eighty-one, he’d known Nonna in Milan, and he owned eleven cars and a parrot. He’d said it on the phone that morning.

“Your grandmother would have looked for nothing, cara. Then called me an idiot for wanting it. So I pay you. And you tell me the truth.”

So here she was. On her back on the pavilion floor, in her sister’s dress, with a torch in her teeth. The truth was on the chassis plate. Right shape. Right number. Wrong rivets. Too clean, too round. Nothing out of a Turin factory in 1974 had rivet heads that pretty. Somebody had drilled the old plate out, put a new one in, and aged the paint round it. She sniffed. Was that tea? They’d used tea?

Amateurs. She took four photos and wriggled out. Brushed the dust off Aurelia’s dress. Looked up.

And there he was.

✦ ✦ ✦

East service door. There were sixty guards in the building. She’d counted them on the way in, a habit she’d caught off her sister and never managed to give back. They all did the same thing. Dark suit. Earpiece. A slow, bored sweep of the room. The one by the bar had been staring at the prawns for ten minutes with real love.

This one wasn’t sweeping. He was watching one man. Tall, fair, grey suit, third chandelier, a glass of champagne he hadn’t touched. The guard looked at the door. At the carpet. At the ceiling. Then back at the fair man. Every time. A compass needle that kept finding north.

Serafina got up and went to the glass to watch him watch.

Thirty, maybe a bit less. A suit that fitted just well enough to forget. The kind of face you stood next to in a lift and couldn’t describe to the police afterwards. A tiny notch through the end of his left eyebrow, like a pen that had skipped. And the details were off. His earpiece tube was brand new, when everyone else’s had gone yellow. The others wore thick rubber soles for standing all night. He wore polished oxfords, resoled with something thin and grippy. Who resoles oxfords for grip? Who expects to run on marble?

Then a waiter dropped a tray of glasses by the orchestra. Half the room jumped. The guards at the bar spun round. The man at the east door didn’t even turn his head. His right hand lifted off his left wrist, a few centimetres, toward the inside of his jacket. Toward nothing. Then it settled again.

She felt it in her stomach. The lurch she got a quarter-second before a car stepped out at the rear.

“Oh.” Her nose was nearly on the glass. “Oh… you’re not a guard at all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went over. Stupid. She knew it halfway across the terrace, same as she always knew a gap was too small about one second after she’d gone for it. She went anyway. Through two hundred people who didn’t see her, because staff were furniture. Oil on her thumb. Torch still in her fist.

“Good evening.”

He looked at a point just above her left shoulder.

“Madam. This door is for staff.”

“I am staff.” She waved the pass. “Vehicle specialist. Lot nine, the red one. It’s a fake, by the way. Well, the plate is. Don’t tell anyone, I haven’t told my client.”

“Please step away from the door.”

“No.”

No accent in his voice at all. Low and level, like the one that tells you the next station. She wanted very badly to make it say something it hadn’t planned.

“You’ve been watching the Belgian for forty-one minutes.”

Nothing. A real guard would have frowned. Laughed. Said what Belgian? This one kept looking politely at the air over her shoulder, like she wasn’t there. Which told her everything.

“I don’t know what you mean, madam.”

“Tall one. Third chandelier. Champagne he isn’t drinking. You check him every eleven seconds. I timed you.”

“Madam—”

“Everyone in this room is looking at somebody. The consul’s wife is looking at the consul’s assistant. The guards are looking at the prawns. You’re the only one looking at the right person.”

Then he looked at her. Two seconds. Maybe three. It went all the way in, like a torch into an engine bay. She had the weirdest feeling he’d just read the scar on her hand, the oil, the boots and her pulse, and filed the lot. In order. Probably alphabetical. His eyes were dark. A lot less empty than his face.

“You should go back to your car.”

“It’s not my car!”

“Then go back to someone else’s car.” The tiniest pause. “And stop timing people.”

“Why? Is it rude?”

“It’s noticeable.”

Then he did something no guard would do. He took the torch out of her hand. It was still switched on, making a bright little circle on his lapel, and she’d forgotten all about it. He clicked it off with his thumb. Put it back in her palm. Folded her fingers round it with his own. Warm. Dry. Much too close for a staff door. He smelled of soap and cold air and nothing else, and her pulse did the thing it only did on the last lap.

“So is that.” He said it low, for her only.

Behind her the orchestra struck up some Strauss. Over his shoulder, the fair man set down his glass, kissed the consulate woman on both cheeks and strolled toward the main doors. The guard’s eyes went with him.

“Excuse me.”

Through the service door. Gone. Serafina looked down at her fist round the torch. So is that? So is what? Her hand? Her pulse? Forgetting she was holding a torch? Rude.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang Signor Bassi from the service yard, between two catering vans.

“The car’s real. The plate isn’t. Somebody swapped it, probably in the eighties, probably to sell a crashed one as clean.”

“So I don’t buy it.”

“You buy it for forty per cent less. Off the man who’ll still own it tomorrow, when nobody bids.”

“Ha! You are wasted on engines, cara.”

“Everyone says that. Everyone’s wrong.”

She hung up and looked up. The staff car park sat behind the vans. Delivery vans, waiters’ scooters, the auction house Mercedes. And at the far end, under the one dead lamp, a grey estate with its engine running and its lights off. A taxi-firm car, big and plain. Except it sat too low on its springs for an empty estate. Something heavy in the doors? In the floor? Her eyes grabbed the number plate without asking her. They always did that.

The guard came out of the dark between the vans. The fair man walked beside him, close, two old friends leaving a party early. The fair man’s face was dead white. The guard had a hand at his elbow, not gripping. The man walked anyway. He got in the back. The guard shut the door without a sound, went round to the driver’s side, and stopped.

He looked straight at her. Forty metres. A dead lamp. A woman in a black dress between two vans with a phone in her hand.

Shouldn’t she be scared? She’d just watched something she wasn’t meant to see, and he knew it. She wasn’t scared. Not even a bit.

He nodded at her. Once. Like she’d held a door for him. Then the grey car rolled out of the gate with its lights off, and they came on at the bottom of the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

Page nine of the business section, next morning. One paragraph. A Belgian logistics consultant called Lucien Marchal had attended the Autumn Reception on Battery Hill, then left the city on an early flight. His office declined to comment.

Serafina read it twice, standing up in the garage, eating cold fried rice out of the pan. An early flight. Sure. She uncapped the red marker and wrote a number plate on the whiteboard over the workbench. Big. Where she’d have to look at it every day.

“What’s that?” Big Wu ducked in under the shutter with the doughnuts.

“A car that’s too heavy for its springs.”

“Whose car?”

“Nobody’s. Yet.”

“Uh-huh…” He looked at the red letters. Then at her face. “That’s not a car face. That’s a man face.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove for three hours. North. The old road, then the new one. The man in the back wore a black cotton hood and breathed too loud for the first hour. Then slower. They always slowed down, once they worked out nobody was going to hit them yet.

Somewhere past the toll gates, the man wet himself. Qin Haozhen cracked a window and made a note to have the seat done.

At a petrol station on the edge of the province, a white van was waiting with two men in it. He handed over the man. Then the man’s phone and passport, in a plastic bag. He signed nothing. Nobody ever signed anything. Back in the grey car, his phone buzzed.

“Delivered?”

“Delivered.”

“Any trouble?”

“He wet the seat.”

“Motor pool won’t like that.” The duty officer yawned down the line. “Go home. Sleep.”

He checked the time. Eleven minutes ahead. He didn’t think about the man in the hood. He’d stopped doing that at eighteen. There was a room in his head where they went, and he kept the door shut, and it was quiet in there.

He thought about boots. Black leather, heels worn on the outside from working pedals. Under a dress that didn’t fit. Oil on her thumb. An old shiny burn on the back of her right hand. A voice far too loud for a staff entrance, that didn’t care who heard it.

Her hand had been under his for one second. With the torch in it. Ten years he’d been walking people to cars, by the wrist, by the elbow. He had never once wanted to keep holding on. What would her mouth have done if he hadn’t let go? Kept talking. Obviously. Would he have stopped it? How?

You’re the only one looking at the right person.

Ten years of doors. Fourteen countries. He was good at it because nobody saw him. Eyes slid off him like rain off glass. Director Duan called him the best she had, in the voice she used for a good knife. Nobody had ever crossed a room to tell him what he was.

SONG S., the pass had said. VEHICLE SPECIALIST.

By the time he reached the city lights, he’d decided he wouldn’t look her up. By the time he parked, he had.

chapters.title: Serafina Finds Out His Name
chapters.desc: Three weeks, one bribed caterer and a note about his terrible brakes. Then the guard turns up in her garage in the middle of the night to ask her to stop.
chapters.epigraph: “A car tells you everything about the man who drives it. His just told me to mind my own business.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
“It’s not real.”

Mouse said it to her screens. Three of them, at the far end of the workbench. Mouse was twenty-two, had a ring through the side of her nose, and had not said one word to Big Wu in four years. She talked to Serafina. Since 2019 she gave Aurelia the odd single word. That was the whole list.

“The plate’s real. I saw it with my own eyes.”

“The plate’s real. The company isn’t.” Mouse turned a screen round. “Silver Line Fleet Solutions. Fourth floor of a block by the old ferry piers. They knocked it down in 2019. Registered to a man who died in 2011. Insurance paid by a bank in the capital.”

“And?”

“No fines. No parking tickets. Four years. Not one.” Mouse finally looked up, pale and worried. “Nobody has no parking tickets, Sera…”

“He does.” Serafina uncapped the red marker and wrote it under the number plate. No parking tickets.

From under Gilded, a pair of enormous legs spoke.

“You’re writing about a man on the wall now. That’s how it starts. My cousin did that. Now she’s married to a dentist.”

“Is that bad?”

“Have you met a dentist?”

✦ ✦ ✦

The security firm for the Autumn Reception was Harbour Guard Services. Their night supervisor was a tired man who said to be honest about every four words. Serafina told him she was from the auction house and had found some keys.

“Sixty on the list, to be honest. Well… fifty-nine. The sixtieth was the delegation’s own man. Came with their paperwork. East service door.”

“What did he look like?”

“To be honest? No idea. Never looked at him. That’s weird, now you say it.” A pause. “Why?”

“The keys. They’re probably his.”

She hung up and wrote Delegation’s own man on the board. Then she stood back with her arms folded and tapped a fingernail on her front teeth. Tap. Tap. Same as when an engine made a noise she couldn’t place. A train went over the bridge. The shelves rattled. A spanner dropped into the bucket.

“Leave it.” Mr. Kwok, at the camping stove, frying garlic in a wok you could bath a toddler in.

Seventy-one. Forty years driving a taxi in this city. Opinions on everything, and annoyingly right about most of them.

“A man who comes in with the delegation and leaves with a Belgian in his back seat? You don’t write that man on a wall. You forget you saw him.”

“I can’t forget him.”

“Try harder.” He threw in a fistful of chilli. Smoke went everywhere.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not try harder. In the second week she went to see Auntie Chu.

Golden Spoon Catering had fed every government party in the city for twenty years. It also owned three refrigerated vans whose brakes made a noise like somebody sitting on a cat. Serafina had heard them in the service yard on Battery Hill. You didn’t forget a noise like that.

“Free.” Her head was under the bonnet of the first van. “All three. Pads, discs, fluid. Plus the rattle in number two’s gearbox. You haven’t heard it yet. You will on the flyover next month.”

Auntie Chu stood over her in a white apron, small and round, arms folded. Thirty years of running big kitchens. She had turned down bribes from consuls.

“What do you want?”

“The sign-in sheet from the Reception. Service door. You keep everything. I saw the clipboard.”

“That is government business.”

“It’s a clipboard, Auntie. I’ll throw in a crate of Chinotto. The real stuff, from Italy. My sister gets it.”

“The bitter orange? The little bottles?”

“Twenty-four little bottles.”

Auntie Chu went inside. She came back with a photocopy and her phone.

“I remember him. The only one who didn’t eat. The consuls eat my prawns. The delegation ate my prawns with their hands. He stood at that door all night and didn’t touch one prawn.” She sniffed. “A man who won’t eat a prawn is hiding something.”

On the photocopy, in a column of sixty scrawls, one line sat apart. Small square letters, each one separate. Like type.

Qin H. East service. 19:02.

Qin. Serafina stared at it until it stopped being a word.

“And this.” Auntie Chu held out the phone. “My nephew takes pictures of the staff for the company page. For morale.”

Four waiters, grinning, with trays. Behind them, a bit blurred, a man in a dark suit at a door. Looking straight at the camera. No expression at all.

“He made my nephew delete it. Very polite. So my nephew deleted it.” Auntie Chu looked smug. “My nephew is an idiot. It went to the cloud.”

“Send it to me!”

“Gearbox first!”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the grey car on a Tuesday, fourth level of the multi-storey by the ferry pier.

Eight nights of looking. Not clever looking. She just drove Nonna round every car park on the harbour side between midnight and dawn. A car like that lived near the water, if its owner might need to leave fast. And she didn’t sleep much anyway. Nonna was a red 1992 Lancia Delta Integrale with three hundred thousand kilometres on her and a gearbox rebuilt four times. Named after their grandmother. Old, Italian, never once did what she was told.

The grey estate was parked nose-out in a corner bay. The camera above it had been turned to face the wall. Huh. Serafina didn’t touch it. She crouched by the back wheel with her torch, creeping up on it like a sleeping dog, and looked through the spokes at the brakes.

Then she sat back on her heels and laughed out loud in the empty car park. Terrible. They were terrible.

She wrote the note on the back of a parts receipt, using Nonna’s roof as a desk.

Your rear pads are down to about three millimetres and the discs are blue. You’re carrying four hundred kilos in the doors and floor that this car was never built for. First long hill with someone behind you, you’ll cook them. Then no brakes. Then a problem. I can fix it.

How to sign it? She chewed the pen. Then she wrote Lot 9 and the address of the garage under the railway bridge, and tucked it under his wiper.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came two nights later.

She was alone. Big Wu had gone home to his mother. Mouse had left at midnight in her headphones. Mr. Kwok always left before the evening news, because a man his age needed it to check he was still alive. Serafina was on her back under Gilded, chasing a hydraulic leak that had been winning for a week. Radio on low. Shutter half up for the fumes.

A train went over. When the noise had gone, so had the radio. She hadn’t touched the radio.

She lay very still on the creeper. Drip of the leak. Tick of the lamp. A dog somewhere down the street of shut workshops. And the plain, prickling feeling of not being alone.

“You’re very good at that.” She didn’t roll out. “Standing in places. Is there a course?”

“Yes.”

A voice by the shutter. She rolled out.

He stood just inside, under the lip of the shutter, the street light behind him. No suit tonight. Dark trousers, black jumper, plain jacket. A thousand men in this city dressed like that. His hands were empty and in plain sight. On purpose, she thought. Like showing your palms to a nervous horse. He held up her note between two fingers.

“You left this on a car you shouldn’t know about.”

“You drove off in it with a man you shouldn’t have had.” She sat up and wiped her hands on the rag at her waist. “Is he okay? The Belgian?”

No answer. She hadn’t expected one. He looked round the garage instead. Shutter, alley door, loft stairs, window, extinguisher. Then the whiteboard. His eyes stopped there. The number plate. No parking tickets. Delegation’s own man. And, in Serafina’s worst capitals, DOESN’T EAT PRAWNS.

The corner of his mouth moved. Not a smile. A smile’s distant relation from the countryside, who’d never been to the city.

“Doesn’t eat prawns.”

“Auntie Chu says a man who won’t eat a prawn is hiding something.”

“I’m allergic.”

“Are you?”

“No.”

She snorted before she could stop it. Another train was coming. She felt it in the concrete first. So did he. His weight shifted a hair toward the side door. Then the whole garage shook, the spanner hit the bucket again, and he didn’t move at all.

“I came to ask you to stop. Looking. Bribing caterers. Driving a red Lancia round car parks in the middle of the night. You’ll be noticed by people less polite than me.”

“You’re not polite. You turned my radio off.”

“It was a long song.” He folded her note and slid it into his inside pocket. Carefully. Like he meant to keep it. “Will you stop, Miss Song?”

“Tell me your name.”

That look again. All the way in. Two seconds, three. She sat on the creeper with oil to her elbows and stared right back. Was something moving in there? Far back? A light coming on in a house she’d thought was empty?

“Qin Haozhen.”

Oh. She’d expected a lie. A good one. She’d been looking forward to it. But she could tell a real plate from a forged one, and this one was real.

“Why tell me?”

“You’d have found it. I’d rather you heard it from me than from someone who wanted to know why you were asking.”

Serafina stood. In her boots she was nearly level with him. She stuck her hand out, looked at it, black to the wrist, wiped it on her overalls, which did nothing, and stuck it out again.

“Serafina Song.”

“I know. I read your pass.”

“That was three weeks ago.”

“Yes.” He shook her hand. Warm. Dry. He let go a beat late, then looked down at the oil on his own palm like he didn’t know where to put it.

“Right. Now. Your brakes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He let her do them. She thought about that a lot, afterwards. A man who signed in at doors like a typewriter and drove cars owned by dead people, standing in her garage in the middle of the night, handing her his keys.

He backed the grey car in under the shutter in one move, a hand’s width either side. She put it on the lift, pulled the wheels and showed him. Blue scored discs. Pads down to metal. Family-estate calipers trying to stop a small tank.

“You need vented discs. Four-pot calipers. Pads that like heat. Fluid that doesn’t boil.” She ran her thumb along the scoring. “Whoever looks after this is either lazy or wants you dead.”

“The motor pool.”

“Then the motor pool wants you dead!”

“Possibly.”

She laughed. Then she looked at him, because he wasn’t joking. He looked back with no expression at all. So she laughed again, harder. It scared her. She didn’t care.

She did the rears with what she had on the shelf. He stood by the workbench and watched her hands, never her face. She dropped a pin, and he had it before it stopped rolling. She reached for the torque wrench without looking, and it was already in her palm.

“You’ve done this before.”

“No.”

“Then how did you know I wanted that?”

“You looked at it four minutes ago. Before the second side. You always look at the next thing before you need it.”

She stopped with the wrench on the bolt. He was leaning on her bench under her whiteboard, oil on one palm, watching her like he’d been taking notes for weeks and found the notes weren’t enough. People looked at her all the time. Her mother, measuring. Boys at street races, wanting her car or her number. Nobody looked at her like that.

“Stop it. Noticing things about me. That’s my job.”

“Then we have a problem.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the shutter, keys in hand, he stopped and looked back across the garage. Too long. Much too long for a man asking about brakes. Then he put the keys in his pocket and came back.

No hurry. Past the lift. Right up to her, closer than he’d stood all night. She still had the torque wrench. He tugged the rag from the waist of her overalls with two fingers and wiped the corner of her mouth with it. Once. Then again, slower.

“You’ve had oil there for two hours.”

“And you just let me—”

He dropped the rag. Took her face in one hand, knuckles under her jaw, thumb where the oil had been. And kissed her in the middle of the word.

He didn’t ask. She worked it out later. He’d decided at the shutter, and the walk back was just the distance. She set the torque wrench down behind her, blind. It rolled. It clanged on the concrete. Who cared?

She’d have guessed he kissed like he wrote. Exact. Neat. It was exact. It was also slow and warm and much too short, just long enough for her to forget to breathe and then remember. When he lifted his head, she had a fist in the front of his jacket. When had she done that?

“I came to ask you to stop.” His thumb moved once at the corner of her mouth. “I’m not going to. The fronts. Thursday. I’ll come at midnight.”

Not a question. She let go of his jacket.

“Night, Guard.”

Something happened at the corners of his eyes. Then he was gone, and she was standing in the middle of the garage with oil to her elbows and the only clean mouth in the building. She pressed the back of her black wrist to it until the next train. At the corner, where every car caught, she heard him brake. The new pads bit clean.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t start the car straight away. He sat at the end of her street with her note in his pocket and the taste of engine oil in his mouth. Annoying. He’d have liked to know what she tasted like without the oil.

Three weeks. She thought she’d found him in eight nights. He’d watched her try every car park in order. The pier, then the market, then the hotels. He knew she slept above the garage four nights in seven, and left the shutter up when she did. He knew her best lap at the circuit in the north to the hundredth. He knew she put chilli on everything except breakfast.

He knew the shutter lock was a joke. He’d have to do something about the shutter.

Thursday was three days away. Far too far.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Big Wu came in with the doughnuts and stopped dead. He crouched by the lift and touched a dark patch on the concrete with one huge finger.

“Brake dust. Not ours.” He squinted up at her. “You did a job last night. For who?”

Serafina took a doughnut. She went to the whiteboard, uncapped the red marker, and above the number plate, in big messy capitals, she wrote a name. Mr. Kwok came in with the shopping and stood in front of it, holding a bag of pak choi.

“So. Does he eat? Or is he still hiding something?”

“Both.”

“Sera.” Mouse, from the end of the bench, eyes on her screens. Talking to Serafina. Only ever to Serafina. “That camera in the car park? He turned it round the night before you got there.”

Serafina choked on her doughnut.

“He knew you were coming.”

chapters.title: A Race, Not a Date
chapters.desc: She makes him race her at Granny Shum’s, his grey taxi of a car against her Lancia. He loses on purpose, and she’s furious about it.
chapters.epigraph: “A circuit is a circuit and a road is a road, and I’m not giving up the road for anybody.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
The calipers from Stuttgart came with the wrong brackets. Of course they did. So the front brakes took Thursday and Friday, and Serafina spent most of Thursday on the floor, swearing in Italian.

“What does that one mean?”

He was on the stool by the kettle. Her stool. He’d just taken it, like he’d been sitting there for years.

“It means the man who packed this box should be buried in it. With his mother.”

“And the one before?”

“You don’t want to know.”

He took a black notebook out of his inside pocket and wrote something down. Small square letters. She was being added to a file. Was that creepy? It should be creepy. It wasn’t, much.

And he didn’t kiss her.

Not on Thursday. He came at midnight like he’d said. He handed her things. He looked at her exactly the way he had before he crossed the garage. And then he did nothing about it. Nothing. She dropped a caliper bolt twice. Both times he caught it before it stopped rolling. Both times, handing it back, his fingers stayed on hers a second longer than a bolt needed. Then he went home. Like a gentleman. The bastard.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Friday he’d stopped standing by the door.

He held the lamp under the car for twenty minutes without being asked, right where she needed it. His arm must have been dying. It never moved. He drank hot water out of her spare mug, the plain one. No coffee. No tea. He would not touch Mr. Kwok’s leftover noodles in the fridge, even though the lid said ANYONE BUT BIG WU.

“Where did you grow up?”

“North.”

“North where?”

“Further north.” He tilted the lamp. “Your bolt’s cross-threaded.”

It was. She swore. By the time she’d fixed it, the question had gone somewhere and she couldn’t find it. Good suspension. You only noticed it when it was gone.

Near dawn she dropped the car off the lift and slapped the bonnet.

“Done! Now you owe me.”

“How much?”

“Not money. A race.”

He looked at her.

“Not a date! I don’t do dates. Dates are two people sitting still, being polite at each other over soup. A race. Tomorrow night. You in this, me in Nonna. Factory roads out past the paint works.” She grinned. “Unless you’re scared, Guard.”

“Street racing carries three years now.”

“I know. My mother posted me a copy of the law.” She leaned on his bonnet. “I’ve got a national licence. A team. My sister’s name on my race car. And I still go to Granny Shum’s on Saturdays. A circuit is a circuit and a road is a road, and I’m not giving up the road for anybody.”

He thought about it. He did it with his face totally still, which she was starting to find as interesting as a sealed gearbox.

“There’ll be phones. I don’t photograph well.”

“You don’t photograph at all. Auntie Chu’s nephew had to dig you out of the cloud.” She held up his car keys and jingled them. “Three o’clock. Bring the taxi.”

He put his hand in hers. Not reaching for the keys. Just his palm, flat on her palm, warm, for one second. She nearly dropped everything. When she looked down, the keys were gone. He was holding them. How?

“Three o’clock.”

And then he didn’t leave. He stood there with the keys and looked at her. The oil on her. The grin she hadn’t put away. She watched him decide something, after two whole nights of watching him decide nothing.

“I’ve been good for two nights.” He said it like it was a fault he’d found in the car.

She opened her mouth to say something rude in Italian. He didn’t wait for it. His hand went flat on the roof of his car beside her head, and he kissed her against the door.

Harder than the first time. Not careful at all. Cold metal at her back. His mouth opening hers. His other hand at her waist, under the knot of her overalls, pinning her there. Where did he think she was going? Nowhere. She was going precisely nowhere. Two nights she’d spent wondering if she’d made the first one up. Nope.

When he let go he stepped back one pace. Only one. He was breathing like he’d run up the street.

“Tomorrow.”

Gone, before she found her voice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum ran the Saturday meet from a folding chair at the junction by the paint works. Thermos of chrysanthemum tea. Blanket over her knees. A police scanner on a string round her neck like a crucifix.

She was eighty, or said so. Her husband had raced these roads in the seventies, in a Datsun with no doors, and died of something boring in bed in 2005. She’d kept the Saturdays going. She called it respect. Everyone else called it spite. A sign hung from the lamp post beside her chair, painted on hardboard. NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING.

Serafina had been coming since she was nineteen, the week she walked out of the house on the Peak. First night, Granny Shum looked her up and down.

“Rich girl. You’ll crash by Christmas.”

On Christmas Eve, Serafina won four in a row in a Fiat she’d built out of two dead ones. Granny Shum handed her a clementine. She never mentioned rich girls again.

“Who’s the taxi?”

The grey estate had rolled down from the gas works with its lights off and parked at the end of the line. Right behind a purple Nissan with a wing like a dining table and a kid on its roof filming himself. Forty people stood about in the floodlight off the paint works. Every single one turned to stare at the grey car. Somebody laughed. Then everybody did.

“A friend. It’s not a taxi. It just looks like one.”

He got out. Dark jacket, black cap pulled low, head down, hands in pockets. When the kid on the Nissan panned his phone down the line, he got a cap and a shoulder. That was all.

“Not a friend.” Granny Shum sipped her tea. “Friends don’t stand like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like they know which way the police will come.” She turned her scanner up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four kilometres and twenty metres. Serafina could drive it asleep. In 2018 she very nearly had.

Off the line at the paint works. The long straight past the container yard, where cars with big engines and nothing else always got ahead. Left at the fish-ball factory. Then the S-bends between the warehouses, tight and blind, where cars with big engines and nothing else went into the wall. Then the long right round the gas works, a lamp post every fifty metres. Sensible people braked at the third lamp post. Serafina braked at the fourth.

Granny Shum’s granddaughter stood between the two cars with the white scarf. Sixteen, purple nails, bored out of her skull.

“One run. No contact. Scanner goes, you go home. Whatever. You know the rules.”

“He doesn’t.”

The granddaughter peered into the grey car. He’d taken off the cap. Both hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, which nobody did. Seat much too far forward for his height. Eyes straight ahead.

“No contact,” she told him.

“No contact.”

Then he got out again. Three steps to Nonna, back to the floodlight. He bent to her open window. Her leather jacket was hanging open over her vest, the way she always raced. He didn’t say a word. He reached in, took the zip, and pulled it up to her chin. Slow. His knuckles brushed her throat at the top.

“It’s cold.”

He went back to his car. Serafina sat there with her mouth open and her jacket zipped up like a schoolgirl’s.

“Friend.” Granny Shum, from her chair, in a voice like a door shutting.

The scarf went up. Serafina brought Nonna to five thousand revs and held her there. The whole car shook like a dog on a lead. She looked left once. Through two windows and a metre of cold air, he looked back.

The scarf came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nonna went off the line like a gunshot.

All four wheels, no slip. The turbo came in at the top of second with that long rising whistle that always made the back of her neck go hot. Half a car up by the paint works. A whole car by the container yard. She checked the mirror for the estate falling back. Heavy cars always fell back on the straight.

It wasn’t falling back. It was there. One length behind. Exactly one, like it had been painted on her mirror. All the way down the straight, through third and fourth, at a speed no family estate with four hundred kilos in its doors had any right to.

“What the HELL have you got in there?”

Left at the fish-ball factory. She braked late, turned in hard, felt Nonna’s tail go light and caught it. Out of the corner sideways on purpose, foot flat. In the mirror the grey car took the same corner on rails. No slide. No fuss. It just turned, and came out one length behind her.

The S-bends. Left, right, left. Warehouse walls a hand’s width from her mirrors. She went through faster than she’d ever gone through them. When she burst out onto the gas works straight, he was closer. Half a length. She could see his face in the glow of his dashboard. He looked like a man doing his taxes.

She started laughing. Flat to the floor, hands loose, gasholders black against the orange sky, and she was cackling like an idiot. Nobody had ever sat on her bumper through the S-bends like it was nothing. When had a car last been this much fun? A year ago? Two?

Lamp posts. First. Second.

And at the second lamp post, a whole lamp post before anyone sane would brake, his brake lights came on. Clean. Perfectly timed. Fifty metres early.

She went to the fourth, like always. Braked. Turned in. Round the gas works with the tail hanging out and the tyres screaming. By the service road he was three lengths back. He stayed there, politely, all the way to the line.

The granddaughter’s stopwatch said four tenths.

The crowd lost its mind. People banged on Nonna’s roof. The Nissan kid was yelling about the taxi. Someone shoved a beer at her. She took it, didn’t drink it, got out, and walked straight down the line to the grey car.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You lifted at the gas works.”

“I didn’t.”

“Your brake lights came on at the second lamp post!” She jabbed a finger at his chest. Not quite touching. “Nobody brakes at the second lamp post. Mr. Kwok brakes at the third, and he’s seventy-one and drives a transporter. You sat on my bumper through the S-bends in a car that weighs as much as a bus. And then you braked at the second lamp post?”

He looked at her from under the cap. In the floodlight his face was all shadow. Calm.

“You were happy.”

That stopped her.

“…What?”

“In the S-bends. You were laughing. I could see you in your mirror.” A plain fact, like the motor pool. “If I’d passed you at the gas works, you’d have stopped.”

She stared at him. Engines revving. Kids shouting. The scanner crackling about somebody’s lost dog two districts over. And a man in a black cap had just told her he’d lost on purpose so she’d keep laughing. Three languages. Not one word in any of them.

“That is the most insulting thing a man has ever done to me.”

“I’m sorry.”

He clearly wasn’t.

“And people were filming. If you’d won, they’d have the man who beat Serafina Song in a taxi.” She narrowed her eyes. “That’s it, isn’t it? You can’t be filmed winning.”

“That too.”

She laughed again. Short. Disbelieving. Hands on hips.

“Rematch!”

“Serafina—”

“Somewhere with no phones. Somewhere I can see every tenth you throw away on a screen. And you drive like yourself. Not a man in a taxi. Whatever you actually are.” Chin up. “Or I write it on the whiteboard. HE LIFTS. In red.”

“And if I drive like myself, and you don’t like it?”

“Then at least I’ll know…”

His eyes dropped to her mouth. Came back up. He didn’t pretend otherwise. Then he took a fistful of her leather jacket and stepped back into the dark between his open door and the car, out of the floodlight. He took her with him.

Nobody saw. She worked out later that he’d made sure. Even then, even with her, part of him had found the one spot on that road no phone was pointing at. The rest of him kissed her like he’d lost a lot more than a race.

Hard. His cap knocked back. His hand spread on her spine under the leather. The edge of the door cold on her shoulder blades. The whole industrial district yelling forty metres away. She bit his lip. Not on purpose. Mostly not on purpose. He made a sound in his chest she felt more than heard, and hauled her closer. Oh. So this was what he did when he wasn’t lifting.

Then Granny Shum’s scanner said something sharp and official. Granny Shum got up out of her chair and blew the whistle she kept for exactly this. Forty people and eleven cars started vanishing into the industrial district like water into sand.

He let her go. Straightened his cap. His hand wasn’t steady. He got in and looked up at her through the open door.

“The circuit in the north has a track day on the tenth. I’ll book it.”

“How do you even know that?”

“I checked. On Thursday.”

He shut the door. The grey car slid off toward the gas works with its lights off, gone before the first blue light came round the paint factory.

Thursday. He’d checked on Thursday. Before she’d even asked him.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a folded paper under Nonna’s wiper. Her own note. The parts receipt from the ferry car park. Your rear pads are down to about three millimetres. He’d kept it ten days. Brought it to a street race. Tucked it back under her wiper while she was marching down the line to yell at him.

Under her signature, in small square letters, a phone number. Under that, one more line.

You brake at the fourth lamp post because you like the noise the tyres make. It’s a beautiful noise. It costs you a tenth.

Serafina read it four times in the dark. Then she saved the number as GUARD. Then she deleted that and typed GUARD (LIFTS).

Then she sat there, furious, because he was right about the tenth.

chapters.title: Rematch
chapters.desc: A track day in the north, one car, two drivers and Mouse on the stopwatch. This time he drives like himself, and she kisses him in the empty paddock.
chapters.epigraph: “Five laps each, same car, Mouse on the clock. Then we both know.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
“Track days aren’t races.”

Serafina said it with her breath smoking. Eight in the morning, second Saturday in December, the paddock at the circuit in the north. Big Wu was rolling Nonna off the transporter. Mr. Kwok was setting up the camping stove under the awning. Mouse sat on an upturned crate with a laptop, plugged into a transponder the size of a matchbox.

“Nobody races. It’s against the rules. You go out, you drive, you come in. You only pass on the straights, and only if the car in front waves you by.” She hauled her helmet bag out of the van. “Forty cars. Mostly dentists in Porsches. Very slow. Very rich. Very angry when you go past.”

“And us?”

“We’re not racing either. We’re timing.”

She’d thought about it all week. Two cars wouldn’t work. Two cars meant armour against turbo, and a fight at the end about whose car did the work. So. One car. Five flying laps each. Timed to the hundredth by a girl who didn’t speak to anyone and couldn’t be bribed.

“Nonna.” She patted the red roof. “Five laps each, same car, Mouse on the clock. Then we both know.”

He looked the Lancia over. Thirty years old. Paint going pink at the edges of the roof. Arches wider than any factory made them, because Serafina had made them wider. A dent in the driver’s door from 2020, when a boy in a Subaru shoved her into a lamp post. She’d never fixed it. The boy had paid in other ways.

“She’s very old.”

“So’s the Pope. Get in.”

She was shivering. She hadn’t noticed till her teeth clicked. He had. He took off his jacket, put it round her shoulders over her race suit, and did up the top button under her chin. Just the one. Then he went to look at the tyres like nothing had happened.

Big Wu, holding a wheel gun, stared at the button. Then at Serafina.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went first. Partly to show him the circuit. Partly, fine, to show off. She took the out lap gently to warm the tyres, talking him round on the intercom she’d wired into both helmets.

“Turn one. Long right. Brake at the hundred board. You’ll think it’s too early. It isn’t. Esses next. Don’t use the kerb on the second one, it’ll throw you. Then the back straight. Nine hundred metres. You’ll see two hundred on the clock if you’re brave.”

“And at the end?”

“The Needle.” They were coming down the straight at a hundred and ninety. A tight grey hairpin rushed at them, under a bridge, gravel behind it, a wall of tyres behind the gravel. “You have to thread it. First time, everyone brakes too late and goes straight into the gravel. Second time, they brake too early and look stupid. Third time—”

She braked. Hard, on the marker. Nonna’s nose dived. Down two gears, heel on the throttle to match the revs. Turn in. The car spun round its own middle like a dancer on one foot, and they came out the other side with the tail wagging and her laughing.

“Third time you thread it!”

Nothing on the intercom. She glanced across. He sat with his hands loose on his knees, watching the track. Not holding on. Every passenger she’d ever had held on.

Her best was 1:58.41. Mouse whispered it over the radio. For a thirty-year-old Lancia on road tyres that wasn’t good. It was great. She rolled into the pit lane with her heart going, stopped by the awning, pulled off her helmet with her hair sticking up in spikes, and turned to him.

“Well?”

“You lift a fraction at the top of the esses. Second lap and fourth. Not the third.” A pause. “I think it’s when the sun gets in your eyes.”

She stared at him. The sun? Was it the sun? It was absolutely the sun.

“Right. Your turn, then.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took off his watch first. She saw him do it. Steel strap undone. Laid face down on the camping table beside Mr. Kwok’s wok, very carefully, like something he meant to come back for. Then her spare helmet. Driver’s seat forward two notches. Both mirrors adjusted. Then he sat for ten seconds with his hands on the wheel at a quarter to three and his eyes shut.

“Is he praying?” Big Wu wanted to know.

“He’s reading, Sera.” Mouse said it to Serafina. Eyes on the laptop. But Big Wu heard, and turned, and very slowly shut his mouth.

Serafina strapped into the passenger seat and plugged in.

“Don’t you want anything else? Braking points? Kerbs?”

“You told me on your laps.” He put it in first.

✦ ✦ ✦

She tried to describe it to Aurelia afterwards. She failed.

He was fast. Nonna had never made that noise in her life, the engine held right at the top, never over, never under, the turbo singing one long note from one end of the straight to the other. But that wasn’t it. What got her was that there was nothing extra. Every driver she’d ever sat beside put something into a car it didn’t need. A twitch of the wheel. A stab at the brakes. A little flick out of a corner to feel the back go. She did it herself. He didn’t. He turned the wheel exactly as far as it had to turn. He braked exactly as hard as the tyres could take. Then he came off the brakes in one long smooth line as the car turned in, so the weight poured across it like water from one cup to another.

Second lap, he was quicker than her through the esses.

Third lap, he went down the back straight at two hundred and three.

“Madonna… two hundred!”

“Two hundred and three.”

He braked for the Needle on her marker. Exactly on it. Down the gears. The car went round the hairpin so neatly she didn’t feel it turn. It was pointing one way. Then it was pointing the other.

She looked across. Through his visor his eyes weren’t empty any more. They were wide awake. And at the corner of his mouth, under the chin strap, something was happening that looked a lot like fun.

He was enjoying himself. When had he last done that? Had he ever?

✦ ✦ ✦

“Same.” Mouse turned the laptop round. Two columns. Five laps each. At the bottom of each, in red, a best lap.

1:58.41.

1:58.41.

“To the hundredth. Same.”

Serafina looked at the screen. Then at him. He was standing by the car with her spare helmet under his arm, his hair flattened on one side, his face back to calm. Except it wasn’t quite. There was colour in it.

“You did that on purpose. You matched me to the hundredth so nobody won.”

“I couldn’t do that if I tried. Nobody could. Ask Mouse.”

Serafina looked at Mouse. Mouse looked at the laptop and shook her head once, which from Mouse was a speech.

Serafina started laughing. She laughed so hard she had to sit down on the transporter ramp. Big Wu looked at her like she’d gone mad. Mr. Kwok said, from the wok, that it was the cold. It went to people’s heads. He’d seen it at the New Year market in 1983.

“Again.” She wiped her eyes. “We’ve got the track till dark. Five more each. Then five more. I’m not going home with a draw.”

He picked his watch up off the table. Looked at it. Didn’t put it on.

“And if I win?”

“What do you want?”

He didn’t answer straight away. He looked at her mouth. Openly. For so long that Big Wu found something urgent to do at the back of the transporter.

“You know what I want. Not a minute at your shutter. Not behind a car door with the police coming.” He didn’t look away. “When they wave the flag, I’m going to do something about it. Win or lose.”

“Win first.” She jammed her helmet on so he wouldn’t see her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch a dentist came over.

Silver Porsche. Gilet. A face the colour of a man who’d been passed on a straight by a thirty-year-old Lancia and hadn’t waved it by. He marched straight under the awning to where Serafina was eating Mr. Kwok’s noodles standing up.

“You. Red car. You came past me on the back straight without a wave. That’s a black flag! I’ve been coming here six years—”

“You did wave.” Serafina slurped a noodle. “With one finger. I saw it.”

“I’ll be reporting you to the organisers. Name?”

He didn’t get an answer from her. Haozhen had put his water down. He came round the camping table and stopped between them. Not close. Not touching anyone. He just stood there with his hands loose at his sides, and the dentist found himself looking at a stranger instead of a girl with noodles.

“Dr. Cheuk.”

The dentist blinked. “How do you—”

“Your car’s parked in bay eleven. Your number’s on the entry list. You live in Mid-Levels, the building with the green awning.” Haozhen’s voice didn’t change at all. Polite. Bored, nearly. “Your daughter has piano on Saturday afternoons. You’ll want to leave soon, if you’re picking her up.”

The dentist went a different colour. Grey. Ash.

“Are you… is that a threat?”

“It’s traffic advice.”

The dentist went back to his Porsche. Then he drove it out of the paddock gate, an hour before his session ended. He did not wave.

Serafina had stopped chewing.

“How did you know where he lives?”

“I read the entry list on the way in.” He picked his water up again. “Then I looked.”

“You looked up forty dentists?”

“Thirty-one. Nine were surgeons.”

She should be horrified. She knew that. She was standing there with noodles going cold, waiting to be horrified. It didn’t come. What came instead was a hot, mean little thrill all the way down her back. Was that bad? That was probably bad.

Big Wu, who had done two stretches inside and never talked about either, watched the Porsche go. He wiped his hands on a rag. Then he walked over and stood beside Haozhen, looking at the gate.

“I know men who talk like that.”

“Yes.”

“Most of them, I wouldn’t let in my mother’s kitchen.” Big Wu folded the rag. “She likes chilli. Sera. Puts it on everything except breakfast.”

“I know.”

Big Wu looked at him sideways for a long, unfriendly second. Then he grunted and went back to the wheels. Mr. Kwok, without a word, put a second bowl of noodles in Haozhen’s hand. It had extra chilli on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove till the light went.

Turn and turn about, the December sun sliding across the valley and down behind the grandstand. The dentists went home one by one. Then it was just them, the noodle man and a bored marshal at the Needle in an orange coat. They got faster. Both of them. He taught her the sun thing at the top of the esses. She taught him to use more kerb at the long right. By mid-afternoon they were trading tenths. Then hundredths. The laptop filled with red numbers, and Mouse started to giggle without making a sound.

He beat her by six hundredths. She beat him back by two.

Then the marshal waved the chequered flag at them with enormous weariness. They rolled into the pit lane for the last time with the brakes glowing and the engine ticking and the tyres smelling of burnt sugar. Big Wu crouched by the front left with the probe.

“Ninety-four.” He stood up. “I’m going to get the van.”

He walked off fast. He took Mr. Kwok with him. He took Mouse too, by the sleeve, and Mouse let him, which had never happened in four years.

The paddock was empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got out first. Cold blue light under the awning. Race suit unzipped to the waist, sleeves tied round her middle, a black vest with steam coming off her shoulders. So happy she didn’t know what to do with her hands.

He came round the bonnet. He still had her spare helmet on, visor down. She could see his eyes through it, dark, and the rest of him buttoned up like always.

“Well. Now I know what you’re like.”

“And?”

She didn’t answer. She stepped in, grabbed the chin of the helmet with both hands, and kissed the visor. Loud. A big smacking kiss, right on the plastic.

He went completely still.

“That’s for the six hundredths.” She was grinning. “You’re the best driver I’ve ever sat next to. And you haven’t been happy in about ten years, have you?”

He didn’t answer. It was in his eyes anyway, for one second, through the plastic. Something old and tired and very surprised. Then she unclipped the strap, pulled the helmet off him, dropped it on Nonna’s roof, grabbed a fistful of his shirt and kissed him for real.

Late and hard. The way she took corners. For one second he didn’t move at all, like a man who’d been passed on the inside where he hadn’t left a gap.

Then his hands came up. One at her jaw, thumb under her ear. One at the small of her back where the race suit was knotted, flat, spread, pulling her in. And then he took it over. Every other time some part of him had been watching a clock. Not now. Slow at first, thorough, like he meant to do it properly or not at all. Then not slow. He walked her back a step, two, till she hit the side of the car. The metal was warm from the engine. She made a noise she would deny until her grave.

He heard it. She felt him smile against her mouth. A real one. Oh, that was so much worse. Her knees went.

“You.” She got a breath. “Are a menace.”

“Is that Italian?”

“It’s English, you idiot.”

He kissed her again before she could say anything else. Short. Hard. Like one hadn’t been enough and he wasn’t going to pretend. Then he rested his forehead on hers and breathed. She could feel him shaking a little. He was not a man who shook.

“You took your watch off. Why?”

His thumb moved once along her jaw. Checking it was there.

“I didn’t want to know what time it was.”

Behind them the transporter came round the end of the paddock with its headlights on and Big Wu leaning on the horn. Two long blasts and a short one. For no reason at all. Mr. Kwok had his hands over his eyes in the passenger seat.

“YOU’VE GOT FOUR MINUTES!” Big Wu bellowed out of the window. Then he heard himself. “Five! FIVE minutes. Not four. Never four.”

chapters.title: 3 A.M., Passenger Seat
chapters.desc: He hasn’t slept properly in ten years. Then he falls asleep in her passenger seat, and she drives round the harbour till dawn so he won’t wake up.
chapters.epigraph: “In ten years I’ve never sat in a car I wasn’t driving or guarding.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
“Big Wu says you’re a vampire.”

“Big Wu has never seen me.”

“That’s his point.”

He came at strange hours after the track day. Never in daylight. One in the morning. Half four. Once just before six, with the sky going grey over the railway bridge. He’d stand under the half-up shutter until she noticed him. She always noticed. The garage felt different with him in it. Fuller. Like someone had shut a window she hadn’t known was open.

Sometimes he stayed ten minutes. Sometimes three hours. He held lamps. He passed her spanners before she asked. He drank hot water out of the plain mug, which was his now. She’d written HIS on it in marker. He’d looked at it for a while, then turned it round so the writing faced the wall.

“Why’d you do that?”

“People would see it.”

“It’s a mug, Guard.”

He left it facing the wall.

And he kissed her. Against workbenches. Under the lift. Once, on the bonnet of Gilded, until she was so dizzy she put a socket wrench in the fridge. He was never the one who stopped. He’d come up behind her at the bench and put his hand on her hip and just leave it there, his thumb moving once on the strip of skin above her overalls, until she lost her place. Then he’d turn her round by the hip, mid-sentence, mid-bolt, and kiss her like the sentence was in his way.

She never finished one of those sentences. After a while she stopped starting them.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sleep. She clocked it in the second week.

He’d come in with clear eyes and leave with clear eyes. Next night, same. She started counting the hours, because she counted everything. They didn’t add up.

“When do you sleep?”

The Thursday before Christmas. He was on the stool by the kettle with a carburettor from a 1971 Alfa in his lap. She’d given it to him to clean. He was cleaning it like he’d been asked to defuse it.

“I sleep.”

“How much?”

He thought about it. She could see him deciding whether to answer. Then deciding he would. That was new. She held very still, so as not to scare it off.

“Four hours a night. Sometimes three. Since I was eighteen.”

She put the spanner down.

“That’s ten years. Of four hours.”

“You get used to it.”

“No, you don’t. You get used to being tired. That’s different. I’ve watched men drive tired. They brake late and swear they braked on time.” She looked at him across the garage. “You never brake late. So you’re the kind of tired where you’ve forgotten what not tired feels like.”

He went on cleaning the carburettor. A whole train went over. Had she pushed too far? Was that it? Then, when she’d given up, he spoke. Eyes on the jet.

“In hotels I sleep in the chair by the door. In my flat I sleep on top of the covers, dressed. I don’t sleep on planes.” He turned the jet over. “In ten years I’ve never sat in a car I wasn’t driving or guarding.”

“Everything’s a choice.”

“Not that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she took him to Granny Shum’s in Nonna’s passenger seat.

“There’ll be phones. I can watch from the gas works.”

“You can watch from my passenger seat or not at all.”

She got in. Started the engine. Waited. After a while he got in beside her, did up his belt and pulled his cap down. She pulled out under the railway bridge with a grin she didn’t bother hiding.

She raced three times. A boy in a white Honda who cried afterwards, which was against the rules, so Granny Shum made him stand by the lamp post till he stopped. A man in a Mitsubishi she’d beaten nine times, who kept coming back out of what he called loyalty. Then a woman in an old BMW who was good. Properly good. She got past in the S-bends and held Serafina off round the gas works. She lost by half a car only because Serafina went to the fifth lamp post, which nobody had ever done, and nearly put Nonna through the gasholder fence.

“Fifth.” Granny Shum held out a clementine through the window. “That was stupid.”

“It worked!”

“Stupid things work until they don’t.” Granny Shum peered past her, at the passenger seat. “Your taxi friend went to sleep.”

Serafina turned round.

He was asleep. Sitting exactly how he’d sat all night. Upright, belt on, cap down, hands loose in his lap. Somewhere between the fifth lamp post and the line, his head had tipped against the window and stayed. His mouth was a bit open. His face under the brim had gone smooth. Not the calm he made himself be. The other thing. The one he’d forgotten.

“Since the gas works.” Granny Shum drank her tea. “Out like a light. Through a fifth-lamp-post braking zone. I’ve seen dead men less relaxed.” She jerked her chin at the road. “Go on. Before the police come and wake him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Take him home? Where was home? She had no idea. Also, if she stopped the car, he might wake.

So she drove.

Down out of the industrial district, the way Mr. Kwok drove. No hard braking. No sudden turns. The turbo never coming in, the engine burbling along in third. Along the harbour road past the container cranes. Over the old bridge. Through the tunnel and out round the long empty loop of the coast road. Black sea on one side, the city lit up on the other. Then round again.

He didn’t wake.

On the coast road, his head slid off the window and landed on her shoulder.

Oh no. Oh no. She kept both hands on the wheel. She drove for twenty minutes with the weight of his head on her and his breath slow and warm through her jacket, his cap knocked crooked, and she did not move that shoulder a millimetre. Not on the corners. Not at the lights. It was harder than the fifth lamp post. A lot harder. If she could do this, she could do anything.

Halfway round the third loop she peeled Granny Shum’s clementine one-handed, against the wheel. She ate half. The other half she left on the dash for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke all at once.

Nothing, then everything. His head came up off something warm. His hand went to the door, then to his jacket, then stopped. Grey light. Sea. A dashboard. Half a peeled clementine on the dashboard, very neatly placed. And her. Driving. Not looking at him, on purpose, with the corner of her mouth trying very hard not to move.

He had been asleep. In a car. In the passenger seat of a car he wasn’t guarding.

He checked himself over like you check for a wound.

“I slept.”

“Two hours and eleven minutes.” She couldn’t hold it any more. She grinned at the windscreen. “I timed it.”

“I don’t sleep in cars.”

“You do in mine.”

He sat back. Looked at the sea. Took his cap off and turned it round in his hands. Then he did something he hadn’t done in ten years. He put his head back against the headrest and shut his eyes on purpose.

“Why does it work in this car?”

She drove for a while.

“Because you know how I drive. You’ve been behind me through the S-bends. You’ve sat next to me through the Needle. You know I won’t crash. Not with you in it.” She swallowed. “You trust my driving. That’s all.”

He opened his eyes and looked at her. The side of her face in the grey light. The hand on the wheel with the burn on it. The shoulder she still hadn’t moved.

“That isn’t all it is.”

He ate the clementine. All of it. Every piece.

✦ ✦ ✦

His flat above the laundry was cold. He didn’t turn the heating on. He never did.

He sat in the chair by the door, dressed, and listed what could have happened while he was asleep in that car. A stopped vehicle beside them at the lights. Someone at the lay-by. A phone pointed through the window. A woman who drove a red Lancia round the same loop three times, where anybody could time her. He got to eleven things. He should have been frightened by every one of them.

He was frightened by number eleven. Only number eleven. His phone buzzed.

Serafina: home??

Haozhen: Yes.

Serafina: u slept 2h11m in my car and now ur AWAKE

Haozhen: Yes.

Serafina: thats insulting to my car

Haozhen: Your car is fine.

Serafina: nonna says u owe her petrol

Haozhen: How much.

Serafina: one (1) more nap. tues. 3am. corner of ur street. dont be late guard

He read it four times. Then he did something he’d never done on any phone in ten years. He saved the number under a name. He typed SONG S., looked at it, deleted it, and typed Sera.

Then he sat in the chair by the door until it was light, wide awake, waiting for Tuesday.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, she picked him up.

Nobody decided it. Two or three nights a week, a text, or no text. She’d just be there in Nonna, on the corner of whatever street he named, and he’d get in, and she’d drive. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. He slept against the window, or on her shoulder. She drove till the sky went grey. Sometimes she raced at Granny Shum’s and he slept through it. That became a joke in the whole industrial district.

“She beat me, and her own passenger couldn’t stay awake for it!” The white Honda boy said it to anyone who’d listen.

She did his car as well. She didn’t ask. Next time he left the grey estate in her garage she rebuilt the front suspension, because she’d felt it wallow. New shocks. Corner-weighted it on her scales so it sat level for once. When he drove it away she heard him take the corner at the end of the street, stop, reverse all the way back and get out by the shutter.

“What did you do?”

“It was falling over. It doesn’t fall over now.”

He stood there for a long time.

“You didn’t ask.”

“You’d have said no.”

“Yes.”

“So I didn’t ask. Duh.”

“Thank you.” He said it like nobody had ever touched his car without a form.

✦ ✦ ✦

On New Year’s Eve, he didn’t sleep.

She drove them out to the lay-by on the coast road above the harbour, where people went for the fireworks. Late. Every space was gone. She parked Nonna half on the grass with two wheels in a ditch.

“You’re in a ditch.”

“I’m parked.”

“Two wheels are in a ditch.”

“Two wheels is still parked. Ask anyone.”

They sat on the bonnet in their coats. The engine was warm under them. Her hands weren’t. He noticed before she did. He took them, one and then the other, and put them in his own coat pockets with his hands over the top. Deep pockets. Hot. She stopped arguing about the ditch.

At midnight the whole harbour went up at once. Gold, red, white, huge slow flowers of fire opening over the water. The bang arrived a second late and rolled up the hill.

She watched the fireworks. He watched her. She could feel him doing it. She turned her head.

“You’re supposed to look at the fireworks!”

“I’ve seen fireworks. Nine countries. From roofs, mostly.” The gold came down over the water and lit his face. “I was always watching somebody else. Somebody I’d been told to watch.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m not told.”

He took one hand out of the pocket, put it round the back of her neck and kissed her. On the bonnet of a car in a ditch, with the sky going off like a war. He pulled her into his lap without seeming to move at all. She ended up with her knees either side of him and her hands in his hair and his coat round them both. His mouth went to her neck. Under her jaw. Slow. The place where her pulse was. He stayed there, like he was counting it.

She laughed into his hair. She couldn’t get her breath.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last smoke drifted out over the water. Cars started leaving.

“So what do you want? For next year?”

He was quiet.

“I don’t know. I don’t think I know how to want things.” No self-pity in it. Just a fact, like the motor pool. “They tell you where to stand. What to eat, when. Which chair to sleep in. For ten years I’ve wanted the job done and the car to start.”

She sat back on his knees and looked at him. Then she poked him in the chest.

“Then start small. Want a sandwich.”

His mouth moved. The real smile. The second time she’d ever seen it. She’d build a whole garage to keep it in.

“A good one. With egg. From the place under the flyover. That’s next year. Once you get the hang of it, you can want something bigger.”

He looked at her in the dark, in the gunpowder smell.

“I want this.”

“The car? The ditch?”

“The passenger seat. You driving. Three in the morning.” His hand flattened on her back, under her coat, and gripped. Hard. Like somebody might try to lift her off him. “And you. Mostly you.”

She had to look at the water for a second before she could talk.

“Then you’ve got it. Get in. I’ll drive.”

“We’re in a ditch.”

“We’re PARKED!”

chapters.title: What He Does for Work
chapters.desc: Mouse finds the missing Belgian in a newspaper. Serafina lays out everything she knows on the workbench, and he doesn’t tell her she’s wrong.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
“Sera.”

Mouse didn’t look up. She just turned a screen round. Second Saturday in January, late morning, the garage smelling of Mr. Kwok’s garlic.

Mouse looked into things. Nobody asked her to. It was what she did after midnight with her headphones on, the way other people did crosswords. Engines, mostly. Wiring. Once, in 2020, the Subaru boy who’d shoved Nonna into a lamp post. She found out some facts about him that he later paid a lot to keep quiet. She looked. She said nothing. Until there was something to say.

It was a Belgian newspaper. Serafina couldn’t read Flemish. She could read a photo. A tall fair man in a grey suit, smiling, at what looked like a wedding. Lucien Marchal (46). Under it, a smaller picture. A woman on a doorstep with her hand over her mouth. Two teenage boys behind her.

“His family. Antwerp. They reported him missing in October. The paper only ran it last week, when the police gave up.” Mouse’s voice was very flat. “His ticket home was used on the twenty-third. He wasn’t on the plane.”

“The police here…?”

“Say he left. The police there say he never arrived.”

Serafina looked at the woman with her hand over her mouth for a long time.

“Print it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She laid it out on the workbench.

Like a diagnosis. When a car came in that nobody could fix, you didn’t guess. You didn’t go with your gut, even when your gut was right. You took every symptom, every noise, every leak and smell, and laid them out on the bench in order. You looked at them all together until they stopped being separate things and turned into one thing. Then you knew. She used parts. She was in that kind of mood.

A spark plug, for the number plate. A dead man’s company. No parking tickets. A brake pad, for the delegation’s paperwork. The sixtieth man.

One black oxford. He’d left it drying by the kettle the night he stood in a puddle at the shutter, and gone home in Big Wu’s boots. Resoled thin. For running on marble.

A shock absorber, for four hundred kilos of steel in the doors. Somebody worried about bullets. A torch, for his right hand reaching for nothing when the tray fell. A clementine, for four hours’ sleep a night. A spent firework from the ditch on New Year’s morning, for nine countries of roofs.

And at the end, in the middle of the bench, the woman on the doorstep in Antwerp.

Big Wu came in from the alley with a crate of oil and stopped. He put the crate down very gently. He looked at the bench for a whole minute.

“Sera…”

“Don’t.”

He didn’t. He went and found Mr. Kwok, who was buying vegetables, and took him to lunch somewhere very far away. They didn’t come back till the afternoon.

When they did, Mr. Kwok went straight to the stove and banged pans. Big Wu came and leaned on the bench next to her. Not looking at the parts. Looking at his own hands.

“You going to tell him to go?”

“I don’t know.”

“Two stretches, me. You know that.”

“I know.”

“You never asked what for. Week I got out, you gave me a key. Said the kettle’s there, the toilet’s out back, don’t touch Gilded’s gearbox.” He rubbed his thumb over a scar on his knuckle. “Nobody else gave me a key.”

“That’s different!”

“Is it?”

“You didn’t take anyone’s dad, Wu.”

Big Wu didn’t say anything for a bit.

“No,” he said finally. “I didn’t.” He pushed off the bench. “I’m just saying. You’re the one with the keys. You decide who gets one. Always have.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in the middle of the night.

She heard the grey car at the end of the street. The pads biting clean at the corner. Hers. Then the alley door. He used that now, because he said the shutter was too loud. She didn’t turn round. She was on the stool by the kettle, his stool, with her back to the door and her hands round the WORLD’S OKAYEST MECHANIC mug. Gone cold an hour ago.

He came in. He stopped. She knew exactly what he was looking at. She’d put it all under the work lamp so he’d see it from the door. Down the line, a train was starting. She could feel it in the floor.

“I’m going to tell you what I think. You’re going to tell me if I’ve got it wrong.” She still didn’t turn. “Okay?”

“Okay.”

She went down the bench. Part by part. The same voice she used to tell a customer his gearbox was done. Flat. Not unkind. The plate. The paperwork. The shoe. The steel. The hand. The sleep. The roofs. She got up off the stool halfway through and walked the bench, touching each thing. He stood by the door and listened and didn’t move. At the end she picked up the photo.

“You don’t guard people. You take them. For somebody with a delegation, and paperwork, and a bank in the capital. You stand at a door till the one you want goes outside.”

He didn’t move.

“Then you walk him to a car with your hand on his arm like you’re friends. And you drive away. And in January his family’s in the paper because he never came home.” She turned round at last and held it up. “That’s what you do for work.”

The train went over. Everything shook. The parts rattled in their row. The clementine rolled off the end of the bench and hit the floor, and nobody picked it up.

He didn’t say she was wrong. He stood by the alley door with the lamp on half his face. His face did none of the things a guilty face does. It didn’t go hard. It didn’t drop. It stayed open, the way it was in the paddock. In her passenger seat. That was worse than any lie.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d thought she was ready. She’d sat on his stool for three hours getting ready. Nope.

“Do you kill them?” Her voice went up. She couldn’t stop it. “When you take them. Do you—do you kill them?”

“Sometimes.”

“The Belgian?”

“No.” Straight away. “I drove him to a petrol station on the edge of the province. I gave him to two men in a van. He was alive. I think he still is. Somewhere he doesn’t want to be, answering questions.”

“What did he do?”

“I don’t know. I’m not told. Mostly I’m not told.”

“And you don’t ask?”

“I was eighteen. They’d told me since I was sixteen that asking was someone else’s job.” He looked at the photo in her hand. “And once you’ve done it without asking, it’s very hard to start.”

She put the photo down. Her hands were shaking. She shoved them in her pockets so he wouldn’t see. She knew he’d seen.

“How many?”

Nothing.

“How many people, Haozhen?”

“I know the number. I know every one. Names. Dates. Where. What they had on.” He hadn’t moved. “I don’t let myself forget them. I won’t tell you tonight.”

“Why not?!”

“Because you’d hear it like this. Standing up, with that photo on your bench. And you’d never be able to hear it any other way.” He breathed in. “Ask me again in a year. If you still want to know, I’ll tell you all of it.”

She laughed. It came out horrible.

“Oh, good. A year. Very reasonable. Shall I put it in my diary?”

“I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked him to go.

She did it badly. She’d be ashamed of that later. She couldn’t look at him. She said it to the bench.

“I think you should go.”

Like a woman in a film. Like her mother ending a phone call. She hated it as it came out. She said it anyway. Because the woman in Antwerp had her hand over her mouth, and there were two boys behind her. Tonight Serafina couldn’t make the man in her garage and the man who walked Lucien Marchal to a car into two different people. She tried. She stood there with her hands in her pockets and really tried.

He didn’t argue. That was the worst part. No orders. No you don’t understand the world. She’d braced for all of it. She’d have had something to push against. He just looked at her a moment longer and nodded. Once. Like she’d told him the time.

He went to the kettle. Picked up the plain mug, his, with HIS on it in her marker, still facing the wall. He turned it round so the writing faced the room. He put it down exactly where it had been.

“If you tell anyone about this—” He was at the alley door, back to her.

She went cold all over.

“Then what?”

He turned his head.

“Then nothing. I’d make sure nobody touched you for it. That’s what I was going to say.” He looked across the garage at her. Across the row of parts. The clementine on the floor. “Lock this door after me. And the shutter. You leave the shutter up at night. You shouldn’t.”

His hand was on the door frame. The knuckles went white. The only part of him that moved.

“You can send me away. You should. But I won’t stop wanting this. I’m not going to lie to you about that either.”

He let go of the frame. He came back across the garage. Not fast. Past the bench. Past the clementine. Until he was right in front of her, close enough that she could feel the cold of the alley still on his jacket. He didn’t touch her. His hands stayed at his sides, where she could see them. Like the first night.

“Once. Before I go.”

He didn’t wait. She could have stepped back. The whole garage was behind her. She knew it like she knew a gap was too small. Her face was wet. When had that started? She was so angry. At him. At herself. At a doorstep in Antwerp. She didn’t move a centimetre.

He kissed her. Nothing in it asked to be forgiven. Slow. One hand came up at last to the side of her face. His thumb went wet from her cheek. He kissed her like he was learning her face well enough to keep it.

She hated him for one second. Then she grabbed his jacket in both fists and kissed him back, hard. Salt. Teeth. Fury. Until she couldn’t breathe.

She was the one who stopped. She put her hand flat on his chest and pushed. Not hard. He went back one step. No further.

“Go! Please.”

“Serafina—”

“PLEASE.”

“Lock the door.”

He went. She heard the grey car start in the alley. Down the street of shut workshops. The brakes at the corner, clean. Then nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t lock the door.

She sat down on the concrete in the middle of the garage with her back against Gilded’s front wheel and her arms round her knees. The trains went over. Every eleven minutes the whole building shook round her like a car on a bad road. She counted them. What else was there to count? Six. Seven. At the eighth she picked the clementine off the floor and peeled it. She didn’t eat it. She just held the peel.

Before dawn she got into Nonna and drove the loop.

Bridge. Tunnel. Coast road. No hard braking. Turbo never coming in. Engine burbling in third. She’d done it so many times with him beside her that her body had learned it that way. On the coast road, at the bend where his head always slid onto her shoulder, she dropped her right shoulder a fraction to catch it.

There was nobody there.

Oh.
