She pulled into the lay-by where the fireworks had been. Turned off the engine. Sat in the dark with both hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, the way he held it. Then the noise came out of her. Not crying. Worse than crying. A sound like something tearing, from low in her chest, with her forehead on the wheel and her mouth open. She howled. She hit the wheel with the heel of her hand until it hurt. There was no one in the passenger seat to hear. So she didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was parked below the lay-by, on the old service road, lights off.

He hadn’t gone home. He’d sat at the end of her street until the red Lancia came out, and then he’d followed it, two hundred metres back. He knew how she drove. He knew where she’d go. He watched her car rock a little on its springs when she hit the wheel.

He didn’t go up. She’d told him to go. He’d gone.

He just made sure nobody else stopped in that lay-by. A van slowed down once. He flashed his lights at it, and it thought better of it. Then he sat with his hands on his own wheel and listened to his own breathing, which was wrong. Too fast. He didn’t know what to do about that. So he did nothing.

He took his phone out once. Typed Are you. Looked at it. Deleted it. Put the phone face down on the passenger seat, where nobody was.

When she drove home, he followed her home. She parked inside. She left the shutter half up.

She hadn’t locked the door. Of course she hadn’t.

He stood in the alley until it was light, so it wouldn’t matter.

chapters.title: She Should Run
chapters.desc: She knows exactly how to run. Instead she turns up outside his flat at six in the morning with two egg sandwiches and four rules.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to run. I’m the one people run with.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
“Gold. Obviously gold. Yes. Fine.”

“Sera, I haven’t asked you anything yet.”

Tuesday. Aurelia, ringing from the boutique about next season’s livery. Serafina was lying under Gilded getting nothing done. She’d been getting nothing done since Sunday.

“Then ask me. I’ll say gold.”

A pause on the line. Then, in the voice from when they were small:

“Sera. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. An engine.”

Aurelia didn’t believe her. Aurelia also didn’t push, which was new, and which Serafina suspected was Chen Si’s fault. They talked about gold for another ten minutes. Serafina couldn’t have said afterwards what shade they picked.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble was, she knew how to run.

She’d known since she was nineteen. In the industrial district there were people who built cars for people who needed to stop existing. Plain cars. False floors. Two sets of plates. A man under the flyover by the fish market could make you a passport in four days. A woman in the Walled City rented rooms by the week and never wrote anything down. Serafina had fixed their cars. Twice, she’d driven through the night to the border with someone lying under a blanket in the back. She didn’t talk about it. Not even to Aurelia, except once, at a fountain in Milan.

She could go. Gone by Thursday. New name, new garage, somewhere nobody had heard of Team AURELIA. Nobody standing at her shutter in the middle of the night with his hands in plain view, ever again.

She thought about it Sunday, lying in the loft listening to the trains. She thought about it Monday under Gilded. She thought about it so hard on Tuesday that she put the same bolt in three times.

Tuesday night Mr. Kwok was washing the wok at the sink by the back door. It came out of her mouth before she could stop it.

“Mr. Kwok. Forty years. Did you ever drive someone who’d done something terrible?”

He kept washing the wok.

“Every night.”

She looked at him.

“Night shift, mostly. You think the people in a taxi at three in the morning are going home from the opera?” He rinsed the wok and turned it upside down on the rack. “Men who hit their wives. Men who robbed their brothers.”

“Mr. Kwok…”

“A man in 1991 got in outside the hospital with blood on his cuffs. Gave me the address of a police station. Sat there the whole way with his hands like this.”

He held his hands out. Flat. Palms up.

“What did he do?”

“I never asked. I asked if he wanted the radio on.”

“Did he?”

“He wanted the news.” Mr. Kwok dried his hands. “Forty years. You want to know what I learned? Since you’re asking, and you never ask.”

“…Yes.”

“Everybody in the back of a cab has done something. That’s not the question. The question is where they’re asking you to take them.” He hung the towel on its hook. “Your guard. Where’s he asking you to take him?”

She didn’t answer.

“Thought so.” He put on his coat and went home for the news.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four days.

He’d spent them the way he spent a job. He drove past the garage under the railway bridge every night, at a different time, from a different end of the street. Shutter half up. Every night. He sat at the window with no curtain and watched the laundry’s cat watch him back from the shop below.

On Monday he wrote a request for a transfer. Somewhere with no harbour. He read it four times and burned it in the sink.

On Tuesday his phone rang. The duty desk.

“Anything to report? Contacts, changes, anything.”

“No.”

It was the first lie he’d told the Bureau in ten years. It came out perfectly. He sat there afterwards and waited to feel something about it, and what he felt was relief. If she talked, he’d have to report her. He’d already decided he wouldn’t. If anyone else came near that garage asking questions about a red Lancia, he’d already decided what he would do about that too. It didn’t take long to decide. It was very calm.

On Wednesday he went down at six to buy nothing, the way he always did, and stood inside the street door to look.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mouse had his address. Of course Mouse had his address.

“Above a laundry.” Wednesday, before dawn. Serafina came down from the loft dressed, keys in hand. Mouse was still at the end of the bench, where she’d been all night. “Old harbour streets. Behind the market. Second floor. The window with no curtain.”

“How do you—never mind.”

“He hasn’t got anything in there. I looked at the electricity.” A pause. “He uses less than the laundry’s cat.”

“How do you know what a cat uses?”

“The cat has a heated bed.” Mouse turned back to her screens.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stopped at the place under the flyover on the way.

A metal stall under the concrete. Corrugated roof. Three plastic tables. An old man who’d been making egg sandwiches since before there was a flyover. Thick white bread off the grill. Butter. An omelette folded so soft it was nearly custard. One slice of ham nobody asked about. Two of those. Two milk teas, too much sugar, in plastic bags with straws.

Then she parked Nonna across from a laundry with its shutter still down. Under a window with no curtain. She leaned on the bonnet in the cold and waited.

The street door beside the laundry opened just after six.

He didn’t come straight out. Of course he didn’t. He stood just inside, in the dark, and she watched him look. Up the street. Down the street. Parked cars. Windows opposite. The alley by the market. All of it, without moving his head much.

Then his eyes came across the road. A red Lancia. A woman on its bonnet with two bags of milk tea hanging off one finger. They stopped there.

He didn’t move for a moment. Then he crossed the road. Not fast. He stopped a metre away in the grey light, hands at his sides, and read her face for damage.

He looked awful. Had he slept at all? Had he even sat down?

“You should have run. You know how. You’ve driven people.”

“Twice.”

“Then why are you here?”

She held out a sandwich. The paper bag was going see-through with butter.

“You wanted a sandwich. For this year. From the place under the flyover. With the egg.” She swallowed. “It’s January. I thought you’d better start.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate on Nonna’s bonnet, because the laundry wasn’t open and there was nowhere else.

He ate with his full attention, like the sandwich had been put in front of him for assessment. Halfway through he stopped and looked at it.

“This is very good.”

“I know.”

“I’ve walked past that stall maybe sixty times. I never stopped.”

“I know. That’s why I brought it, Guard.”

A woman came and rattled the laundry shutter up with a long screech. She looked at them. Two people on a red car at six in the morning. She went inside. She came back out holding a fat grey cat, so the cat could look at them too.

“I’ve got rules.”

He turned his head.

“Three. Maybe four. You don’t have to agree. But if you don’t, I drive off and you eat the sandwiches by yourself from now on.”

“Go on.”

She held up one finger. “One. You don’t lie to me. You don’t already, I know. Keep not doing it. If you can’t tell me something, say I can’t tell you that. I’d rather have that than anything made up.”

“Yes.”

“Two. You never bring it into my garage. Not the job. Not a gun. Not a person. Not a file.” Her voice wobbled. She ignored it. “Big Wu’s done two stretches and I’ve never once asked. The garage is where you don’t have to. That’s yours too. If you leave the rest outside.”

“Yes.”

“Three. If you’re going to be gone, you tell me. You don’t have to say where, or what for. Just I’ll be gone, and roughly how long. So I’m not standing at the shutter all night wondering if I’ll ever hear your brakes at the corner again.”

He was quiet on that one.

“I’ll always tell you. If I can.”

“If you can?”

“Sometimes they don’t tell me till I’m in the car.”

She looked at him. He looked back. The open look. The one with nothing guilty in it. Oh. This was going to be the whole of it, wasn’t it? Him telling her the truth. Her deciding, every single day, whether she could stand it.

“Then you tell me from the car.”

“Okay.”

“And four.” It came out rough. “If you ever want out. Of all of it. You tell me first. Before anyone. Before you’ve got a plan. Before you’ve even said it to yourself properly. You come to the garage and you say Sera, I want out. And I’ll have the car outside.”

He didn’t move a muscle.

“Serafina.”

“I know what I’m saying.”

“You don’t. You don’t know who they are.”

“I know they’ve got a bank in the capital and men in a white van at a petrol station. I know they’d be very cross.” She put her milk tea down on the bonnet. “I’m not going to run.”

“Listen—”

“I thought about it for four days! I could’ve been gone by Thursday. But I’ve watched people run since I was nineteen. I’ve driven them. I know what I am.”

“And what’s that?”

“I’m the one people run with.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything for so long the laundry woman put the cat down and went inside.

Then he took her right hand. The one with the old shiny burn across the back. He turned it palm up in both of his and looked at it, the way he’d looked at the oil on his own palm that first night. He ran his thumb along a cut across the base of her fingers. Monday’s bracket.

“The first time I didn’t ask, I was eighteen. A man in a hotel in the capital. A teacher. They said he’d written something.” He was still looking at her hand. “I didn’t read it.”

She didn’t move.

“I’ve never told anyone that. They make you see a doctor every year, and you tell the doctor you sleep fine.” His thumb moved on her palm. “I don’t know what you’re doing, Sera. I don’t know why you’re here.”

Sera. Out loud. He’d never said it out loud.

She couldn’t speak. So she didn’t. There was sesame from the bread on his lower lip. She wiped it off with her thumb. Then she leaned in and kissed the place where it had been. Slow. Until he made a sound in his throat, low and surprised, and his hand came up and caught her jaw.

Then he wasn’t surprised any more. He pulled her off the bonnet and into him, right there in the street, both hands in her short hair. He kissed her back hard and deep, like he’d spent four days at a window with no curtain telling himself he’d never get to do this again. She lost the milk tea. She heard it hit the road. Who cared? Nobody. Nobody cared.

“ABOUT TIME!”

The laundry woman. In her doorway. Arms folded.

“Two years he’s lived up there! Never once brought anyone home!”

He shut his eyes.

“She knows you!” Serafina was delighted.

“She knows my electricity. Her cat has a heated bed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday was Lunar New Year’s Eve. Mr. Kwok cooked.

He did it every year in the garage, for whoever turned up. Two trestle tables pushed together under the hanging lamp. A tablecloth from his own home. Chairs borrowed from the noodle shop at the end of the street. A team was a family whether it liked it or not, he said, and families ate together on New Year’s Eve. Even ones with criminal records.

Big Wu’s mother came. Tiny and fierce. She sat at the head of the table and told everyone what to eat. Mouse came, and sat at the end, and ate four bowls of rice in total silence. Serafina wore a red jumper Aurelia had sent by courier. The note said For luck. Wear it, or I’ll know.

At seven the alley door opened.

He came in with a net bag of mandarins and stopped dead. Trestle tables. Tablecloth. Borrowed chairs. Big Wu’s mother at the head. He looked like a man who’d walked into the wrong building.

Big Wu stood up. He was enormous and he took his time. He crossed the garage. He looked down at the net bag. He counted.

“Eight. Not four.”

“I asked at the market. The man said never four. Never an odd number. Never the ones with no leaves.”

Every mandarin had two green leaves still on its stem. Big Wu looked at them for a long time. Then he took the bag, carried it to the table, put it down in front of his mother and pulled out the chair beside his own.

“Ma. This is the guard.”

“Too thin!” Big Wu’s mother started piling food into his bowl before he’d sat down. “Eat. Eat. Why are you so thin?”

“I don’t know, Auntie.”

“Eat and find out!”

Then she reached across and dumped half a steamed fish into Serafina’s bowl. Head and all. For abundance.

Serafina hated fish. Everybody at that table knew Serafina hated fish, except Big Wu’s mother, who was now watching her with tiny ferocious eyes. Serafina picked up her chopsticks. Oh God. Was she going to have to—

Her bowl moved. Under the table edge, smooth as a gear change, he’d swapped it for his. She looked down. Rice. Pork. Greens. No fish. Beside her, he was already eating the fish, neatly, bones and all, like he’d been looking forward to it all week.

Big Wu’s mother nodded at Serafina. Satisfied.

At the stove, Mr. Kwok put his mouth by Serafina’s ear.

“Is Big Wu crying? Is that what that is?”

“It’s the onions.”

She wiped her own eyes on her red sleeve. Mr. Kwok looked at her. Then at the pot, which had no onions in it at all.

chapters.title: The First Time He Bleeds in Her Garage
chapters.desc: He’s late for Valentine’s dinner because of a knife in a stairwell. She stitches his arm with fishing line and swears the whole way through.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule two doesn’t cover blood. Sit down before you fall on my car.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
“It’s a florists’ holiday. And a restaurant holiday. And a jewellers’ holiday.”

Sunday. She was under Nonna. He was on the stool by the kettle. She’d already told him once.

“My sister sells eleven per cent of her whole year in the first two weeks of February. She lights a candle to Saint Valentine in her workshop every year as a joke. I don’t think it’s a joke any more.”

“I know. You told me.”

“I don’t need flowers! I don’t need a man playing the violin at me over a steak. I don’t do dates.”

“I’ll come at eight. With dinner.”

She rolled out on the creeper and glared at him upside down.

“Not a date. Dinner. Here. From the dumpling place by the tram depot. The one with the chilli oil.” He wrote something in his notebook. “You eat standing up at the bench every night anyway. I’ll stand up with you.”

She thought about it. That was a mistake. Thinking about it meant thinking about him standing next to her, eating dumplings, in her garage, on purpose.

“Pork and chive. Not the cabbage ones.”

“Not the cabbage ones.” He wrote that down too. Underlined it.

“And the good vinegar.”

“I know which vinegar.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The stairwell smelled of bleach and cigarettes. Third floor of a hotel nobody had renovated since the nineties.

He was supposed to be at the bottom of it. Watching a door. That was all. Then the door opened early, and the man who came through it wasn’t the man in the file. This one had a knife. He was fast, and he was scared, and scared men did stupid things with knives.

Qin Haozhen put his left arm up. The blade went down the outside of it from elbow to wrist. Long. Not deep. Then he had the man’s knife hand in both of his and turned it until the man stopped holding anything. The man made a noise. Haozhen sat him down on the stairs. He took the knife and folded it and put it in his pocket.

Blood was running into his cuff. Annoying. It was a good shirt.

He checked his watch. The dumplings would have been ready an hour ago.

He called it in. The van came. He wrapped the arm in a grey wool scarf from the lost property box behind the hotel desk. On the way back to the car he thought about the Bureau doctor. A form. A desk. Someone at the desk asking why a man watching a door had been close enough to get cut.

No. No doctor.

He got in the grey car. Took out his phone with his right hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight he didn’t come.

At nine he didn’t come. She’d been under Nonna since seven doing a clutch she didn’t need, so she’d look busy when he arrived. At nine she rolled out and checked her phone. Nothing. At ten, nothing. She found herself standing at the shutter, which she’d left half up again in spite of him, staring down the street toward the corner where his brakes always bit.

Pathetic. She went back in. She was so angry with herself she kicked the creeper across the floor.

At eleven, her phone buzzed.

Haozhen: Late. I’m sorry. In the car. Coming.

Rule three. From the car. She looked at the four words for ages. Then she went back under Nonna and finished the clutch. She did need to do it now. She’d taken it apart.

Serafina: ok

Serafina: are u ok

No answer. Was that a yes? A no? She turned the phone face down on the floor.

It was nearly one when she heard the brakes at the corner.

Wrong. They bit late. Hard. A bit crooked. She was out from under the car and on her feet before the grey estate stopped in the alley. She knew every noise that car made now. That one was wrong.

✦ ✦ ✦

The alley door opened.

He came in holding a plastic bag from the dumpling place. In his right hand. His left arm was folded against his chest, inside his jacket. The left sleeve was black and wet from elbow to cuff, and it was dripping. Not much. A drop every few seconds onto her concrete. Black under the work lamp.

“I’m breaking rule two. I’m sorry. I couldn’t go to the doctor.”

She’d been furious since eight. Somewhere in the last three seconds she’d stopped. She couldn’t have said when.

“What happened?”

“A knife. In a stairwell.” Like he was saying a puncture. “It isn’t deep. It’s long. I’ve stopped most of it. But the Bureau doctor puts everything on a form.”

“The Bureau…?”

“I brought the dumplings.” He looked at the bag. “They’re cold.”

“You brought the…” She stared at him. “You got STABBED and you stopped for DUMPLINGS?”

“I’d ordered them. They were waiting.” A pause. “Pork and chive. Not the cabbage.”

“And the man with the knife?”

“He won’t hold anything in that hand for a while.” Exactly the same voice as the dumplings. “He’s in a van.”

She heard how flat it was. She’d think about that later. More than once. Right then she found she didn’t care about the man’s hand at all.

“Good.”

That surprised her. She crossed the garage, took the bag off him, put it on the bench without looking. Then she took his good arm and walked him to the stool by the kettle. He let her. That frightened her more than the blood.

“Rule two doesn’t cover blood. Sit down before you fall on my car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The cut ran down the outside of his left forearm, from just below the elbow almost to the wrist. Long and clean. Gaping a bit in the middle, where it was deepest. He’d wrapped it tight in a grey wool scarf that wasn’t his, soaked right through. When she unwound it he didn’t make a sound. The muscle in his jaw went tight and stayed tight.

She looked at it under the lamp and made herself breathe.

She’d seen cuts. Big Wu had opened his palm to the bone on a bonnet catch once and gaffer-taped it and finished the job. She’d done her own forearms a hundred times. Small ones. She had never stitched anybody in her life.

“It needs stitches. I can’t stitch.”

“You can. You do the wiring on a thirty-year-old Lancia’s dashboard with tweezers. I’ve watched you.” He was looking at her face, not his arm. “Wash it out first. Boiled water, cooled. Lots of it. Fishing line, if you’ve got it. Boil that too. Boil a needle. Then just close it. One stitch at a time. Don’t pull them tight.”

“You’ve done this.”

“Twice. On myself.” A breath. “It’s easier when someone else does it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Kwok kept his fishing things in a red tin box under the bench. On Sundays he went to the breakwater, caught nothing and loved it. She found the line, clear and light. She found a needle in Mouse’s drawer, where Mouse kept everything, and bent it into a curve with two pairs of pliers. She boiled them in the saucepan on the camping stove. He sat on the stool with his arm held out over a clean rag and watched her the whole time.

The strongest thing in the garage was Big Wu’s emergency bottle. Scotch. Somebody gave it to him in 2017, and he was saving it for a death. She poured it over her own hands. Over the needle. Then, while he watched her, over the cut.

He made a noise then. Short. Through his teeth.

“Porca miseria—sorry, sorry, scusa—”

“It’s fine.”

“It is NOT fine, you’re bleeding on my floor, I just poured a dead man’s whisky on you—”

“Is Big Wu dead?”

“He’s saving it for when he is!”

She picked up the needle. Her hands were shaking so hard she couldn’t hold it. She put it down again. Then picked it up. Down again. Her breath was coming in little hitches she couldn’t stop. Oh God. What if she did it wrong? What if it went bad? What if he—

He reached out with his good hand and took her right wrist. He held it. His thumb sat on the inside, where her pulse was going like a piston. He didn’t say anything. He just held it until it slowed.

“One at a time. Like a wiring loom.”

She picked up the needle.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fourteen stitches.

She swore through every single one. Italian, mostly, the Milanese kind, the kind Nonna had used on watchmakers. Cantonese at the fishing line when it wouldn’t knot. English, at him, under her breath, every time the needle went in and his jaw went tight.

“Idiot. Lunatic. Stopping for dumplings with a knife in you. Who goes into a stairwell? What kind of man goes into a stairwell?”

“I was in it already.”

“If you die in my garage, I’m telling the whole industrial district a dumpling killed you!”

He sat on the stool with his arm on the rag and his eyes on her face. He didn’t once look down at what she was doing.

“Why aren’t you looking?”

“I’m looking at what I want to.”

The eighth stitch went wrong. She pulled too tight. The edge of the skin puckered. She said something in Cantonese that would’ve made Granny Shum put down her tea.

“Leave it. It’s fine.”

“It is not fine. It’ll leave a mark.”

“Sera. I’ve got plenty of marks. This one’s from you. Leave it.”

She had to stop after that. She sat back on her heels on the concrete with the bloody needle in her fingers and the lamp in her eyes, and didn’t look at him until she could. Then she did the other six.

✦ ✦ ✦

She dressed it with gauze from the first-aid kit in the van and a crepe bandage, firm, taped. A train went over. The bloody rag, the empty whisky bottle, the saucepan and the bent needle lay round the stool like the aftermath of a very small war.

He looked at his arm for the first time.

“That’s good. That’s better than mine.”

“Shut up!”

“It is.”

His shirt was ruined, the left sleeve stiff with blood up to the shoulder. She told him to take it off while she found him one of Big Wu’s T-shirts. He took it off one-handed. She stopped with the T-shirt halfway out of the locker.

She’d known there’d be scars. Ten years of what he did? Obviously. She hadn’t known there’d be so many. Or that they’d all be so neat. A short white line under his right collarbone. A round pucker low on his left side, old. Three faint parallel marks across his ribs, like a fork. A long thin one down his back she could only see the start of. All healed flat and pale.

“Don’t.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were going to count them.”

She was. She put the T-shirt down. She walked over and stood between his knees and put her hand flat on his chest, over the white line under the collarbone. His heart was going much faster than it had while she was stitching him.

“I don’t want to count them. Which ones still hurt?”

“None.” He looked up at her. “This one, a bit.” He tipped his head at the bandage. “Mostly the whisky.”

She laughed. It came out wet. And he didn’t wait. His good hand came up, took a fistful of the front of her vest and pulled her down to him.

Nothing careful in it. She tried to go slow, because he’d lost blood. He wouldn’t let her. His good hand let go of her vest and went to her waist, found the gap between vest and overalls and stayed there, flat and hot on her bare back. She had both hands on his face. Stubble rough under her palms. His mouth opening under hers. Whisky on him where she’d splashed it. He pulled her closer by the waist. She went. She went until she was pressed between his knees and his face was against her collarbone and he was breathing hard against her skin. She could feel him trembling all through. Like an engine at the limiter.

Then something warm on her hip. She looked down. He was bleeding through the gauze.

“No.” She took his face in both hands and held it away. “No. Absolutely not.”

“It’s fine.” He was already reaching for her again.

“It’s leaking. You’re leaking on my overalls! You’ve got fourteen stitches put in by a woman who’s never stitched anything but a seat cover.” She was laughing, and breathless, and her face was on fire. “Not tonight. You’ll bleed on my car.”

He looked up at her with his hair wrecked and his mouth red. Dazed. Deeply offended. She laughed harder.

“You’re a menace. I’ve said this before.”

“In English. You said it in English.”

“Then I’ll learn it in Mandarin. So you understand.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let him drive home.

While he struggled into Big Wu’s T-shirt, which came down nearly to his knees, she went out to look at the grey estate in the alley. There was a hole in the driver’s door. Small and neat and round, about level with where his hip would be, with a bright ring of torn paint round it. She put her finger in it. She touched steel. The armour in the door had stopped whatever made it.

He hadn’t mentioned that. A knife in a stairwell, he’d said. Had there been a gun as well? Before? After? Was that rule one? Not lying, just not saying?

She stood in the alley with her finger in the hole for a long time. Then she went back in and took his keys off the bench and put them in her pocket.

“You’re sleeping here.”

“Where?” He looked up the stairs at the loft.

“Not there. Not tonight. You’d bleed on that too.”

She found the painkillers in the van kit. She read the label. Then read it again, slower, because her eyes kept sliding off the words. Two. Not more than eight in a day. She shook two into his palm and stood over him until he’d swallowed them with the hot water from his own mug. HIS. Facing the room.

Then she opened Nonna’s passenger door.

He looked at it. At her. Then he got in carefully, arm across his chest, and put the seat back two notches. She got in the driver’s side. They sat in the red Lancia in the middle of the garage under the hanging lamp with the engine off. She reached back for the blanket on the rear seat and tucked it over him, up to his chin, round the bad arm.

“Happy Valentine’s Day. This isn’t a date.”

“No.” His eyes were already closing. “It’s better than a date.”

He was asleep before the next train. She sat beside him and ate four cold pork and chive dumplings with her fingers, with the good vinegar. She didn’t take her eyes off the bandage.

It stayed white till morning. She checked it eleven times.

chapters.title: Twelve Days and a Postcard
chapters.desc: He’s gone for twelve days with no phone. She nearly puts Gilded into the tyre wall, Aurelia notices, and then a postcard comes with nothing written on it.
chapters.epigraph: “When you can tell me, tell me. That’s how it works in my house.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
She took the stitches out on the Friday. Ten days after she put them in.

He sat on the stool by the kettle with his sleeve rolled up. She sat on an upturned crate with Mouse’s tweezers and a pair of nail scissors she’d boiled in the saucepan. Snip. Pull. Snip. Pull. All fourteen. The cut had closed into a long pink line, puckered at the eighth stitch where she’d pulled too tight. When she’d finished she ran her thumb down the whole length of it.

“It’s ugly.”

“It’s yours. I like it.”

She kept her thumb on it. Something about the way he was sitting. Too straight. Like a man with a bag already packed.

“You’re going somewhere.”

He didn’t ask how she knew. He’d stopped asking that in January.

“Sunday. I’ll be gone. Maybe two weeks. Maybe a bit more.” He looked at her thumb on his arm. “I can’t tell you where.”

“Rule three.”

“Rule three.”

“Can you ring? Text?”

“No. There won’t be a phone that’s mine.” He was quiet. “If I could, I would. You know I would.”

She did know. That was the worst part. She sat on the crate with her hand on the long pink line she’d made and thought about stairwells. About fourteen countries and roofs. About a neat round hole in a car door with steel at the bottom of it.

“Come back with that arm. I want to see it heal.”

“I’ll come back with the arm.”

“The whole arm. Attached.”

“Attached.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning he left his grey car in her garage. They’d give him a different one, he said. He wanted this one somewhere he knew it would be looked after. He left the keys on the bench by the kettle. He left the plain mug, HIS, facing the room.

He kissed her at the alley door, early, with the dustcarts going past at the end of the street. Careful at first. Like he was memorising something. Then not careful at all. He pushed her back against the door frame and kissed her like he was taking her with him and meant to take every bit. When he let go, he didn’t step back. He stood with his forehead on hers.

“Wait for me.”

Then he walked to the corner and turned it and was gone. She stood in the alley till the dustcarts had finished and the sun had come up over the railway bridge.

That was Day Nothing. She didn’t count it. Day One was Monday.

✦ ✦ ✦

She counted.

Day Two, she rebuilt his grey car’s gearbox. It didn’t need it. Day Three, she did Nonna’s. Day Four, Big Wu took a spanner out of her hand.

“Go to bed.”

“I’m not tired.”

“You’ve put that bolt in and taken it out four times. Four, Sera…” He looked genuinely upset about the number. “Go to bed.”

Day Five, Mouse turned a screen round without being asked. A page of numbers that meant nothing to Serafina.

“There’s been nothing. On anything. No news. No reports. No names.” A pause. “That’s good, I think. When it’s bad, there’s always something.”

“How do you know?”

“I looked. In January. At what happens when it’s bad.”

Mr. Kwok made her lunch every day and stood over her until she ate it. At night she drove the loop. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. On her own. She kept forgetting and dropping her shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

The pawnshop was on a street by a river, in a city he would never tell her the name of.

He walked past it on the first day, on the way to the building he was watching. He walked past it again in the evening. Day Two, he went in. He didn’t know why. He told himself it was cover. A man browsing in a pawnshop is just a man. That was true. It wasn’t why.

It was in a tray at the back, under scratched glass, with forty other rings. Old gold. A plain band, worn thin on one side. A square setting. One red stone. Red like her car. Exactly like her car. He stood there looking at it far longer than cover needed.

“That one?” The old man behind the counter had glasses on a cord. “From a family who left in a hurry. Long time ago. The stone is old. The lady who wore it worked with her hands. See how the band’s gone thin? Forty years of work, that.”

“How much?”

The old man named a price. It was too high. Haozhen could see it was too high. The old man could see that he could see it, and waited, smiling, for the haggling.

Haozhen paid it. All of it. Cash, from the job money.

The old man stopped smiling. He looked at the notes. Then at Haozhen.

“You didn’t argue.”

“No.”

“Everyone argues.” He put the ring in a worn red leather box with a brass clasp, very slowly, like he wasn’t sure he should. “She must be something.”

That night Haozhen took a man home from the building he’d been watching. It went cleanly. It took eleven minutes. On the way back to his room he touched the box in his inside pocket four times, to make sure it was still there.

He started on the speech on Day Three. He practised it on a ferry. In a stairwell, waiting. On the floor of a hotel room by the door, where he slept. It had four parts. It had reasons. The reasons were in order.

On Day Ten he found the postcard on a market stall. He bought it. He didn’t write anything on it. There was nothing he was allowed to write.

✦ ✦ ✦

Day Six was the pre-season test at the circuit in the north. Saturday, the fourth of March.

Every team in the series came. Twenty-two cars. Two days of running before the season opened in April. Sponsors came to see their logos. People who might give you money stood in the pit lane with their arms folded and watched how fast you went.

Aurelia came at ten. Cream coat, fur collar, dark glasses, coffee. Lily from the boutique trotted behind her with the new livery proofs. Aurelia walked into the pit garage and looked at Gilded. Matte black. AURELIA in gold on the bonnet, freshly painted.

“It’s crooked.”

“It is NOT.”

Big Wu got the tape measure out. Four millimetres. Aurelia took her glasses off and looked at her sister.

“Sera. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. It’s four millimetres.”

“You’ve never once in your life let anything be four millimetres out.” Aurelia put her coffee down on the tyre rack. “And you’ve looked at your phone eleven times since I walked in. I counted.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afternoon session. Ninth lap. Serafina lifted at the top of the esses.

The sun. She knew it was the sun. He’d told her it was the sun, in December, and she’d fixed it, and for three months she hadn’t done it once. She did it now. She came over the crest with the sun full in her visor. Her foot came up off the throttle without asking her. The car went light. She caught it. Then she was so angry at herself that she went down the back straight at two hundred and forty-one without deciding to, and braked for the Needle ten metres late.

Ten metres. In a race car, at that speed, ten metres is everything.

The front tyres went. That long sick slither, like missing a stair in the dark. The car wouldn’t turn. She came off the brakes to get the steering back and the car went straight on. Off the tarmac. Over the kerb with a bang that went up her spine. Into the gravel. The gravel grabbed at the wheels, the way it was meant to. And the tyre wall came at her, red and white and huge, and she thought, very calmly, well, he’ll have to come back now, to see this—

The car stopped.

A metre from the tyres. Less. She could see the bolts in the belt that held them together.

She sat in the gravel with both hands on the wheel. Her heart was so loud she could hear it inside her helmet. The red flag went out all round the circuit. Marshals came running with extinguishers. Was that it? Was that how it would have gone? Gravel, and a tyre wall, and him finding out from a stranger? She couldn’t get her fingers to open. She tried. They wouldn’t.

“MISS SONG? Can you hear me? Miss Song!”

A marshal had to unclip her belts for her. She sat there with her hands still locked on the wheel and her whole body shaking in long hard waves. When he lifted her visor, she was sick down the front of her race suit.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu didn’t speak to her for an hour.

He got the car on the truck and back to the garage. He went over every centimetre with a torch. Gravel in everything. Radiator ducts. Wheel arches. Undertray. A crack in the splitter that would cost four thousand to replace. He didn’t say one word. Mouse sat at the laptop with the crash data up. Speed going up and up. The brake trace, a fraction late. The steering doing something wild. Mouse didn’t say a word either. Mr. Kwok made tea.

When the pit lane was emptying, Aurelia came and sat on the tyre stack next to her. In the cream coat. In the gravel and oil. She didn’t say anything for a while.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“You went off at the Needle. You never go off at the Needle. You told me it was the only corner on earth you trusted.”

Serafina didn’t answer.

“I’m not going to ask who he is.”

Serafina turned her head.

“Oh, please… You think I don’t know what this looks like? I’m married to a man who leaves at three in the morning and comes home at six smelling of the docks and says it’s handled.” Aurelia’s voice was dry. “I know the phone. I know the face.”

“Lia…”

“I’m not going to ask. When you can tell me, tell me. That’s how it works in my house. We say I can’t tell you that yet, and the other one waits.”

“And if I never can?”

Aurelia was quiet.

“Then I’ll pay for the splitter. And wait anyway.”

Serafina put her head on her sister’s shoulder. Aurelia smelled of polishing rouge and something French and coffee. She let the head stay there, oil and sick and all, on the cream coat. Nobody in their family ever let anybody’s head stay anywhere.

Big Wu came over eventually.

“Van’s loaded. If anyone wants a lift back, they’d better stop crying on the tyres.”

“Nobody’s crying.”

“Course not.” He gave Serafina his handkerchief anyway. It was enormous. Then he gave Aurelia the other one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Day Seven. Mr. Kwok made her the noodles. The long ones, for long life, the ones he made when somebody had died.

“Eat.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“Nobody asked if you were hungry.”

She ate them. When she’d finished he took the bowl and patted her once on the top of the head. Four years, and he’d never done that.

Day Eight. Where was he? Was he cold? Was he eating anything that wasn’t out of a machine? Day Nine. She didn’t drive at all. She sat in his grey car in the garage with the door open and her feet on the dash and looked at the round hole in the driver’s door. She hadn’t filled it. She wasn’t going to fill it till he could see.

Day Ten. Day Eleven. Day Twelve. Friday the tenth. The post came. A tyre catalogue. A gas bill. A letter from the series about the splitter. And a postcard.

Foreign stamp. Smudged postmark. The address was hers, the garage under the railway bridge, in small square separate letters. The same hand as the caterer’s clipboard. Nothing else written on it. Not one word.

She turned it over.

An old hand-tinted photo, in colours that never existed. The banking at Monza. The huge concrete curve of the old oval tilted up like a wall against a too-blue sky. One silver car from the fifties, high up at the top, leaning in. Impossible.

She’d told him that. On the coast road, in January, at three in the morning, when he was supposed to be asleep and wasn’t. Nonna had taken her to the old banking when she was nine. They didn’t race on it any more. Nonna let her walk on it. It was so steep. She tried to run up it, slid down and skinned both knees, and Nonna laughed.

That’s where the brave ones went, cara. Round the top. Where it’s steepest. Never the bottom.

He’d remembered. Somewhere, in whatever country he was in, he’d found a postcard of a place he’d never seen, because she’d mentioned it once in the middle of the night.

She could read it anyway. Alive. Thinking of you. The brave ones go round the top.

Big Wu came in with the doughnuts and found her on the floor by the door with the postcard in both hands. He looked at it over her shoulder. He grunted.

“Monza. He went to Italy?”

“There’s nothing on it.”

“Then how do you know it’s from him?”

“Look at the writing!”

“I don’t know.” She laughed, wet, with her face in the postcard. “I don’t know where he went. I don’t care where he went!”

She put it on the whiteboard. Right in the middle. Over the number plate, which she wiped off for the first time since October.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she lay on the mattress in the loft with the window open, not sleeping, listening to the trains.

She heard the car before the brakes. Not his. His was downstairs. Something diesel, with a loose exhaust bracket. A taxi. Coming down the street much too slowly. It stopped at the corner.

Footsteps.

Then, at the bottom of the stairs, in the dark garage, somebody stopped by the kettle. Picked up a mug. Put it down again, carefully, exactly where it had been.

She was down the stairs before she knew she’d moved.

chapters.title: The Ring Was in the Glovebox
chapters.desc: She goes into his glovebox for the tyre gauge and finds a ring. He had a speech in four parts, and she says yes before he gets to part two.
chapters.epigraph: “I had a plan. It had four parts. You were supposed to let me finish.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
He did the glovebox first.

The grey car was under the work lamp, where he’d left it. He opened the passenger door without a sound and slid the red leather box in behind the handbook, next to the tyre gauge. Part one was the lay-by on the coast road. Three in the morning. Tomorrow. Everything in order.

Then he went to the kettle. HIS was still facing the room, where he’d left it twelve days ago.

He picked it up. Put it down again. Exactly where it had been.

Upstairs, the mattress creaked.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d lost weight. That was the first thing she saw. His face was thinner, the shadows under his eyes gone nearly black. A brown hooded jacket she’d never seen. Cheap trainers. Like a man who’d bought everything at an airport.

“Sera—”

She didn’t let him get further. She jumped the last two stairs, grabbed the brown jacket in both fists and kissed him. Hard. Fast. Teeth. He staggered back into the bench. He caught her. Both arms. He made a sound she’d never heard from him, rough, from deep in his chest.

Then he was holding her so tight she couldn’t breathe. She didn’t want to.

“The arm.” She said it into his neck. “Show me the arm.”

He pushed up his left sleeve. There it was under the street light. Her long pink line. Paler now. The pucker at the eighth stitch.

She ran her thumb down it. Then she bent her head and kissed it. The whole length, elbow to wrist. Slow. He stood in the dark garage and let her, and didn’t breathe.

“You came back with it.”

“Twelve days.” His voice wasn’t steady. She’d never heard it not be steady. “I counted.”

“So did I.” She laughed. Then she was crying. Ugly, sudden, the snotty kind, with her forehead on his collarbone. “I went off at the Needle, you idiot. I went in the gravel…”

He went cold under her hands. She felt it.

“Are you hurt?”

“No! A metre from the tyres. I’m fine. I was sick on a marshal.”

He took her face in both hands. He tilted it up to the street light and looked at it, every bit, like he was checking a car after a crash. Then he kissed her eyelids. The left. The right. Wet and salty. She cried harder. That wasn’t fair at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove him the loop.

He was asleep before the tunnel. How much had he slept in twelve days? Ten hours? He went down like a building being knocked over, all at once. His head landed on her shoulder at the bridge. She drove till the sun came up. When she rolled back in under the railway bridge, he woke.

“How long?”

“Four hours and six minutes.”

“That’s the longest since I was eighteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon he slept again, upstairs, in his airport clothes. She finished his car. Then she filled the bullet hole in the driver’s door at last, because he’d seen it now. When he came down with a blanket crease on his cheek, she was jingling the keys.

“Test drive.”

“Now?”

“The gearbox needs bedding in. And you need waking up. Get in.”

He got in the passenger side without even thinking about it. She shoved the seat back four notches and fixed his mirrors, which he watched with real pain. Then she leaned across him to the glovebox.

“Tyre gauge. You keep one in here. I saw it in November.”

“Sera—”

The glovebox was already open.

The tyre gauge was there. Cheap. Black. And next to it, pushed in behind the handbook, a little box. Dark red leather gone pale at the corners. A brass clasp.

Her hand stopped on the gauge.

Beside her, he’d frozen. The east-service-door kind.

“That’s not.” A breath. “I was going to.”

She took the box out. She held it in her oily palm. She looked at it. Then at him. He’d shut his eyes.

“I had a plan. It had four parts.” His voice was level. Too level. That was how she knew. “Part one was the coast road. The lay-by. Three in the morning. Because that’s where you asked me what I wanted, at New Year.”

She couldn’t breathe.

“Part two was what I was going to say. I’ve had eleven days to practise. I practised on a ferry. In a stairwell. On a hotel floor by the door. It was quite long. It had reasons, in order. It started with the fact that I don’t know how to want things, and you said start small—”

“Yes.”

His eyes opened.

“—and that I’d tried. And this was the smallest thing I could find that was still true. And part three was the ring, and part four was an apology. In advance. For what I am. For the stairwells—”

“YES.”

“You were supposed to let me finish.”

“I’m not letting you finish!” She was laughing. Her eyes were burning. “You can finish later. In the lay-by. Every night for the rest of your life, with the reasons in order. But I’m saying yes now, Haozhen.”

He stared at her.

“In a car. In my garage. With a tyre gauge in my hand. Because if you think I’m waiting till three in the morning to say it, you’ve learned nothing about how I drive.”

He put his face in his hands. His shoulders shook. For one horrible second she thought he was crying. Then she heard it. He was laughing. Helplessly, into his palms, like a man who couldn’t find where it went.

“Open it.” Muffled, through his fingers.

“No.”

He lifted his face.

“No?”

“You didn’t ask me anything. You did a speech about a speech.” Her voice cracked right down the middle. “I said yes to nothing. Ask me properly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at her. Then he got out of the car.

He walked round the bonnet and opened her door. Then he knelt on her garage floor, in the oil and the brake dust, in his cheap airport jeans. He took the box out of her hands and opened it himself.

Her mouth fell open. Was he really—on the floor—?

“Serafina.”

A train was coming. He waited for it. The whole garage shook. The spanner hit the bucket. He didn’t take his eyes off her once. Then it was gone.

“Will you marry me?”

She’d said yes twice already. Loudly. Now her throat had shut. She nodded. She nodded harder, and her face crumpled.

“I need you to say it.”

“Yes.” Barely a sound. “Yes. Yes, you stupid… yes.”

He breathed out. Like he’d been holding it since the pawnshop.

The ring was from before the war. She knew that straight away. She’d grown up in a family that bought jewellery like bread. Old yellow gold, worn thin on one side. A square setting. Four claws. One stone.

Red. Brake-light red. 1992-Lancia-going-pink-at-the-edges red.

“It’s the colour of your car.”

She made a noise. It wasn’t a word.

“There was a pawnshop. In a city by a river. I walked past it every day on the way to—on the way. On the second day I went in.”

“And?”

“The man said the woman who wore it worked with her hands. Because of how the band’s worn.”

“Haozhen…”

“I don’t know anything about rings. I know it’s red. I know someone wore it a long time doing something hard, and kept it on.”

She held out her left hand. It was shaking. Black round the nails.

He tried her ring finger. It stuck at the knuckle. Of course it did. She had her father’s hands, long and bony. He looked up at her, stricken. The man who’d walked out of a stairwell with a knife cut down his arm, looking like the world had ended.

“Little finger.” She was laughing through it. “Try the little one.”

It went on the little finger. It sat there, red and old and perfect, next to a fresh nick from a hose clamp.

“Aurelia’s going to have opinions about the size. She’ll want to resize it.”

“Let her. Just don’t let her make it new.”

He turned her hand over. He kissed the inside of her wrist, just under the ring. Then he stayed there, his mouth on her pulse, his eyes shut, kneeling on her floor.

That did it. She grabbed his collar and hauled him up off the concrete and kissed him. Half in the car, half out, the steering wheel in her ribs. She kissed him till his hands came up and held her head. Then she kissed him some more.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove the coast road with the ring on her little finger.

Not gently. She put her foot down like it was Granny Shum’s. The new gearbox snicked through like butter. She took the long bends above the harbour flat, the sea going by gold and enormous. She rolled the window down, stuck her head out and screamed.

“FIDANZATO!”

A man on a bicycle wobbled.

“What does that mean?”

“It means fiancé! You’re my fiancé! How do you say it? Properly. Your way.”

He told her. She yelled it out of the window. Wrong.

“The tone goes down. On the second one.”

She yelled it again. Worse.

“Down, Sera. Not sideways.”

She yelled it a third time, all wrong on purpose, at a bus. He laughed. Out loud. Head back against the seat, laughing so she could hear it over the engine. She’d drive a car into the sea for that sound.

At the lights at the bottom of the hill she stopped. Panting. Grinning like an idiot. She looked at the ring.

“Oh God. Mamma.”

“Yes.”

“She’s going to have a heart attack. Then she’s going to have you investigated. Then another heart attack.”

“She won’t find anything.”

“That’s what she’ll hate!”

He didn’t laugh at that one. He was looking at the ring too. His hand came across and settled on the back of her neck, warm, his thumb in her short hair.

“I’ll have to tell them. At work.”

“Tell them what?”

“That I’m engaged. It goes on a form.”

The light went green. She didn’t move. Somebody behind them honked.

“So I’m on a form.”

“You’ll be on a form.”

A white van. A petrol station. Her own name in capitals in a drawer somewhere. Her stomach dropped. Then she looked at his arm, with her stitches down it.

“Fine. Put me on your stupid form.” She put the car in gear. “Spell my name right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back down into the industrial district at dusk and pulled in under the railway bridge so fast the tyres squealed on the concrete. Handbrake. Engine off.

The engine ticked. Tick. Tick. Metal cooling in the dark garage.

She turned in her seat. He was already reaching for her.

She climbed over the gearstick. It wasn’t graceful. She banged her knee on the handbrake and swore. He caught her hips and pulled her the rest of the way. She landed in his lap with her head bumping the roof. They were both laughing too hard to kiss. Then they weren’t laughing.

He kissed her slow. Thorough. She didn’t let him. She kissed him fast and hard, the way she’d just taken the coast road. She felt him try to take control. She wouldn’t give it to him. She held his face and kissed him till his breath went ragged and his hands on her hips weren’t steady. The windows fogged. Her elbow hit the horn. Nobody stopped.

“Sera. Sera, the gearstick—”

“I know where the gearstick is.”

She dragged the airport jacket off his shoulders and threw it in the back. She got her hands under his shirt, flat on his bare back, on the long thin scar she’d only ever seen the start of. His whole body jolted under her palms like a car going over a kerb.

He caught her wrists. Not hard. He looked up at her in the fogged dark with his hair wrecked and his eyes nearly black. Breathing like he’d run up a flight of stairs.

“I’m trained to keep control. Of everything. Always. Every room.”

“I know.”

“I can’t. With you. I can’t keep it.”

She leaned down till her mouth was at his ear.

“Then don’t. Let me have it. Just tonight.” She kissed the corner of his mouth. “Let me drive.”

He let go of her wrists.

✦ ✦ ✦

They made it to the loft. Eventually. She was never sure how.

His shirt was on the third stair. Her vest on the landing. Then her boots, which took forever. He knelt on the top step to unlace them while she sat on the edge of the mattress and laughed at him.

“Double knots? Who double-knots their boots?”

“You. Every day. Since October.”

She stopped laughing. Halfway through the second boot he stopped too, and looked up at her from the step, his hands still on her ankle.

“I’ve wanted this since Battery Hill. Since the torch.”

“Since the torch?”

“You were holding it like a spanner.”

She grabbed his hair and pulled him up off the step. Then there was nothing between them but the dark and the window open onto the railway. The cold coming in. The heat of him. He was careful. He was careful with everything. He kissed her like he was reading her. Slow. Exact. Her shoulder. The inside of her elbow. The old burn on her hand. Every time she made a sound, he went back to wherever he’d just been. Then did it again.

“You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Yes.”

“Haozhen—”

“I’m learning it. Be quiet.”

She was not quiet. She told him exactly what she thought of him, in Italian, in the dark. Then she rolled him over, pinned his wrists and kissed him until he forgot to be careful. She felt it go. Ten years of doors and chairs by the door, going out of him under her hands. What was left was a man who laughed into her shoulder and said her name like it was something he’d found.

Then it was him. Once it had gone, it didn’t come back. He turned her under him. Not slow. Not careful. He wouldn’t let her go anywhere. His hands laced through hers on the pillow. His mouth at her ear.

“Sera. Sera. Look at me.”

She looked. His face was right above hers in the orange light from the tracks. Nothing put away. Nothing at all.

“Okay?”

“If you stop, I’ll kill you.”

He laughed. Breathless. He didn’t stop.

The first train went over and the whole loft shook. The window rattled in its frame. The mattress trembled under them like a car on the line. She laughed into his neck. She felt him laughing too.

“That’s one.”

“You’re counting?”

“I count everything. Don’t you?”

“Not tonight.” His hands were on her back. His mouth was in her hair. “Tonight you can do it for both of us.”

She counted six.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late. The window still open. The red ring catching the light every time a train went by.

“Go on, then.” Her head was on his chest. “Part two.”

“Now?”

“You practised for eleven days. On a ferry. I want it.”

He was quiet for a while. His fingers moved in her hair.

“I don’t know how to want things.”

“I know. That’s reason one.”

“You said start small. I tried.” His voice was low in the dark. Rough. “A sandwich. The passenger seat. Your hands. It didn’t stay small. I tried to find the smallest thing that was still true.”

“And?”

“And it was this. I couldn’t get it any smaller.”

She kept her mouth shut. She didn’t trust it. He kept going. All four parts. In order, with the reasons. She lay there and listened to every word and didn’t interrupt him once. Part four was the apology. For what he was. For the stairwells. She let him get all the way to the end of it.

“Done?”

“Done.”

“Still yes.” She bit his shoulder. Not hard. “Idiot.”

He was asleep before the seventh train. In a bed. No chair. No door. His hand had ended up spread flat across her stomach, warm and heavy, keeping her there. She stayed awake for the seventh. The eighth. The ninth. He didn’t wake when the building shook. Not once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday morning, Big Wu came in under the shutter with the doughnuts and stopped dead.

Serafina was on the bench in the brown airport jacket, eating cold rice from the pan. Haozhen was on the stool by the kettle with his hot water. Big Wu looked at them. Then at the ring on her little finger.

He put the doughnuts down. He went to his locker. He came back holding the empty whisky bottle and turned it upside down. One drop came out.

“You poured it on him.”

“He was bleeding!”

“That was for a death, Sera. This is a wedding.” He pointed the bottle at Haozhen. “You owe me a bottle.”

“Two.”

“…Two.” Big Wu’s face did something complicated. He turned round fast and went and stood very close to the transporter, with his back to everyone.

Mouse came in last, sat at the end of the bench and looked at the ring for a long time.

“Sera. That’s your little finger.”

“I know which finger it is.”

“I know you know.” Mouse turned on her screens. Then, still only to Serafina, very flat: “He’s going to make a list now.”

On the stool by the kettle, Haozhen had already taken out his black notebook. He opened it to a clean page.

“What are you writing?”

He didn’t look up.

“A list.”

chapters.title: Qin Haozhen Has Never Planned a Party
chapters.desc: He has stood at the door of eleven weddings and never been inside one, so he makes a list. Then he puts the engagement on a Bureau form, forgets his own toast, and she buys a burnt-out race car for scrap.
chapters.epigraph: “Depends how many people love you. Start counting.” — Mr. Kwok
chapters.content:
The list was called WEDDING. Underlined twice.

He'd started it on the Sunday morning, on the stool by the kettle, while Big Wu was still pretending to look at the transporter. By the next Sunday it had a column.

“Date. Venue. Guests, number. Guests, who. Food.” Serafina read it upside down from the creeper. “Her family, two question marks. My mother. Clothes. Rings, resize, not new. Music.” She stopped. “What happens in the middle?”

“That one’s a question.”

“I can see it’s a question. It’s got a question mark.”

He turned the notebook round so she could read it the right way up. Like that helped.

“I’ve been to eleven weddings. Six countries. A minister’s daughter. Two ambassadors. A man who ran a port.” He took the notebook back. “I stood at the door at every one. I’ve never been inside.”

“Never?”

“I know how they end. Somebody’s uncle makes a speech. The bride’s mother cries in the car park.” He wrote something. “I know where the fire exits are at the Harbour Hotel. I don’t know what happens in the middle.”

“The middle’s the good bit, Haozhen.”

“I assumed it must be.”

At the bottom of the page, on its own, circled: Ask Mr. Kwok.

She looked at the ring on her little finger. Then at him, writing. The man had a list for their wedding before she’d told her own sister properly.

Was that sweet or terrifying? Both. Definitely both.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Kwok put down his wok.

He’d been waiting thirty years for somebody to ask. His daughter had married in a registry office in Vancouver in 1994, in jeans, and he had never recovered. He pulled the other stool over and sat on it with his hands on his knees.

“Nine courses.”

Haozhen wrote 9.

“Not eight. Not ten. NINE. Suckling pig first, red skin, the groom cuts it. Crab claw. Scallops with the green vegetable. Chicken, whole, head on, so the marriage has a beginning and an end. Then the fish.” A finger went up. “Whole. You never turn it over. Anybody turns it over, they get out.”

“She hates fish.”

“The FISH isn’t for HER.”

Serafina, under Gilded, snorted so hard she hit her head on the sump.

“Noodles, long. Fried rice. Red bean soup. Little peach buns for the old people. Round tables, ten to a table, never square.” He breathed. “Then you go round every table with her and drink. Every one. You don’t sit down till you’ve done them all.”

“How many tables?”

Mr. Kwok picked up his wok again and gave him a hard look over it.

“Depends how many people love you. Start counting.”

Haozhen wrote that down too. Word for word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu’s advice came from under the transporter.

“Don’t let her mother near it.”

“I haven’t met her mother.”

“Good. Keep it that way. Whole industrial district’s heard about her mother. She had a man following Sera for two years.” He rolled out, oil on his face, and pointed a spanner. “You find that man. If he’s still at it. You find him and you explain things.”

“He stopped in 2019. Her brother-in-law spoke to him.”

Big Wu stared.

“How do you know that?”

Nothing. Haozhen turned a page.

Big Wu lay back down on the creeper. He rolled under the transporter again. From underneath, in a different voice: “Right. Course you know that.”

Mouse gave no advice at all. But that night there was a printed sheet by the kettle. Forty numbered rows, mostly empty. Seven filled in, tiny writing. Big Wu. Big Wu’s ma. Mr. Kwok. Me. Aurelia. Aurelia’s husband. Granny Shum (she won’t come but ask).

At the top: GUESTS (WHO).

He looked at it for a while. Then he folded it once and put it in the notebook, at the page that said WEDDING.

✦ ✦ ✦

The date was the problem.

Coast road, three in the morning, the harbour black on the left. Spring was meant to have arrived. Nobody had told the wind. She drove one-handed, the other hand stuffed in his coat pocket with his, because he’d taken it off the gearstick at the bridge and put it there without asking.

“October. When it’s cool. Before the rain.”

He didn’t answer.

“Hello? October?”

He was looking out at the water. His face had gone the way it went in rooms. Counting exits.

“I can’t give you a date.”

“Because of them.”

“They give me dates. A week before. Sometimes a day.” His thumb moved over her knuckles in the pocket. “If I say the fourteenth of October and they put me on a plane on the twelfth, you’re standing in a room with nine courses and a whole fish. No groom. Your mother in the car park.”

“I don’t care about the fish!”

“I do. I’ve stood at the door of eleven weddings. I’m not missing the middle of mine.”

She drove. The ring was cold against his fingers in the pocket. She could feel him turning it. Round and round. Like he was checking it was still on.

“Then we don’t set a date. We set a when.”

“A when.”

“When it’s safe. When you can sit through nine courses and nobody rings you. Whenever that is.” She glanced at him. “I don’t need a party, Hao. I need you at the end of an aisle that isn’t in a stairwell. The rest is extra.”

Hao.

Where had that come from? She hadn’t planned it. It just came out, the way the turbo came in at the top of second. By itself. With a whistle.

He turned from the window.

“Say that again.”

“No.”

“Sera.”

“Absolutely not. You’ll get a big head.”

He didn’t argue. He just kept looking at her. The whole length of the coast road. She could feel it on the side of her face like a heat lamp. At the tunnel she cracked.

“…Hao. Happy?”

He took her hand out of his pocket, kissed her knuckles, ring and all, and put it back in. Then he faced the road like nothing had happened.

Her ears were on fire till the bridge.

✦ ✦ ✦

He filled in the form on the Thursday. Five in the morning, at the table in his two rooms above the laundry, with the laundry’s cat asleep on the warm floor over the dryers.

Two pages. A crest at the top. NOTIFICATION OF CHANGE IN PERSONAL CIRCUMSTANCES.

He’d filled in eleven of these in ten years. Address, twice. Dentist. Medicals. This one took him forty minutes.

Nature of change: Engagement to be married.

Name of other party: SONG Serafina.

Occupation: Racing driver. Mechanic.

Known associations: Song family (Milan, the Peak). Sister married to CHEN Si.

He looked at that last line for a long time. Then, smaller, underneath: No relevant concerns.

Page two asked about her habits. Her movements. Any irregular activity.

He thought about Granny Shum’s folding chair. A red Lancia at the gas works. Three years, since 2019, for anyone who cared to write it down.

He wrote None known.

It was the neatest lie he’d ever put on paper. He checked the spelling of her name four times. Then he went to get the egg sandwiches from the place under the flyover. Egg for her. Not ham.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found it on the bench by the kettle.

She was still holding it when he came in with the bag.

“You’re telling them.”

He put the sandwiches down.

“The white van people. The petrol-station people.” She shook the form. “SONG Serafina. In CAPITALS. You’re telling them you’re marrying me?”

“Yes.”

“WHY?”

He took the form out of her hand. Smoothed it flat on the bench.

“Because they’ll know anyway. A month. Six. Someone sees the ring. Someone sees me at the circuit. They watch everybody.” He touched her name. “If I report it, you’re a fact. On a form, in a drawer. A fact is boring.”

“And if you don’t?”

“Then one day they find it. Then you’re a secret.” He looked up. “They look at secrets very carefully, Sera. For years.”

She read the line again. No relevant concerns.

“I don’t like it. I’d rather they didn’t know I existed.”

“So would I. But you walked across a ballroom in your sister’s dress and told me what I was.” He folded the form in three. Envelope. “You were never going to be someone who didn’t exist. This is the next best thing. It makes you boring.”

“I’m NOT boring.”

“No.” He licked the envelope. “That’s why I lied on page two.”

She opened her mouth. Shut it. Grabbed an egg sandwich instead and ate half of it in one go, furious, while he watched with his hot water like this was a perfectly normal Thursday.

Then she got her phone out. Found GUARD (LIFTS). Deleted GUARD.

He leaned over to look.

FIDANZATO (LIFTS).

“I don’t lift any more.”

“You lifted at the gas works. It stays till you’ve earned it off.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The engagement drinks were on the second Saturday in April. He planned them like an operation.

She found the run sheet later, in the notebook. One page. Arrivals, side door, shutter down. Drinks: Chinotto (Mouse), beer (Big Wu), Big Wu’s ma brandy SMALL. Mr. Kwok’s food. Toast, me, forty seconds. Ring shown. Aurelia arrives (late. She will be late). Cake. Guests leave. And at the bottom: Contingencies. 1. Big Wu cries. 2. Rain. 3. Granny Shum.

It went wrong in minute two.

Big Wu’s mother came early. She was eighty-three, the height of a fire hydrant, and she had a whole roast duck under her arm in a plastic bag.

“I’m doing the food.”

Mr. Kwok came out from behind the trestle table with his ladle.

“Over my DEAD BODY you’re doing the food.”

“That can be arranged.”

“Ma—”

“Sit down, Ah Wu.”

Big Wu sat down.

It went wrong again in minute four. Granny Shum came. Nobody had thought she would. She came in on the arm of her bored granddaughter with her folding chair and her thermos and her scanner round her neck, set the chair up in the middle of the floor and sat in it.

“Where’s the taxi?”

Haozhen came and stood in front of her. She looked him up and down. A long way up. Then she dug in her coat and held out a clementine.

“You’ll do.”

He took it like it was a medal. Serafina had to go and stand behind the transporter for a minute.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the toast, she yanked his collar straight. Hard, like a seat belt. He let her.

“Forty seconds,” she whispered. “I timed the run sheet.”

“Thirty-eight. I cut a bit.”

He stood up with his beer. Opened his mouth.

A train came.

The whole garage shook. The spanner fell in the bucket. Granny Shum’s scanner squawked. He stood there with his beer up and his mouth open and waited, very politely, for a train to finish going over his engagement.

When it had gone, everyone looked at him.

Serafina felt him go still beside her. Oh no. Oh, no no no.

“I had a speech.” He looked round. Big Wu’s mother’s duck. Mr. Kwok’s nine dishes, because Mr. Kwok had done nine anyway. Big Wu, already crying, contingency one. Mouse with her Chinotto. The postcard on the whiteboard. “It was thirty-eight seconds. I’ve forgotten it.”

Granny Shum folded her hands on her thermos.

“We’ll wait.”

“I’ve stood at the door of eleven weddings. I always wondered what happened in the middle.” He lifted the beer a little higher. “I think it’s this. To the middle.”

“To the middle.” Big Wu’s voice had gone thick. He drank. So did everybody.

She was halfway through saying “That was the worst speech I’ve ever—” when he put the beer down, took her face in both hands and kissed her.

Right there. In front of all of them. Not a peck. He tipped her head back and kissed her like the room was empty and he had all night. Her hands didn’t know where to go. They went to his shirt. She heard Big Wu’s mother start counting out loud.

“…nine… ten… eleven…”

She lost track after that. So did Big Wu’s mother, apparently, because when he finally let go, the old lady was saying “twenty-six” with great disapproval and Mr. Kwok was saying it was a terrible speech and the best one he’d heard since 1994.

Serafina stood there with her mouth wet and her brain gone.

He wiped a smear of duck sauce off the corner of her lip with his thumb. Then licked his thumb. In front of everyone.

“That,” she managed, “was not on the run sheet.”

“No.”

The side door opened. Aurelia. Gold coat, alone, because Chen Si was in Rotterdam. A box of pastries from the Milanese bakery on Harbour Road. One minute later than the run sheet said, exactly.

“What did I miss?”

Nobody could tell her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car came on the Monday.

On a flatbed, under a tarpaulin, from a salvage auction at the port. The driver backed in under the shutter, tipped it onto the concrete with a noise like a skip landing, and left fast. Before anyone could make him take it back.

They stood round it.

It had been a car once. Now it was a long, low, burnt carbon tub, black and blistered. No engine. No wheels. No glass. Something had melted across the nose and set in a frozen dribble. The tail still swept back like a shark’s.

Big Wu found his voice first.

“What is THAT.”

“A 1991 endurance prototype!” She was walking round it with her hands in her pockets and her whole face lit. “Built for the long straight at Le Mans. It was in a museum warehouse that burned down in 2009. Nobody wanted it. Nine thousand. That’s scrap price for the carbon!”

“It’s a coffin.”

“It’s a CAR.”

“It’s a coffin that used to be a car.”

Haozhen crouched by the nose. He looked at the melted bit the way she’d looked at the rivets on the fake chassis plate in October. Close. Patient.

“What are you going to do with it?”

“Make it go two hundred miles an hour.”

“Three hundred and twenty-two kilometres.”

“Miles. Everything fast sounds better in miles. Nonna said so.” She crouched next to him and put her hand flat on the burnt carbon. “When I was nine I asked her what the fastest was. She said, two hundred miles an hour, cara. That’s the top. So.” She shrugged. “I want to go to the top. Once. In something I built.”

He looked at her. A train went over. He kept looking.

Then he took out the notebook. Not the WEDDING page. A clean one.

She leaned over his arm to read it.

Two hundred.

And under it, smaller, like it was just one more thing to do this week:

Find out how.

chapters.title: Aurelia Finds Out Who Pays for the Racing Team
chapters.desc: Aurelia does the team’s books and finds sixty thousand she didn’t pay. At Da Gianni the whole restaurant hears whose salary bought Sera’s gearbox.
chapters.epigraph: “He overpaid by a third. I like him.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
Aurelia did the team’s books on the first Friday of every quarter. Middle of the night, at her bench behind the boutique, pencil behind her ear, cold coffee, Enzo’s radio playing opera to nobody.

She’d done it since December 2019. It was the only part of Serafina’s life her sister let her touch without a fight. Every tyre. Every entry fee. Every tank of fuel. She knew what Team AURELIA had spent on brake pads in the third quarter of 2021 to the cent, and she’d rung the supplier personally about it.

So she noticed the splitter.

Four thousand two hundred. From the March test, when Sera had gone into the gravel at the Needle. Aurelia had said she’d pay. She went to pay.

PAID IN FULL. The eighth of March.

Not by her.

She took the pencil out from behind her ear. Then she went back through the whole quarter, line by line, the way she’d once gone through four ledgers at a basement table in the old town.

There was more.

✦ ✦ ✦

“A gearbox.”

Da Gianni, Saturday lunch, the table by the window. Aurelia laid the first invoice on the tablecloth between the bread and the olive oil.

“Sequential. From the Germans you’ve been begging since 2021. Thirty-eight thousand. Paid direct, first of April.” Second invoice. “Brakes, both axles, eleven thousand.” Third. “A new engine in the transporter. Mr. Kwok has been lighting incense for that engine. Nine thousand four hundred.” Fourth. “And my splitter.”

Serafina had stopped with a forkful of risotto halfway to her mouth.

“…Your splitter?”

“Sixty-two thousand six hundred. One quarter. Not me. Not a sponsor.” Aurelia lined the edges up. “A company called Northgate Services. One director. No staff. No website. The address is a post box in the capital.”

“I don’t know who that is.”

“I know you don’t, darling. I saw your face at gearbox.” Aurelia picked up her wine. “So I asked Qian.”

“Chen Si’s Qian?”

“There is only one Qian. He took a day and a half and four antacids.”

She put a fifth sheet on the table.

A bank statement. A state bank in the capital. A salary account. Ten years of it fitted on one page, because it was so simple. The same deposit every month since June 2012. A second column, bigger, irregular, each line just a code. Aurelia had seen codes like that in her husband’s accounts and learned not to ask.

Going out? Almost nothing. Rent on two rooms above a laundry. A transfer every month to a mining town in the north. A dentist, once, in 2017.

Then four huge withdrawals this spring. To Northgate Services.

The balance at the bottom, after all of it, was still more than Serafina had earned in her life.

She read the name at the top.

She put her fork down.

“He did WHAT?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Da Gianni was full at Saturday lunch. Bankers. Shoppers from Harbour Road. A long table of Italian businessmen at the back toasting something. It got a lot quieter when Serafina Song stood up out of her chair.

“He paid for my GEARBOX?”

“Sit down.”

“With his SALARY?”

“Sera. The man at the next table has stopped chewing.”

“I don’t CARE about the man at the next table!” She was waving the statement. “Ten years! He doesn’t spend anything! He lives above a laundry! He hasn’t got curtains! Mouse says he uses less electricity than the cat!”

“What cat?”

“The laundry’s cat! It’s got a heated bed!” She slapped the statement on the table. “And he took sixty thousand out and gave it to a POST BOX so the post box could buy me a gearbox, and he didn’t even—”

“I know exactly how that feels.”

Serafina stopped.

Aurelia was looking at her over her glass. That look. The one from a garage in October 2019, the two of them over a folder of receipts from a bank in Luxembourg.

Oh.

Serafina sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I didn’t tell you either. For two years. Remember why?”

“Because I’d have stopped taking it.”

“And because I couldn’t go with you.” Aurelia tapped the statement. “So. A man who hasn’t spent a cent on himself in ten years spends sixty thousand on you in one spring. And says nothing.” She folded her hands. “Why?”

Serafina didn’t answer.

“I’ll tell you what I think. You tell me if I’m wrong.” Aurelia’s voice went low. “I think he isn’t sure he can stay.”

Outside, Harbour Road went by in the April sun. Trams. Shoppers. Gold letters over the door of number eighteen, two hundred metres down.

“He’s in the kind of work where people don’t always get to stay. He knows it. He’s done the sum.” Aurelia looked at her. “He wants the car to keep running whatever happens to him. That’s what I’d do. That’s what Chen Si would do. Zhao would buy you a tank.”

“I don’t WANT a tank.”

“Nobody wants a tank, Sera. That’s not what tanks are for.” Aurelia held out her hand across the table. “Now give me the left one. I’ve been looking at that ring for a week and you keep putting it in your pocket.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Out came the loupe. The little gold one Aurelia kept for clients who thought they could fool her.

She held Serafina’s hand flat on the tablecloth and bent over the ruby on its little finger. Serafina sat there with her face still red and her hand out like she was at the doctor.

“Yellow gold. Eighteen carat. Handmade, not cast. File marks inside the shank. Nineteen-thirties, probably.” Aurelia tilted the hand to the window. “Worn thin on the side toward the middle finger. She worked with her hands, whoever she was. Sewing, maybe.”

“And the stone?”

“Ruby. Old cut. Burmese, from the colour.” A pause. “It’s a very good stone, Sera.”

“Is it?”

“It’s a very good stone he overpaid for by about a third. To a man who saw him coming.” She lowered the loupe. Her face had gone soft. “He didn’t haggle. He had no idea what it was worth. He just saw it was red.”

“He said it’s the colour of my car.”

Aurelia looked at her.

Then Aurelia Chen put down the loupe and laughed out loud. The bark. The one from the balcony. In front of the bankers and the shoppers and the whole table of Italians. She had to wipe her eyes with her napkin.

“He overpaid by a third. I like him.” She pressed the napkin to her mouth. “Oh God. I like him.”

“You’ve met him ONCE. For an hour. He forgot his speech!”

“That was plenty.”

At the long table at the back, a fat man in a pink tie had seen the loupe and the ring and the laughing. He stood up with his glass.

“Auguri alla sposa!”

The whole table of Italians stood up. Glasses everywhere. Auguri! Auguri!

“I’m not a BRIDE.” Serafina was crimson. “I’m a—I’m just—”

“She’s a bride.” Aurelia raised her own glass to them, gracious as a queen. “Grazie.” Then, to her sister, not moving her lips: “Smile. You’re engaged in public now. It’s the law.”

Serafina smiled. It came out like a dog showing its teeth.

Aurelia took a breath. “I’ll resize it. For the right finger.”

“Not new. He said don’t make it new.”

“Of course not new, I’m not an animal.” She turned the hand to the light again. “I’ll open the shank at the back and put in a piece of old gold. Same period. I’ve got some. Nonna’s earrings. The last pair.” She was quiet a second. “You won’t see the join.”

“Lia…”

“What does he do?”

“Security.”

Aurelia looked at her sister for a long, long moment over the rim of her glass. She didn’t say what she thought about that.

She said, “Chen Si will want him to dinner.”

Which was worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat in Nonna outside Da Gianni with the engine off and the bank statement on the passenger seat. She typed so hard the screen complained.

Serafina: northgate services

It came back before she’d put the phone down.

FIDANZATO (LIFTS): Yes.

Serafina: YES??

Serafina: thats it?? thats all u have to say

FIDANZATO (LIFTS): You’re angry.

Serafina: im on harbour road SHOUTING at my phone

FIDANZATO (LIFTS): I can see.

She whipped round in her seat.

Tram stop. A woman with shopping. A boy on a scooter. Bankers going back to work. No grey car. No dark jacket. Where was he? Up a building? In a shop? How did he SEE?

Serafina: WHERE ARE U

FIDANZATO (LIFTS): Tonight. Garage.

Serafina: u better

Serafina: and bring ur stupid notebook
