She threw the phone on the bank statement and pulled out into the traffic so fast a taxi hooted. She checked every mirror the whole way home. Nothing. Not once.

That was the worst part. He was better at it than her mirrors.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in the middle of the night, through the side door.

She was waiting. Sitting on Gilded’s bonnet under the hanging lamp with five pieces of paper laid out on the matte black paint beside her. Splitter. Gearbox. Brakes. Transporter. Bank statement.

He stopped.

He looked at the row of paper. Then at her face. She watched him read it all the way to the end. He didn’t try to get out of it. Not even a little.

“Your sister.”

“My sister. And Qian, with four antacids.”

He shut the door. Stood with his back to it.

“You needed a gearbox.”

“I’ve needed a gearbox since 2021!”

“The old one was going. Big Wu said so in January. You’d have lost third at the first race and gone into the wall at the long right on lap two.” Flat. Like a weather report. “I heard it at the track day. The noise in third.”

“And the splitter? You were GONE in March. No phone. You said.”

“There was a computer in a hotel.” He didn’t blink. “The series puts the timing up live. Red flag, car seven, the Needle. Then nothing for nine minutes.”

She stared at him.

“You watched my test. From wherever you were.”

“Every session.” He looked at the bank statement. “I couldn’t ring. I could pay for the splitter.”

Nine minutes. He’d sat at some hotel computer for nine minutes not knowing if she was alive. And then he’d gone and paid a bill.

Her throat did something horrible.

“With your salary, Haozhen.”

“I never spent it. I didn’t want anything. Ten years.” A pause. “Then I did. And it was a gearbox, and I could get it. It’s the first thing I’ve bought in ten years that wasn’t on a form.”

She slid off the bonnet. Walked over. Stood right in front of him.

“Aurelia thinks you’re not sure you can stay.”

A train went over. The garage shook round them. He waited for it.

“Your sister pays because she can’t come with you. Me…” He looked at the paper on the bonnet. “I might not get to stay. That’s all it is.” His voice didn’t change. “If one day I don’t come back from a stairwell, you’ll still have third gear at the long right. I didn’t tell you because you’d ask why. Then I’d have to say it. Like this.”

She hit him.

Flat hand, on the chest. Once. Again. Then she grabbed his jacket in both fists and put her forehead on his collarbone.

“You don’t get to buy me a gearbox in case you DIE. That’s not a thing! You don’t get to do that!”

“All right.”

“You come back from every stairwell. That’s the deal. That’s the whole deal.”

“All right.” His hand was on the back of her head. “Every stairwell.”

“And next time you pay for something, put your NAME on it. Like Aurelia. Gold on the bonnet, where everybody can see.”

He went still under her hands.

“I can’t put my name on a car, Sera.”

She lifted her head. She knew. She’d known before she said it. A form in an envelope. No relevant concerns. A man who walked round cameras.

“No. I know you can’t.”

She pulled him down by the jacket and kissed him. Angry. Teeth. She wanted it to hurt a bit. He let it, for about three seconds. Then he turned it slow. Slow and hard, his back against the door, his hand spread on her skull, until she forgot she was angry and just held on.

When he lifted his head, he didn’t let go.

He reached past her to the whiteboard ledge and picked up her red marker. Took her left hand. Turned it over.

On the inside of her wrist, under the ring, in small square letters, he wrote QIN H.

Same as the caterer’s clipboard. Same as the postcard.

“Not on the car,” he said. “On you. If you’ll have it. As soon as they let me.”

She looked at her wrist. She didn’t trust her mouth.

She didn’t wash it for three days. On the second, Big Wu caught her wrist in the coffee queue.

“What’s that?”

“Part number.”

“For what part?”

“A big one. It’s on order.” She took her wrist back. “Go away, Wu.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Big Wu found something on Gilded.

Driver’s door, low down, just above the sill. Where you’d only see it crouching to check the tyres. A sticker the size of a thumbnail, cut from grey vinyl with a craft knife. Somebody had sat up late at the end of the bench with Mouse’s magnifying lamp to do it.

The shape of a plain estate car. The kind taxi firms bought by the dozen.

Big Wu crouched and looked at it for ages.

Then he went and got the good clear lacquer and gave it three coats. So it would stay on through anything.

chapters.title: Two Professionals at One Table
chapters.desc: Dinner on the forty-fourth floor. Two men go for the same chair, the ruby moves to the right finger, and Chen Si takes Haozhen out on the balcony.
chapters.epigraph: “Mr. Qin. Welcome. You don’t exist.” — Qian
chapters.content:
“Chen Si will sit facing the door. So will you. You’ll both go for the same chair, and one of you will have to sit with his back to the room. And I want to WATCH.”

The lift went up the Coastal High-Rise like it was holding its breath. Forty-four floors of little white numbers.

“I won’t fight him for a chair.”

“You will. You won’t even know you’re doing it.”

He was in the forgettable suit. White shirt. No tie. He’d shaved twice. She’d heard the razor go, and then go again, and she hadn’t said a word, because she was a good person. He was holding a bottle of wine he’d chosen after forty minutes and a conversation with the shop owner on Harbour Road that she’d watched through the window and was still laughing about.

At floor twenty he reached over and did up the top button of her shirt.

“What are you doing?”

“It’s your sister’s house.”

She undid it.

He did it up again. Very calmly. Like adjusting a mirror.

“Haozhen. I will bite you.”

“After dinner.”

Her ears went hot. She left the button. Traitor ears.

“I’ve read about him,” he said, to the numbers. “There’s a file on everybody who matters in this city. His is very thick and says very little. That’s how you know someone’s good.”

“And yours?”

“Mine’s thin. And says nothing at all.”

The doors opened on a corridor with one door at the end. In it, holding it open, stood a small tired man in glasses with a packet of antacids in his top pocket. He looked at Haozhen for three full seconds without blinking.

“Mr. Qin. Welcome. You don’t exist.”

“Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat facing the door.

So did Chen Si.

Same moment, opposite ends of the long table, the whole harbour lit up behind the glass. Both of them pulled out the one chair that could see the corridor door, the kitchen door, and both of those in the window. Both of them stopped with their hands on the chair backs. They looked at each other down the table.

At the counter, Aurelia put down her wine.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake.”

Serafina had to bite her lip so hard it hurt. Best. Night. Ever.

It lasted maybe a second and a half. Then Chen Si gave a small nod, like a man conceding a point he’d expected to lose, and walked round to the side and sat with his back to the harbour. Haozhen stayed where he was. He didn’t look like he’d won. He looked faintly apologetic.

“Thank you.”

“You’re a guest. And she’d have made us flip a coin.” Chen Si turned the wine label to the light. “This is good. The man on Harbour Road doesn’t sell this one to people he doesn’t like.”

“He asked me a lot of questions. I answered them.”

Chen Si looked at him across the table. Serafina had seen that look once before, at a circuit in December 2019. Total, quiet attention. Like he was filing something.

“I’ll open it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si cooked. Braised beef with star anise and dried tangerine peel, going since the afternoon. Greens with garlic. Lotus root soup. Rice.

No fish.

“I was told.” He set the beef down. “In red ink. On a sheet of my own paper. No fish. Underlined.”

“She hates fish.” Aurelia, pouring.

“I’ve noticed.”

Serafina turned in her chair.

“You’ve never seen me not eat fish.”

“The reunion dinner. Mr. Kwok made a whole one. You put rice over your piece so he wouldn’t see. Then you gave it to Big Wu’s mother when she wasn’t looking.” He picked up his chopsticks. “She was looking. She ate it anyway.”

Aurelia set down the bottle. She looked at her sister’s fiancé properly for the first time all evening.

“How long have you been watching my sister?”

“Since the twenty-second of October.” He took some greens. “Nine twenty-two.”

Nobody said anything. The harbour went on glittering.

Then Aurelia laughed. The bark.

“Oh, he’s as bad as you.”

“Worse.” Chen Si served the beef. “I didn’t know the minute.”

Aurelia wasn’t finished.

“And your mother? Does she know about my sister?”

“Not yet. I ring her on Sundays.”

“And?”

“Four minutes. Usually.”

“Four minutes!” Aurelia looked at Serafina. “You can’t explain Sera in four minutes. I’ve had twenty-five years. I’m not done.”

“No.” He looked at his bowl. “I’ll need longer.”

Under the table, Serafina found Haozhen’s ankle with her boot and kicked it. Not hard. Then she left her boot there.

He put the best piece of beef in her bowl without looking. Then the second best.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the beef, Aurelia gave back the ring.

A plain cream box from the boutique, AURELIA in gold on the lid. She put it on the table between the soup bowls. For once in her life, she said nothing at all.

Serafina opened it.

The ruby in its old claws. Brake-light red. The band looked exactly the same. She turned it to the harbour light. Where was the join? She looked again. She couldn’t find it.

“It’s there. Inside, at the back. Four millimetres.” Aurelia was looking at her own hands. “Nonna’s. The last of the earrings. The pair she wore to Geneva.”

Serafina couldn’t say anything. Her mouth wouldn’t work.

So she held it out. On her open palm, across the corner of the table, to the man beside her.

He looked at it. Then at her.

He took it. He took her left hand, and slid the ring onto her ring finger. Over the knuckle this time. All the way. It stopped where it should, and sat there like it had never been anywhere else.

“Oh no… Mouse is going to be devastated.” Her voice came out wobbly. “She had a whole bit about my little finger.”

“She’ll find a new bit.”

He didn’t give the hand back. He kept it, under the edge of the table, on his knee, his thumb going back and forth over the ruby. He ate the rest of dinner left-handed. Badly. He didn’t seem to care.

Across the table, Aurelia had picked up her wine and was staring out at the harbour very, very hard.

“Lia—”

“Don’t. Don’t say ANYTHING. If you say anything I’ll cry on my own tablecloth and Chen Si will never let me forget it.”

“I won’t.” Chen Si didn’t look up. “I’ll write it in the margin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner Chen Si picked up the wine and two glasses and went to the long glass door. He looked back once. Haozhen got up and followed him out.

The sisters stayed on the grey sofa with their feet tucked under them. Neither pretended not to watch.

“Look at them.” Serafina had her nose almost on the glass. “Same. Exactly the same. Backs to the wall. Facing the door.”

“There’s no door. It’s a balcony. On the forty-fourth floor.”

“They’re facing where a door WOULD be.”

Aurelia looked. Then she put her face in a cushion.

“Oh God. There’s two of them.”

“I know!”

“I married one and you’re marrying the other!” Aurelia came up out of the cushion. Her eyes went to the ring. Then her voice dropped. “Sera. Mamma will find out.”

Serafina stopped grinning.

“She’s got someone in the series office. She always has. The minute there’s a photo of that ring…”

“So she finds out.”

“So when she does, you ring me first. Before you answer her. Before you do anything stupid with a car.” Aurelia took her hand. The ringed one. “Promise.”

What was the worst Mamma could do? Cut her off? Done. Not speak to her? Seven years. Done.

Somehow that didn’t help at all.

“…Promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The balcony went round the corner of the building. Forty-four floors down, the harbour lay black and glittering. The wind came up off the water.

Chen Si poured two glasses and held one out. Haozhen took it and didn’t drink. Chen Si noticed. He didn’t drink his either.

“The Eleventh.”

Said pleasantly. To the view.

Haozhen didn’t move.

“I can’t tell you that.”

“You just did. By how long you took.” Chen Si turned the glass in his fingers. “I’ve met three of you in twelve years. A customs officer at a port in 2014. A man at a funeral. A man at a hotel breakfast in the capital, holding a teapot.”

“A teapot.”

“A teapot.” He looked at the water. “You all stand the same. Weight on the back foot. Hands where people can see them. Looking just past whoever’s talking.”

“And?”

“The teapot one was very good.” A pause. “You’re better.”

“Thank you.”

“It wasn’t a compliment. It was a description.” Chen Si was quiet a moment. “I read about your kind before I met one. At sixteen. In a cell. They had a file on my father. Then they had one on me. Sixteen, and somebody had decided I was worth a file.”

“I know. I’ve read it.”

Chen Si turned his head.

It wasn’t a long look. But it went right through Haozhen, the way his own went through people. He let it. He didn’t put anything in its way.

“Block C.”

“The riot. The bed slat. The drain.” Haozhen looked at the wine. “Three pages. You and another boy went into the drain in the snow and came out the other side. It doesn’t say how. It doesn’t say much about the other boy. A surname. Wang.” He paused. “Nobody ever found a Wang.”

“No. Nobody would have.” Chen Si looked down at the harbour. “It was the first name we could think of. In the snow.”

Behind the glass, Serafina said something and Aurelia laughed and clapped a hand over her mouth.

“Does she know?”

“Yes.”

“All of it?”

He took his time.

“No. She knows what I am. She guessed. She laid it out on her workbench in January with car parts, in order, and I told her she was right.” He turned the glass once. “She doesn’t know the number. I told her to ask again in a year.”

“And when she asks?”

“I’ll tell her. Names. Dates. What they were wearing.”

Chen Si nodded slowly.

“In my house there’s a contract. Eleven pages. My wife wrote it in red ink. Clause three: neither of us lies to the other. About anything.”

“Anything.”

“It’s very inconvenient.” He looked at Haozhen. “And there’s a sentence for when the truth is something we can’t say yet. I can’t tell you that yet. You say it. The other one waits. Then one day you can, and you do.” A pause. “It saves furniture.”

“She has a rule. Rule one. It’s the same.”

“Of course it is. They had the same grandmother.”

He took a card from his inside pocket. Cream. Heavy. A phone number in black ink. Nothing else.

“If you ever need a door.” He held it out. “Not a car. She’ll be the car. A door.”

Haozhen took it. Looked at it. Put it in his inside pocket, against his chest, by the notebook.

“And if anything ever comes to her through you.” Same voice. Same view. “Anything. From anyone in the capital. I will know before you do. And I won’t be polite.”

“Good.”

Chen Si glanced at him.

“Good,” said Haozhen again. “I’d rather there were two of us.”

Something happened at the corner of Chen Si’s mouth. Gone almost before it came.

Then they both drank. Same moment. Like a signal nobody else could see.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He’s very good.”

Going down. Serafina was leaning on the mirrored wall with her left hand up in front of her face, turning it so the ruby caught the light. She’d been doing it since the front door. Ring finger. RING finger. She couldn’t stop.

“At what?”

“Everything I’m good at.”

“Is that a problem?”

“No. It’s a relief.” He was watching her in the mirror. The ring. Her face. “He’d have found me anyway. Now he knows I’m not hiding.”

“What did he say to you out there? You were gone ages. Aurelia had to physically hold me on the sofa.”

“He gave me a phone number.”

“And?”

“And he said if anything happens to you because of me, he’ll know before I do.”

She stopped turning the ring.

“That’s a THREAT!”

“Yes.” He sounded pleased. “It was a good one.”

Thirty. Twenty-nine.

He didn’t wait for twenty-eight. He crossed the lift in one step, caught her left hand, ring and all, and pinned it flat to the mirror beside her head. He kissed her like he’d sat through four courses and a balcony waiting for exactly this and was done waiting.

She made a noise into his mouth. The ruby was cold under his palm. His other hand was on her waist, under her jacket, pulling her off the wall into him. She got her free hand in his hair and hung on.

Twenty. Fifteen. The floor where the lift always lurched. It lurched. Her teeth clicked his. She laughed into his mouth. He didn’t stop. He kissed her through the laugh and out the other side of it, until she forgot which floor they were on, and which way was up, and what her own name was.

At some point, with his mouth on her jaw, he undid her top button himself.

“You said—”

“Dinner’s over.”

The doors opened on the lobby.

Qian was standing there with his coat on and his car keys in his hand.

He looked at them for three seconds without blinking. Serafina, flattened against the mirror, with her shirt open and her hair wrecked. Haozhen, not moving his hand off the ring at all.

Qian took out the antacids. Took two. Walked past them into the lift and pressed forty-four.

“Congratulations, Miss Song.” The doors began to close. “He still doesn’t exist.”

chapters.title: Director Duan Sends Congratulations
chapters.desc: His director has read the form. She brings congratulations, a silver pen with a 7 on it, and a folder for Lisbon. Serafina uses the pen to enter a hill climb.
chapters.epigraph: “We look after our families. It’s in the training.” — Director Duan Qiuyan
chapters.content:
The Pavilion of Clear Springs had no spring, and nothing in it was clear. Second floor, old town, up a wooden stair from a lane that smelled of dried fish. Twelve tables. A man with a copper kettle who never looked at anybody’s face.

She was at the back by the window. She was always at the back.

Director Duan Qiuyan. Fifty-five. Neat grey bob, reading glasses on a chain, a grey cardigan darned at one elbow in a slightly different grey. Knitting. Red wool on two bamboo needles. The same scarf she’d had on her lap in June 2012, the day she walked into the commandant’s office at the academy and asked for the eighteen-year-old who never hesitated.

It was about two metres long now. Nobody had ever seen it finished.

“Sit. I’ve ordered for you. Hot water.” She didn’t look up. “You still don’t drink tea.”

He sat. She’d left him the chair that saw the door in the window. She always did.

“Director.”

“Haozhen.” Click. Click. “Congratulations.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took his form out of a canvas shopping bag. It had been sitting between a bag of oranges and the spare wool. She smoothed it flat between the teacups.

“No relevant concerns.” She looked at him over her glasses. “You wrote that.”

“Yes.”

“I nearly had it framed.” The needles went on. “Ten years of your forms. Change of address, twice. Dentist, once. Annual medical, sleeping well, every single year.”

“I sleep well.”

“It’s a lie, Haozhen. The doctor knows it’s a lie. He writes it down anyway, because you’re so convincing.” She tapped the form with a needle. “Then this. I read it on the train. A woman across the aisle asked if I’d had good news.”

He said nothing.

“I’m pleased for you. Truly.” Click. “You were the youngest I ever took. You never had anything.”

He waited.

“You’d sit outside a door for a week. Then come back and fill in the form. Never once complained.” Click. “I used to think, one day that boy will find something. And then I’ll have to decide what to do about it.”

“And have you?”

“Decided?” She looked up. Kind face. Grandmother’s face. “Of course. Last night. On the train.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew everything.

He’d known she would. It still went into him like cold water down a collar.

She didn’t list it. She was too good to list it. She dropped it between rows, while the kettle man came and filled the cups and went away.

“Team AURELIA. Second in the series last year, on a very small budget. A new gearbox this spring. German.”

He didn’t move.

“Such a nice gearbox.” A row. “I hear she still goes to the industrial district on Saturdays. To an old lady with a folding chair. They changed the law on that, didn’t they? 2019. Three years.” A row. “And you had dinner on the forty-fourth floor. With Chen Si. Braised beef. You sat facing the door, and he let you.”

He held his cup and didn’t drink.

Who had been in the building? The doorman? Qian? No. Not Qian. A cleaner, then. A delivery. Somebody he hadn’t looked at twice. He would look now.

“Chen Si has a very thick file.”

“I know.”

“And so little in it. I’ve always rather admired him.” She turned the work and started back the other way. “His father had a very unpleasant time. A vice-minister called Fu, I believe. Who is going to have a very unpleasant summer.” She smiled at the wool. “Things come round.”

“Director—”

“Oh, don’t look like that. It isn’t us. It’s other people. We just read about it first.”

“Then why tell me?”

“Because you’re family, dear.” Click. Click. “My point is only that your fiancée’s family is extremely interesting. Her sister’s married to a man who sits on the docks like a spider. Her parents are about to lose everything they own. And she races against the law on Saturday nights.” Over the glasses again. “No relevant concerns.”

“She’s a mechanic.”

“She’s a lovely girl. I’ve seen the photographs. Such a loud laugh.”

She put the knitting down.

First time all afternoon. Her hands went still in her lap. She looked at him properly.

“I’m not threatening her, Haozhen. I want to be clear. I don’t threaten people. You know that.” Gentle as milk. “We look after our families. It’s in the training.”

He looked back at her. Polite. Empty. The east-service-door face.

Behind it, he was thinking very clearly. She lived on the ninth floor of a building by the north station. She took the early train from the north station on weekdays. She had a sister in the south with a dog called Bao and a bad hip. He’d known all that for six years and never once needed it.

He filed it somewhere closer to the front.

Then he picked up the hot water and drank.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end, she gave him a box.

Red lacquer, the size of a pencil case, a gold clasp. Out of the canvas bag from between the oranges.

“For the wedding list. When you have one. She’ll want to write thank-you notes. Brides always do.”

He opened it.

A fountain pen on red silk. Silver. Heavy. The kind that lived in glass cases in the old shops on Harbour Road. On the barrel, under the clip, engraved very small and neat, a single number.

7.

The white 7 on the side of a matte black car with a gold name on the bonnet.

He looked at it for a while.

“Thank you, Director.”

“You’re welcome.” She picked the knitting back up. “Have you a date?”

“Not yet.”

“No.” Click. “I wouldn’t think so. Not yet.” Click. “Now. Lisbon.”

A grey folder slid across under the form. Thin. He didn’t open it.

“June. Mid-month. Four weeks, perhaps five. A man there took something of ours in 2021. He’s been living very happily by the sea ever since. Upstairs would like it back.” Click. “And him. You’ll have Tianyi. He’s been asking for you. He says nobody else lets him have the window seat.”

He looked at the folder.

“What did he take?”

The needles stopped.

Half a second. A row left hanging, the red wool lying still over the bamboo. Eleven years, and he had never once asked her what anyone had taken. He took folders. He read them. He went.

She looked at him over her glasses. Not angry. Careful. Like a woman watching a dog she’d raised from a puppy look at the door for the first time.

“Ledgers.”

The needles started again.

“You never used to ask,” said the Director, to the scarf.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t bring the pen into the garage. Rule two. It went in the grey car’s glovebox, where the ring had been.

He came in through the side door late. Big Wu and Mr. Kwok had gone home. Mouse was a shape at the end of the bench in the light of her screens. Serafina was on the floor by Gilded with a wheel off and a brake caliper in her lap, fighting a piston that wouldn’t go back.

She looked up. She saw his face.

“Rule one. What is it?”

He crouched on the concrete in front of her. He took the caliper out of her lap, seated the piston with his thumbs in one push, and gave it back. Then he took her left hand. Oily. Ring on the right finger now.

“My director sends her congratulations.”

“…That’s nice?”

“No. It isn’t.”

He told her. All of it, in order, word for word, because he remembered everything and because it was rule one. The form on the table. The gearbox. Granny Shum’s on Saturdays, three years. The braised beef and the chair. A vice-minister’s unpleasant summer. A loud laugh in a photograph.

“She knows about Granny Shum’s?”

“Yes.”

“She knows about the BEEF?”

“She knows which chair.”

“Who told her? Qian? I’ll kill Qian—”

“Not Qian.” He’d already been through it, on the stairs of the tea house. “Somebody we didn’t look at.”

He watched her face go puzzled. Then white. Then something else. Flat and cold and furious.

Oh. There it was. Her mother’s face. He’d only ever heard about it.

“Show me the pen.”

“It’s in the car.”

“Rule two. I know. Go and get it.”

He got it.

She held it under the work lamp. She found the 7 in about one second. She’d painted that number on cars forty times.

“That’s a threat.”

“Yes.”

“She said she doesn’t make threats!”

“She doesn’t. She gives presents.”

At the end of the bench, without a sound, Mouse took her headphones off.

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while Serafina sat on the floor with a silver pen in one hand and a brake caliper in the other and said nothing at all.

A train went over. The building shook.

Was she going to cry? Throw the pen? Throw him? He knelt in front of her and waited. Since October he had never once known what she would do next. He’d stopped trying to guess. It was better not knowing.

She got up.

She went to the pile of team paperwork by the kettle and dug through it, swearing in Cantonese. Out came a form. Three pages, the series logo, a box for a signature at the bottom.

Baizhang Pass Hill Climb. Sunday 18 June. Twelve point four kilometres up a mountain in the north of the province. A hundred and fifty-six corners. She’d been putting it off for a month because Big Wu said it was a waste of tyres.

She unscrewed the cap of the silver pen.

“Sera. What are you doing?”

“She’s watching. She SAID so. She’s got photographs. She knows I’ve got a loud laugh.” She smoothed the form flat under the lamp. “So she can watch me do this.”

She signed it. Serafina Song. Big, messy, fast, right across the box and out the other side. The S went off the paper onto the bench.

She capped the pen. Calmly. She handed it back to him.

“Send that to your director. With a thank-you note.”

“Sera…”

“Tell her I’ve used her present.” Her chin came up. “Tell her I’m racing up a mountain on the eighteenth, number seven, and she’s very welcome to watch. Tell her I’ll wave!”

He stood at the bench looking at the signature going off the edge.

Then he started to laugh.

Not the glovebox laugh. Lower. Darker. A lot of fear in it, and a lot of something else. He put his hand over his eyes. When he took it away his eyes were wet.

“You’re going to get us both killed.”

“Probably. Not this year.” She took his face in her oily hands. Black thumbprints on his cheekbones. “When’s the plane?”

He went still.

“How did you know?”

“You came in and didn’t pick up your mug. You ALWAYS pick up your mug. You only don’t when you’re going.”

He looked at her. She looked back. She didn’t blink first. She never did.

“The twelfth. Of June. Early.”

“Then I’ll drive you. Five in the morning. In Nonna.” She kissed him once, hard, with the director’s pen in his pocket between them. “And you’ll be back to watch me win.”

“I don’t know if I’ll be back.”

“Then you’ll watch from wherever you are. Like her.”

She let go. He didn’t.

He caught her wrist and pulled, and she went down onto the concrete with him, half in his lap, and he kissed her like a man holding on to something in a strong wind. Not careful. Not slow. His fist was in the back of her vest. A woman with a red scarf had photographs of her. He didn’t say so. No need. She could feel it in how long it took him to make himself let go.

When he did, his forehead stayed on hers.

“She said I’ve got a loud laugh.” It came out small. She hated that.

“You have.”

“Is that bad?”

“No.” He breathed her in. “It’s how I find you in a paddock. Every time. Before I can see you.”

She laughed. Loud. On purpose. Right in his face, until he cracked and laughed too.

“Five o’clock,” she said. “Don’t you dare get a taxi.”

At the end of the bench, Mouse put her headphones back on.

But first she reached over and took the entry form off the bench. The one with the signature going off the edge. She scanned it, both sides, at the highest resolution the scanner would do, and saved it in a folder on her desktop that had no name.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she wrote the thank-you note herself. On team letterhead. At the bench, with the silver pen, tongue between her teeth.

Big Wu read it over her shoulder.

“You can’t send that to the GOVERNMENT.”

“It’s polite!”

“Dear Director. Thank you for the pen. It writes very fast.” He jabbed a finger. “Very fast is underlined, Sera. Three times!”

“Because it does.”

Mr. Kwok took the page off her, read it, and corrected two of her characters with a biro. He handed it back.

“Now it’s rude in the right words.”

She signed it. S. Song. (Loud laugh.) Then she handed it to Haozhen with the entry form, both folded together.

He read it. All of it. Twice. His face did nothing at all.

Then he put it in an envelope and licked it shut.

“Will she even read it?”

“She’ll keep it.”

“How do you know?”

He put the envelope in his inside pocket. Left side. With the folder about Lisbon.

“She keeps everything.”

chapters.title: Five A.M., Departures
chapters.desc: The last night before Lisbon, then the airport at five in the morning. She gives him her grandmother’s tyre gauge, and he says it through the car window.
chapters.epigraph: “You have to bring it back. It’s the only one that reads true. I’ll need it for the hill climb.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
He didn’t sleep the night before. Neither did she. They didn’t pretend.

Sunday, and hot. The first proper hot night of the summer. The loft held the day’s heat like an oven, so she shoved the window open onto the railway as far as it would go. Hot iron. Diesel. The jasmine that grew wild on the fence by the tracks.

He’d packed already. One black bag by the top of the stairs. She’d watched him do it, sitting cross-legged on the mattress. Four shirts, folded flat and square like envelopes. Trousers. Washbag. A book he didn’t read.

Six minutes. She’d timed him.

“That’s it?”

“They give you the rest.”

“What rest?”

“Like what?”

“Sera.”

“Socks? Do they give you SOCKS? A toothbrush? A whole other man?”

He zipped the bag. Which was an answer.

Now they lay with the sheet kicked off and the train light sliding orange across the ceiling. He was on his back with an arm under his head. She was on her side with her hand flat on his chest, over the white scar under his collarbone. His heart went slow. Even. Annoying.

“Talk to me.”

“About what?”

“Anything you’re allowed. I want your voice.” Her hand moved on his chest. “For however long.”

“I’m not allowed much.”

“Then the stuff from before. Before them.”

He was quiet so long she thought he wouldn’t.

Then it came out of him in bits. Like rust off a bolt. The mining town. Two streets. Coal dust on everything, on the washing, on the windowsills, in the creases of his father’s knuckles where it never washed out. The winding gear at the pithead. A groan and a clank, every four minutes, day and night.

“Every four minutes?”

“You stop hearing it. Then it’s gone and you hear nothing else.” He looked at the ceiling. “When I went to the academy, I couldn’t sleep for a month. It was too quiet.”

She went very still.

“That’s why you like the trains.”

He turned his head on the pillow.

“Something big goes over every eleven minutes. The building shakes.” She was grinning in the dark. She couldn’t help it. “You sleep through the trains. You don’t sleep anywhere else.”

“I sleep in your car.”

“My car makes a noise too, genius.”

He looked at her in the orange light. Then he touched her cheekbone with two fingers. Light. Checking she was there.

“What else have you noticed about me that I don’t know?”

“Loads.” She caught his fingers and bit one. “One a day when you get back. It’ll take years.”

“Years.”

“Decades. You’re very badly made. It’s going to need a lot of work.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, he stopped talking.

He pulled her on top of him by the hips and kissed her like he was already late. Fast. Hungry. She put her hand flat on his chest and pushed him back down into the mattress.

“No.”

He stopped dead.

“Not fast. Not tonight.” She was breathing hard already. “I want to remember it. Every bit. So shut up and let me.”

He let her.

Everything between them had been fast. The coast road. The gas works. The gearstick. Tonight she went slow on purpose, and it nearly killed both of them. She kissed him the way he kissed her. Thorough. Exact. His mouth. His jaw. The notch at the end of his eyebrow, which made him laugh, and then not laugh. Down his left arm to the long pink line. All fourteen stitches, one at a time, while a train went over and the whole loft shook.

“Sera.”

“Thirteen. Fourteen.” She looked up at him. “I counted.”

His hands were on her hips. Gripping. His eyes were shut and his breathing was coming apart at the edges. She loved that. She could have done it for an hour. She nearly did.

“You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Yes.” Back at him. His own word. “Be quiet. I’m learning it.”

He made a sound that was half a laugh and half something much worse. Then he flipped her over in one move. His hand was already behind her head so she wouldn’t hit the wall. When had he put it there? He’d planned that. Of course he’d planned that.

He held himself over her in the orange light and just looked. Like he was learning her face by heart for wherever he was going. She couldn’t stand it.

“Hao—”

He kissed it out of her mouth.

It was hot. Sweat on his back under her palms. The sheet somewhere on the floor. His mouth at her throat, her ear, saying her name in that low wrecked voice like he was checking it still worked. She told him what she wanted, out loud, in two languages. He did all of it. He did it until she couldn’t remember either language. Then he did it slower.

“Look at me.” Against her mouth. “Stay with me. Don’t shut your eyes.”

“I’m not going anywhere. You’re the one going.”

His whole body flinched. Then he held on to her so hard she couldn’t breathe. She didn’t want to. The next train went over. She never heard it.

Afterwards he lay with his face in her hair. His heart under her palm was going fast and not slowing down.

“Sera?”

Like a question.

“I’m here.”

“I know.” His arm tightened round her. “I know you are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The alarm went before five. They didn’t need it. She’d been lying on his chest for an hour listening to him not sleep.

He got dressed in the dark. Envelope shirt. Grey trousers. The forgettable jacket. He went down the stairs. She heard him at the kettle. She heard him pick up the plain mug. Hold it. Put it down.

She lay there one more second with her fists shut.

Then she got up. Dressed. Went down. Sat on the bottom stair to do her boots.

He knelt in front of her and took the laces out of her hands.

“I can do my own boots.”

He tied them. Double knots. Both. Then he tugged each one once, to check, like a man checking a harness.

She looked down at the top of his head. Her eyes stung. Stupid boots.

“That’s my thing,” she said. “The double knots.”

“I know. I’ve watched you do it every morning since October.”

She went and started Nonna before she could do anything stupid.

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was forty minutes out, over the long bridge to the island. Five in the morning on a Monday, the road was empty. She drove with the windows down and the sky going from black to dirty purple over the sea. The bridge lights went over them one by one.

Not gently. Not fast either. She drove the way she did when she was thinking. Right on the limit. Smooth as glass.

He didn’t sleep. Halfway across the bridge he checked the wing mirror. Again four seconds later. Again.

“Stop it.”

“There’s a lorry.”

“It’s a FISH lorry. It’s five in the morning. There’s me, and a fish lorry, and the sea.” She didn’t look away from the road. “You’ve got thirty minutes of me left. Don’t you dare spend them on a lorry.”

“What do I look at, then?”

“Me. Obviously.”

“You’re driving.”

“I’m extremely good to look at when I’m driving. Ask anyone.”

He turned his head and looked at her instead. For the rest of the bridge. She could feel it on the side of her face like sun.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the turn-off for departures, she reached into the door pocket and held something out. Without looking.

“Here.”

A tyre gauge. Not the cheap black petrol-station one from his glovebox. Brass, round, the size of a pocket watch, with a scratched glass and a needle that had been bent once and straightened. Initials scratched on the back with a nail. S.S. And under it, older, smaller: A.C.

“It was Nonna’s. For her Alfa.” She swallowed. “She gave it to me when I was twelve. She said never trust a tyre gauge from a petrol station.”

He turned it over in his fingers.

“Sera. I can’t take this.”

“You have to bring it back. That’s the point. It’s the only one that reads true. I’ll need it for the hill climb.” She glanced at him. “So bring it back. Before the eighteenth, if you can. After, if you can’t. But you bring it BACK.”

He looked at it a long time. The bent needle. The two sets of initials.

Then he put it in his inside pocket. Left side. Against his chest, with Chen Si’s card and the black notebook.

“I’ll bring it back.”

“Promise on something.”

“On what?”

“I don’t know! Your notebook.”

He put his hand flat over the pocket.

“On the notebook.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Departures was a concrete lane under a concrete roof. Signs every twenty metres: NO WAITING. A few taxis. A coach. A traffic warden in a yellow vest, about twenty-two, who’d clearly been looking forward to his whistle all night.

She pulled in. She didn’t turn the engine off.

He got out. Bag on his shoulder. He shut the door and bent down to the open window.

She wasn’t going to cry. She’d told herself in the loft, and on the bridge, and at the turn-off. Hands on the wheel. Chin up.

“Go on, then. You’ll miss it.”

He didn’t go.

He stood bent at her window with one hand on the roof, close, the purple light coming in under the canopy. She watched him decide something. It went across his face like the smile had in the paddock in December. Fast. Total.

“I love you.”

Just like that. Not careful. Not testing it, the way he’d said I slept, like he wasn’t sure he was allowed. Straight. Through the window of a red Lancia, under a sign that said NO WAITING, like telling her the time.

She opened her mouth—

The whistle went. Long. Loud. Right behind him.

“NO WAITING! Sir! That means YOU, sir! Move it!”

Haozhen straightened up and turned and looked at the warden.

That was all. He looked at him.

The warden took one step back. His arm came down. The whistle came out of his mouth on its own.

Haozhen bent to the window one more time. Looked at her. Then he stepped away and walked to the sliding doors with his bag on his shoulder. Not fast. Not looking back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was out of the car.

When had that happened? She was standing in the road. Door open. Engine running. The warden was blowing his whistle again, weakly. Taxi drivers staring. A family with a luggage trolley stopped dead.

“QIN HAOZHEN!”

He stopped at the doors. Ten metres. He turned round.

She had a voice for pit walls and street races and a restaurant full of bankers. She used all of it.

“I LOVE YOU! YOU IDIOT! YOU SAID IT THROUGH A WINDOW! YOU COULDN’T WAIT TILL I’D PARKED?”

The family with the trolley turned round to watch.

“FIDANZATO! BRING BACK MY GAUGE!”

The warden had his whistle halfway to his mouth and had forgotten it was there. He looked from her to the man at the doors.

“Is that your wife?”

“Fiancée.”

And Qin Haozhen, a man whose eyes slid off cameras, who had stood unseen at the doors of eleven weddings in six countries, stood in front of the sliding doors at departures in full view of everybody and smiled at her. The real one. All the way across his face. In front of strangers.

He put his hand flat on his chest. Left side. Over the gauge.

Then he went through the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry till the middle of the bridge.

Then she cried so hard she had to pull into the emergency lane and put the hazards on. She sat with her forehead on the wheel while the fish lorries went past and rocked the car. Twice in the middle of it she laughed out loud, because of the warden’s face.

What was she supposed to do now? Go home? Make coffee? Change a tyre like a normal person?

When she got back under the railway bridge, Mr. Kwok was already there.

Mr. Kwok was never there before nine. He was on the stool by the kettle in his cardigan, with a bag from the place under the flyover beside him. When she came in under the shutter with her face all swollen, he didn’t say a word. He held out a sandwich.

“Mr. Kwok… why are you here?”

“Eat.”

“How did you KNOW?”

“He rang me. Last night. He said he was going away, and would I come in early.” He pushed the sandwich at her. “He said you shouldn’t have to come back to an empty garage.”

She just looked at him.

“He said you’d want the egg one. Not the ham.”

She made a noise like a kettle.

“Big Wu’s coming in early too.” Mr. Kwok unfolded his newspaper. “He says to tell you he isn’t.”

Serafina sat down on the floor with her back to the workbench and held the egg sandwich in both hands and didn’t eat it.

From down there she could see the corner by the shutter. Eight new tyres in two towers, still in their wrappers. The soft compound Big Wu rationed like medicine. When had they come? Saturday? She’d been too busy looking at him to notice who carried what.

The delivery note was taped to the top one. At the bottom, under Paid by, in small square separate letters:

QIN H.

Not a post box in the capital. His name. Where she would see it.

She turned her wrist over. The marker had gone weeks ago. She looked anyway.

On the bench, the plain mug that said HIS sat exactly where he’d left it. Facing the room.

chapters.title: Baizhang Pass
chapters.desc: She races up a mountain without her gauge. On the other side of the world, a man and a night porter watch the stream at four in the morning.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a waste of good tyres. His tyres.” — Big Wu
chapters.content:
“A hill climb is a race against a mountain.”

Saturday. The paddock, which was the village car park. Big Wu had his arms folded and a face like a thunderstorm.

“Are you listening?”

“No.”

“The mountain doesn’t care. That’s what makes it fair. That’s ALSO what makes it stupid.” He pointed up. “No run-off. No gravel. You go off at the Needle, you sit in the gravel and cry on your sister. You go off up there, you go off the MOUNTAIN.”

“You said this in the van.”

“Twice.”

“Three times, Wu.”

“Then this is four, and four’s bad luck, so listen to it.” He glared at Gilded on the transporter. Matte black. White 7. Gold name. A little grey taxi on the driver’s door, just above the sill. “Circuit car. Circuit tyres. Against a field of specials built for nothing but this. It’s a waste of good tyres.” His glare got worse. “His tyres.”

She patted his enormous arm and went to unload her own car. The Baizhang Pass climbed eleven hundred metres in twelve point four kilometres. From a village of tea sheds and noodle stalls at the bottom to a concrete car park and a temple at the top. Somebody had cut the road into the mountain in the sixties without believing in guard rails. Rock on the left, going up. On the right, mostly, air.

✦ ✦ ✦

Forty-one entries. Nine classes. Men from the provinces in old saloons with roll cages. A woman from the city in a Lotus. Two brothers from the coast in identical hatchbacks who’d slept in their cars. And at the top of the list, where he’d been nine years out of the last eleven, Lau Kam-wing.

Sixty-two. He’d built his car in a shed in the next valley over thirty years. It wasn’t really a car. A frame of steel tubes, a motorbike engine in the back, an open cockpit, four fat tyres and a wing on the back like an upside-down table. It weighed less than Lau did. It did exactly one thing, which was go up the Baizhang Pass faster than anything else alive. Six minutes, eleven point four. His record. 2018.

“Nobody beats Old Lau in a circuit car!” One of the coast brothers, at the noodle stall that night, loud. “Can’t be done. Too heavy. Too wide. The top corners are too tight.”

Serafina was at the next table, eating her noodles standing up.

“Can’t be done is what they said about the Needle.”

The brother turned round. Saw who it was. Went pink.

At the end of the stall, Lau Kam-wing put down his chopsticks and looked at her over his glasses. Small. Brown. Like a walnut in a fleece.

“Circuit car?”

“Circuit car.”

“Good luck, girl.” He picked his chopsticks up again. “Bring a spare neck.”

“Keep your record warm, uncle. I’ll be borrowing it.”

The whole stall went ooooh. Big Wu put his face in his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday morning, she set her tyres without the gauge.

She’d known on the departures lane, handing it over. She’d done it anyway. Big Wu had a digital one from the team kit. Black plastic, a screen that read to two decimal places. She crouched by the front left in the cold mountain air with her breath smoking and looked at it.

“It’s accurate. Calibrated it in March. It’s more accurate than that old brass thing ever was.”

“I know.” She didn’t pick it up yet. “It’s not hers.”

She used it anyway. One point five two cold on the fronts. One point four eight on the rears. A shade under her circuit numbers, because the top was eleven hundred metres up and every tyre on the mountain would read a tenth high by the time it got there. She wrote the numbers on her forearm in marker, the way Nonna used to write them on her driving glove.

Then she did something she hadn’t done since she was twelve. Bare palm flat on each tyre in turn. Held it. Shut her eyes.

“What are you DOING?”

“Feeling it.”

“You can’t feel point oh four of a bar!”

“Nonna could.”

Before the second run, Mouse was on an upturned crate under the awning with the laptop. She wasn’t looking at the screen. She was looking at Serafina. When Serafina looked back, Mouse held up her phone and turned it round.

The series stream. Under the video, a little grey number. People watching.

Two hundred and eighty-one.

“It’s four in the morning in Lisbon.” So low only Serafina could hear.

Serafina stared at her.

“You don’t know he’s in Lisbon.”

“No.” Mouse put the phone away. “I don’t know anything.”

How long had Mouse known? Since Thursday? Since the plane? Had she followed a flight? Serafina decided she didn’t want to know, and hugged her. Mouse went rigid as a plank and let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel was narrow and yellow with green shutters, on a steep street in the old part of the city. The lobby was the size of a lift. At that hour it was dark except for one lamp on the desk and the glow of the guest computer in the corner.

The night porter was called Fernando. Seventy. Fifty years of night shifts in four hotels. He had seen everything that could happen in a lobby between midnight and six. So the quiet Asian guest from room nine, coming down before four and sitting at the guest computer, was nothing.

The car race was something.

Fernando came round the desk in his slippers with his coffee and stood behind the chair. A mountain road, steep and grey, cut into rock. A drop into green nothing on one side. And a car going up it. Black. Low. A gold word on the front. Faster than Fernando had known a car could go up anything.

“Formula One?” In Portuguese.

“No.” Good Portuguese. He didn’t turn round. “A hill. On the other side of the world.”

“Who’s driving?”

The guest didn’t answer straight away. He had something in his left hand, held against the desk by the keyboard. Round. Brass. A short rubber tube. He held it the way Fernando’s mother had held her rosary.

“My fiancée.”

Fernando put his coffee down. He pulled up the other chair.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had watched the first run alone. Two in the morning here, nine there. Tianyi asleep upstairs with his mouth open and a stick of cinnamon gum in his fist. Six minutes, fourteen point eight. Second. Three point four behind Lau. On a mountain, that was a lifetime.

Then he watched it again. And again. Nine times, frame by frame, until he knew where every camera post was and where there wasn’t one. Where the rock came right out to the edge of the road. The twelve corners after the first bridge, where she’d been careful because the tyres were cold. The long left at halfway, where she’d been perfect.

The hundred and twelfth. The tightest on the mountain. A hairpin with nothing on the outside but a white-painted rock and a view. She’d lost a second and a half there.

He knew why. He’d known by the third viewing. She’d braked where a circuit driver brakes. Lau braked where a goat would.

He could have told her. He had no phone that was his. Just a hotel computer, a brass gauge, two hours. So he sat.

“Is it the last one?” Fernando, beside him.

“Yes.”

“And she is behind?”

“Three seconds.”

“Is that a lot?”

“On a mountain? Yes.”

“Is she careful?”

“No.”

“Good.” Fernando crossed himself anyway. “Careful ones lose.”

She went off the line in the village with the tea sheds. The stream cut to a camera on a pole. The black car went up the first straight into the trees, and Haozhen stopped breathing.

Faster through the twelve after the bridge. The tyres were warm this time. She’d done something to them. A hair lower at the front. Biting. Faster through the long left. Faster through the cutting where the rock hung over the road like a roof.

“What is that? The green?”

“Faster than the old man.”

The split times came up in a box at the bottom of the screen.

Green. Green. Green.

“Meu Deus…”

The hundred and twelfth. The camera on the white rock. The black car came up the last steep straight at it. Too fast. Much too fast. Much too late. She’s going to the fifth lamp post—

She braked.

Late. Goat late. The nose went down. The back of the car stepped out. Just a little. Just enough. On purpose. She went round the hairpin with the outside wheels on the very edge of the tarmac, a hand’s width from the white rock and the drop behind it, and came out the other side already flat.

The split came up.

Green.

“GOAL!” Fernando grabbed his arm. “That is a goal, yes? That is like a goal?”

Haozhen found his hand was locked round the gauge so hard the rim of the dial had cut into his palm. He didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

Six minutes, ten point nine.

Half a second under Lau’s record. The first time in the history of the Baizhang Pass that anything with a roof had won outright. The stream cut to the top. The temple car park. She was getting out. Helmet off. Hair in spikes. Face red and wet and laughing, shouting at Big Wu, who had picked her up off the ground, all of her, and was turning in a circle with her held to his chest like a sack of rice. Mouse was jumping up and down. Mr. Kwok was holding a camping stove. Why was he holding a camping stove?

Behind them Lau Kam-wing pulled off his helmet. He walked over to Gilded and put his hand flat on its roof. An old jockey touching the horse that just beat his.

“Who is the old man?”

“The one she beat.”

“He is touching her car!”

“He’s allowed.”

Then the camera found her face. Close. Somebody was holding out a microphone. She didn’t take it.

She looked straight past it into the lens and grinned and waved. A huge stupid wave with her whole arm over her head. Number seven on top of a mountain, waving.

Tell her I’ll wave.

Then she held up her left hand to the camera. Palm out. Something red on the ring finger caught the sun. She mouthed three words. Slowly. So anybody could read them.

Bring it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fernando was crying into his coffee. Seventy years old, fifty years of night shifts, and crying into his coffee like a boy.

“She waved at you!”

“Yes.” Haozhen didn’t look away from the screen. “And at somebody else.”

Fernando didn’t ask who. Fifty years. He went round the desk. Two small glasses. A bottle from under the counter, very old, very brown.

“It’s four in the morning.”

“It’s eleven in the morning on the other side of the world. And she won.” Fernando raised his glass. “To your fiancée!”

The guest from room nine drank it all at once, like medicine.

Then he went back to the start of the stream. A black car at the bottom of a mountain. Waiting.

He pressed play.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eleven times. Fernando stayed for four. Then a German couple came down with suitcases for an early flight. Then the street outside went grey and a man went past with a cart of bread and the first tram came groaning up the hill. Haozhen sat at the guest computer with the gauge in his fist and watched her climb the mountain over and over. On the eleventh time, at the hundred and twelfth, when the back stepped out and she held it a hand’s width from the drop, he found he was laughing.

And under the laughing, something much worse.

He wanted to stand up and walk out of the lobby. Get on the first plane east. File or no file. Stand in that car park on the mountain, take her helmet off her himself, and kiss her in front of every camera until somebody pulled them apart.

He sat still and waited for it to pass. It didn’t pass.

Upstairs, on his bed, there was a folder. A street. A house. A family. A man who took ledgers. In the other bed was a man he’d trained beside at sixteen, who would wake at seven wanting breakfast. The window seat. The details.

He stopped laughing. There was a half-moon cut in his palm from the gauge. A little blood. He wiped it on his trousers. He looked at the back of the gauge. S.S. A.C.

“Fernando.”

The porter looked up from the desk.

“If I asked you to keep something for me. In your desk. For a few weeks.” He held the gauge out. “And if I didn’t come back for it, to post it to an address on the other side of the world. Would you?”

Fernando looked at the gauge. Then at the man.

“No.”

“No?”

“No. I would not.” He shook his head. “You keep it in your pocket. You take it back to her yourself. She asked you. On the television. In front of everybody!” He picked up his coffee. “I saw her face. I would not like to be the man who posted it.”

Haozhen looked at him for a moment. Then he put the gauge back in his inside pocket. Left side.

Upstairs, Tianyi was just waking up. Stretching. Reaching for the gum on the bedside table.

“You’re up early.” A yawn, in Mandarin. “Couldn’t sleep?”

“No. I slept fine.”

It was the first lie he had ever told Tianyi. He noticed it. He filed it. Then he went and stood at the window, where the street ran down the hill to the river. On the corner stood a yellow house with blue tiles. A boy’s bicycle was leaning against the door.

chapters.title: The Target Has a Family
chapters.desc: Lisbon. Twenty-three days in a chair by a door, counting a boy’s keepy-ups. Then the job.
chapters.epigraph: “Not in front of the house. Please. That’s my son’s window.” — Gong Ruiming
chapters.content:
“Twenty-two. Twenty-three.”

Tianyi didn’t turn round from the window.

“He’ll drop it at twenty-four. He always drops it on the evens after twenty. He gets excited.”

The ball hit the cobbles.

“Twenty-four.” Tianyi chewed his gum. “You’re counting.”

“No.”

“You are. Under your breath. Since about day five.” He shifted the binoculars on the sill. “You’ve changed, Haozhen.”

Haozhen sat in the chair by the door and didn’t answer. Day fourteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The yellow house stood on the corner where the street turned down to the river. Three storeys. Green shutters. A front of old blue-and-white tiles, ships, some of them cracked. Geraniums in a box on the first floor. A boy’s bike against the door. Blue. A bell that didn’t work. A football wedged in the basket.

Their room was across the street and two doors up, third floor of a guesthouse. Tianyi had the window seat. Tianyi always had the window seat. Feet on the sill, binoculars, cinnamon gum, and twelve hours of jokes under his breath. Haozhen had the chair by the door.

The man’s name was Gong Ruiming. Forty-six. Nine years in the accounts section of a building in the capital that wasn’t on any map. Then one Friday in the spring of 2021 he’d walked out with a briefcase and never walked back. Seven weeks later he was here. Teaching maths to diplomats’ children at a language school by the river. A different surname. He’d married a nurse called Ana. She worked nights at the big hospital on the hill. There was a boy. Tomás. Eleven. Ana’s from before, the file said. The boy called Gong Pai anyway.

Every Saturday Gong walked him to football with a hand on the back of his neck and stood on the touchline in a raincoat, even when it wasn’t raining, and shouted. He watered the geraniums every evening. He put the bins out on Saturday nights. He had a custard tart from the bakery at the bottom of the street with his coffee, and he gave the last bite to the bakery’s dog. Every single time.

And every evening after dinner Tomás came down into the little square by the side wall and did keepy-ups. An hour. Until his mother leaned out of the window and called him in.

He was trying to get to thirty-two. Why thirty-two? Some player. Some boy at school. On day nine he got to thirty-one and stopped, ball under his foot, and yelled something up at the window that made his mother laugh. Since then he hadn’t got past twenty-six.

Haozhen couldn’t see him from the chair. He could hear him. The flat soft slap of the ball. Foot. Knee. Foot.

“Why thirty-two?” Tianyi, day eleven, to nobody.

“I don’t know.”

“I bet it’s a girl. It’s always a girl.” Chew. “You’d know about that now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“The Director told us at the section dinner.” Day sixteen. Feet on the sill. “April. Stood up at the end with her glass. Haozhen is getting married.”

Haozhen looked up.

“Half the section didn’t believe her. Other half thought it was a code.” Tianyi grinned at the street. “I knew it was true. She had the face she has when something’s surprised her and she doesn’t like it.”

“You never said.”

“I was waiting for you to!” He swung round, finally, all delighted teeth. “A racing driver. Haozhen. A RACING DRIVER. That’s the best thing I’ve ever heard. You, who drives like a hearse.”

“I don’t drive like a hearse.”

“You drive like a very fast hearse. With great respect for the deceased.” Back to the window. Chew. Chew. “Is she pretty?”

Haozhen said nothing.

Tianyi laughed into his shoulder.

“Oh, she is. Look at your face. Oh, Haozhen…”

“Watch the house.”

“I’m watching it. It’s a house.” A pause. “When’s the wedding?”

“There isn’t a date.”

“No.” The grin went thinner. “There never is, in this job.” He held out the packet of gum without looking. “Have one. For the bride.”

Haozhen took one. He didn’t chew it. He put it in his inside pocket, next to the brass gauge.

“Name?”

“No.”

“Initial?”

“No.”

“Does she know? What we do?”

“Yes.”

Tianyi stopped chewing. He took his feet off the sill.

“She KNOWS?”

“She guessed. In January.”

“And she still…”

“Yes.”

Tianyi looked at him for a long time. Then he put his feet back up and laughed at the street, not his usual laugh.

“Well, she’s mad. I like her already.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Day twenty, he asked.

“What did he take?”

Tianyi turned his whole head from the street. First time in twenty days.

“Ledgers. Accounts. Nine years of who paid who for what in the building with no map.” He turned back. “Upstairs wants them. And they want to know who he’s shown them to. That’s why it’s him and the books.”

“Has he shown anyone?”

“Don’t know. Not told.” Chew. “Does it matter?”

Haozhen didn’t answer that either.

Day twenty-one, Tianyi found a key in a biscuit tin on top of a wardrobe. Gong at the language school, Ana asleep after nights, Tomás at football. In and out in four minutes. Haozhen watched the street from the corner.

“Locker,” Tianyi said, when he came out. Breathless. Happy. “Railway station. Number on the tag. Easy.”

Day twenty-two, they opened it.

Four ledgers. Old-fashioned, hardbacked, grey cloth. Columns of dates and figures in a small, neat accountant’s hand. Haozhen turned the pages in front of the locker while Tianyi watched the concourse. He wasn’t supposed to read them. He was supposed to put them in the bag.

“Bag them. Come on. There’s a policeman buying a sandwich.”

He read one line.

Spring 2020. Third ledger, halfway down. A date. A figure. A company he didn’t know. In the authorisation column, three small initials. D.Q.Y. And in the last column, where every other line said section or upstairs or a department number, this one said, underlined once:

Private.

He shut the ledger. He put all four in the bag. Slowly. Corners squared. Tianyi didn’t see his face. He filed it in the room in his head where he put things, and shut the door.

“Anything good?”

“Numbers.”

It wasn’t the usual room. It wasn’t the room where the people went.

He noticed that. He filed that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Day twenty-three was a Saturday.

Football. The touchline. The raincoat. The custard tart, the last bite to the dog. Geraniums. Dinner at the first-floor window, Ana in her tunic for nights, Tomás talking with his mouth full, Gong laughing.

Then the boy came down with the ball. Haozhen sat in the chair by the door.

“Nineteen. Twenty.”

The slap of it.

“Twenty-one. Twenty-two. Twenty-three.”

“Twenty-four,” Tianyi whispered. “Drop it. Go on.”

It didn’t drop.

“Twenty-five. Twenty-six.”

Haozhen was standing up. When had he stood up?

“Twenty-seven. Twenty-eight.”

“Haozhen…” Tianyi had stopped chewing.

“Twenty-nine. Thirty…”

Thirty-one.

The ball hit the cobbles.

Down in the square the boy shouted something, furious and laughing at once, and booted the ball against the wall.

“Trinta e um! MÃE! Trinta e um!”

His mother leaned out and called something back. The boy stood in the evening light with his hands on his hips and his face turned up to the window.

“Thirty-one.” Tianyi let out a breath. “Again.”

Haozhen sat down.

Ana left for the hospital. She kissed the boy in the doorway. She kissed Gong on the step. She walked down the hill to the tram. Later, Gong put the bins out.

✦ ✦ ✦

The street was empty. It was always empty, Saturday nights. Gong came out in his slippers with two black bags, one in each hand, carried them to the bins on the corner by the bakery, dropped them in, and turned round.

Haozhen was standing on the pavement between him and his front door.

He had come down the guesthouse stairs and across the street without a sound. Dark jacket. Hands at his sides, where people could see them.

“Gong Ruiming.”

Gong stopped. He didn’t run. Haozhen had known he wouldn’t. After ten years you could tell who would run, and Gong wasn’t a runner. Gong was a man who had walked out of a building with a briefcase and known, every day since, that one evening someone would be standing on his pavement saying his real name.

He looked at the jacket. The hands. The car at the corner, engine running, Tianyi at the wheel.

“Yes.” In Mandarin. A capital accent, gone soft at the edges by the sea. “All right.”

Haozhen waited.

“Not in front of the house. Please.” Gong looked past his shoulder at the first floor. “That’s my son’s window.”

“All right.”

They walked to the car side by side. Close. Two friends leaving a party. Haozhen’s hand was on Gong’s elbow. Not hard. Gong was walking anyway.

Four steps. The light came on in the first-floor window.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bare feet on the stairs. Fast. Then the front door was open and Tomás was on the step in a T-shirt and pyjama shorts with the football under his arm. He’d been lying in bed with it. Of course he had. Lying in bed thinking about thirty-one.

He looked at his father walking away toward a car with a strange man holding his elbow.

“Pai?”

Gong stopped. He didn’t turn all the way. Just his head.

“Vai para dentro, Tomás.” Go inside. The touchline voice. Easy. “É trabalho. Volto logo.” It’s work. I’ll be back soon.

The boy didn’t go inside.

He stood on the step with the ball and looked at Haozhen. Not at his father. At Haozhen. Straight at him. The way kids look before they’ve learned not to.

A great many people had looked at Haozhen in ten years. Frightened ones. Angry ones. A man in a hood at a petrol station. A woman across a ballroom on Battery Hill without one bit of fear in her. Nobody had looked at him like this. Like he was the thing under the bed.

“Tomás. Por favor.”

Further down the street, a light came on. A woman’s voice called a question. Haozhen opened the rear door. Gong got in without being pushed. He folded himself into the back seat, put his hands on his knees, palms up, and looked straight ahead through the windscreen. He didn’t look at the house again.

Haozhen shut the door. The ball hit the car.

The boy had thrown it from the step with both hands, as hard as he could. It bounced off the rear window a hand’s width from Haozhen’s face with a flat hollow bang. It rolled away down the cobbles toward the river. Into the gutter. It stopped against a drain.

Haozhen looked at it. Then he walked round the car and got in the front. Tianyi drove off down the hill. Not fast. Lights on. Like anybody.

In the wing mirror the boy was standing in the middle of the street in his pyjamas, in the light from the bakery, with his hands at his sides.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody spoke for half an hour. Then, on the long road out by the river, Gong did. Conversationally. From the back seat.

“You have someone.”

Haozhen didn’t answer.

“You keep touching your pocket. The left one.” A pause. “I did that the first year. With a photograph of the boy. In case I had to leave in a hurry.”

Tianyi glanced across at the passenger seat. Back at the road.

“Is she waiting for you?”

“Be quiet.” Tianyi, eyes on the road.

“Then you know.” Gong didn’t raise his voice. “You know exactly what this is.”

Nobody said anything else all the way to the marina.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a boat. Two men on it who didn’t give names. Haozhen walked Gong down the pontoon in the dark with his hand on his elbow. At the edge of the boat Gong stopped.

“The bakery. Somebody should tell them the dog—” He stopped. “No. Nobody will tell them anything.”

He got on. Haozhen handed over the bag of ledgers. He signed nothing. He walked back up the pontoon alone.

Halfway, he stopped. He went to the edge. He was sick into the black water.

Not since he was eighteen. Not since the hotel in the capital. He knelt on the wet planks and was sick until there was nothing left. Then he kept retching. Behind him the boat’s engine started and went away across the river toward the sea.

Tianyi was waiting at the top. He held out a stick of cinnamon gum. Haozhen took it.

“First time I’ve seen you do that.” For once in his life, Tianyi wasn’t joking. He looked at Haozhen’s face under the marina lights. “Haozhen. Are you all right?”

“Yes. I’m fine.”

The second lie.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, on the way to the airport, he told the taxi to go the long way. Up the hill. Past the yellow house.

Nobody had watered the geraniums. The boy was sitting on the front step in his school tracksuit with the football in his lap. Somebody had gone down to the drain and got it for him. He was holding it in both arms against his chest and looking down the hill toward the river. At nothing. The way you look at a road somebody went down.

The taxi went past. The boy didn’t look up.

“Aeroporto?” said the driver.

“Yes.”

Haozhen put his hand flat on his chest. Left side. The gauge. The stick of gum for the bride. He kept it there all the way to the airport, and all the way through it, and through two weeks of debriefing rooms in the capital, and most of the way home.

chapters.title: He Comes Home Wrong
chapters.desc: He comes home, sits in her passenger seat and says nothing for two days. Her father’s company is falling apart, and in the end he tells her about the boy.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to ask. I’m going to sit here. You talk when there’s something you can say.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
Unknown: Back Saturday. Late. H.

Friday. A number she didn’t know. She read it at the bench with a socket in her hand.

“Saturday.”

“Good.” Big Wu, from under the transporter.

“Late, he says.”

“Then he’s late. Hand me the twelve.”

That was all, all day. That was how she knew Big Wu had been worried too.

She saved the number. Then she deleted it, because it wouldn’t be his by Monday. Then she sat on the bottom stair and turned the ring round and round on her finger until Mr. Kwok told her she’d wear it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited up.

Sunday, nearly four in the morning, a taxi. Not his grey estate, which was still in her garage with the bullet hole filled and primed. The taxi stopped at the corner. A door. The taxi leaving. Then nothing. She stood at the bottom of the loft stairs in her vest and shorts and listened to the nothing.

Four minutes. Five. What was he doing out there? Standing in the street? She was halfway to the side door when it opened. He came in.

Black bag on his shoulder. Envelope shirt, grey trousers, the forgettable jacket. All clean. All pressed. He’d shaved. His hair was cut. He looked like a photograph of himself. Like the blurry one Auntie Chu’s nephew took in the service corridor on Battery Hill. A man at a door with no face at all.

He looked at her across the garage. Then he came to her. Took her hand. Opened it. Put something in it and closed her fingers round it.

Brass. Round. Warm from his chest.

“I brought it back.”

The voice from the east service door. Please step away, madam. She hadn’t heard it in months.

“Haozhen…”

He let go of her hand. He walked past her, careful not to brush her, to Nonna under the hanging lamp. Opened the passenger door. Got in. Shut it. Sat there with his hands on his knees, looking through the windscreen at the postcard of the Monza banking. He didn’t move.

“Haozhen? Hao. Talk to me.”

Nothing.

She stood in the middle of the garage with Nonna’s gauge in her fist. Then she went and got the blanket off the back seat of his grey car, got in the driver’s side, and put it over his knees.

“Okay. Okay. I’m here.”

She didn’t ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t speak on Sunday.

He didn’t sleep either. That was the bit that terrified her. All six weeks she’d been so sure. Whatever he came back as, the passenger seat would work. It always worked. It didn’t work. He sat with his eyes open on the whiteboard and his breathing never changed. Not once.

Big Wu came in under the shutter with the doughnuts and stopped. The red Lancia in the middle of the floor. Serafina in the driver’s seat with her bare feet on the dashboard. The man in the passenger seat.

Big Wu had done two prison sentences and would never say what for. He looked at Haozhen’s face through the windscreen. She saw him know it. She saw his own face shut like a door.

He put the doughnuts on the bench. He went out again.

“Wu?”

Gone. An hour later he came back with a pot wrapped in a towel. His mother’s soup. Pork bone and old cucumber, the one she made for people coming out of hospital. He put it on the camping stove with two bowls next to it. He stood at Nonna’s passenger window for a second. Haozhen didn’t look at him. Big Wu nodded once, to himself.

“Radio stays off,” he told her. Nothing else.

It stayed off all day.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fed him. Like a bird that had flown into a window. She brought the soup in the plain mug, the one that said HIS, and blew on it, and held it out. And waited.

Nothing.

“It’s Big Wu’s mother’s. If you don’t drink it she’ll come here personally.”

Nothing.

“She’s eighty-three and she’ll climb in, Haozhen.”

After a while his hand came up and took the mug. After a longer while he drank some. She brought it again an hour later.

“Good. Good boy. That’s two.”

In the afternoon Mr. Kwok made congee. Plain. Ginger, salt. She took that to the car too, with a spoon.

“Four spoons. Just four. Then I leave you alone.”

He ate four spoons. He gave it back.

At six, Mouse came over from the end of the bench. Mouse never came over from the end of the bench. She stood at the passenger window with her headphones round her neck and put something on the dashboard, very carefully, next to the brass gauge. A clementine. Then she went back to her screens.

“Mouse…” Serafina’s throat closed. “Thanks.”

“Granny Shum’s.” Mouse didn’t look round. “She gives them to people who need one.”

He looked at it. It was the first thing all day he’d looked at that wasn’t the whiteboard.

✦ ✦ ✦

At night she drove him. It had always worked. The loop, gently, like all winter. Bridge. Tunnel. Coast road. Ferries and cranes. He didn’t sleep.

“Remember this bit? You always go here. Right here. Every time.”

At the bend on the coast road where his head always slid off the window onto her shoulder, he stayed upright. She went round three times. Four. The sky started going grey over the water. Nothing.

She pulled into the lay-by above the harbour, where they’d watched the fireworks. Engine off. The engine ticked.

“I’m not going to ask.” She kept her eyes on the windscreen. “I want you to know that. I’m not going to ask where you went or what happened or what you did. I’m going to sit here. You talk when there’s something you can say.”

“If that’s tomorrow, it’s tomorrow. If it’s next year, it’s next year.” Her voice went. She got it back. “I’ve got nowhere to be.”

He didn’t answer.

But on the dashboard between them, he reached out and picked up Mouse’s clementine. And held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Monday, he didn’t speak either.

He got out of the car twice. Once for the toilet. Once to stand at the side door with his back to the garage, looking at the alley. Nine minutes. She counted every one. Then he got back in and shut the door.

Big Wu took the day off the transporter and rebuilt the grey car’s front suspension instead. Serafina had already rebuilt it in December. She didn’t say so. He did it slowly, two metres from Nonna’s window, making as little noise as a man his size could, for eight hours.

Mr. Kwok didn’t go home for the news. He sat on the stool by the kettle in his cardigan and read the newspaper out loud. To nobody. To Haozhen, mostly. Racing results. Weather. A long story about a dog that lived in a fire station. In Cantonese. Calm. Flat. An hour and a half of it.

“My wife liked the dog stories,” he told her, when she brought him tea. “At the end. I read her every one.”

She had to go and stand in the alley for a minute.

Late, she sent them all home.

“Ring me,” said Big Wu at the shutter. “Any time. I mean it, Sera. Any time.”

“I know.”

“I sleep with it on my chest.”

She was in the driver’s seat before dawn with her knees up, eating cold congee out of the pot, when her phone rang.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia. Who didn’t ring at that hour. Who sent messages with full stops on them at civilised times.

“Lia?”

“Papà rang me.” Steady. Far away. The voice she used when she was holding something with both hands. “From the tower. He couldn’t go home. I’m in the corridor outside his office.”

“What? What’s—”

“It’s going, Sera. The Group. All of it. The banks meet on Friday, all eleven of them, and if nothing comes they call everything in. Four towers up the river nobody will buy.” A breath. “The house.”

Serafina sat very still with the pot in her lap. Beside her, she felt him turn his head.

“He was crying. On the phone. I’ve never heard him cry.” Aurelia’s voice wobbled once and came back. “He said Mamma told him not to build them.”

“The house…”

“If Friday goes how he thinks, they’ll sell it. In the autumn. Everything with a sticker on.” Quiet. “I wanted you to know before it’s in the papers. You don’t have to come.”

Serafina looked through the windscreen at the whiteboard.

“I can’t. Lia, I can’t, not tonight. I’ve got someone in my car who—” It broke. She tried again. “I can’t leave him tonight.”

A long pause on the line. She heard her sister breathe.

“Then stay with him. Stay with him, Sera.” Another pause. “Is he all right?”

“No.”

“I know.” Very low. “They don’t come home all right. Not always. Not the first time it’s bad.” Then, in the voice from when they were small: “Stay with him. Papà’s got me. And Chen Si’s awake. He’s always awake.”

The line went dead. She sat with the phone in her hand.

“Your father.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first thing he’d said in two days.

She turned. He was looking at her. Not the whiteboard. Her. His face was pale and tired, and something had gone out of it. The thing far back behind the calm she’d always been able to see. A light in a house she’d thought was empty.

“The Group’s gone. Four towers. He’s selling the house.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I haven’t been in it for seven years! I haven’t spoken to him in seven years.”

“I know. You should have gone.”

“I’m not leaving you in a car!”

He looked at her.

Then down at the clementine in his hand. He’d held it since Sunday night. It had gone soft and warm.

“He had a son.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her.

Not all of it. Not the city. Not the name, or the building with no map, or the ledgers. She didn’t ask and he didn’t give it. A yellow house with blue tiles. Geraniums. A man who gave the last bite of his custard tart to the bakery’s dog. A boy of eleven doing keepy-ups against the side wall every evening, trying to get to thirty-two. Haozhen counted every one from a chair by a door for twenty-three days and never once saw him.

“He always dropped it on the even numbers. After twenty. He got excited.”

“Hao…”

“The last night, he got to thirty-one.” Level. The east-door voice, the whole way. “Then the bins. The slippers. The light coming on upstairs. And he came down. Pyjamas. The football under his arm.” He turned the clementine over. “He looked at me.”

She waited.

“Like I was what’s under the bed.”

“He threw the ball at the car. At my window. It missed my face by about this much.” His fingers, a hand’s width. “In the morning nobody had watered the geraniums.”

“I did it anyway. He threw the ball and I got in the car.” He looked at the clementine. “I didn’t even slow down.”

She reached across the gearstick and took his face in both hands. The ruby was cold against his jaw.

“Look at me.”

He looked.

“You did it. I know. I’m not going to tell you it wasn’t you, or it was them. It was you.” Her thumbs moved on his cheekbones. “And you’ve been sitting in my car for two days because you can’t stand that you did. That’s what this is. That’s ALL this is.” Her voice cracked right down the middle. “A man who could stand it would be asleep.”

Then his face started to go. His mouth first. A tremor, there and gone. Then his jaw. Then his eyes, dry and fixed for two days, went bright. She watched it come up through him like water through a cracked floor. Slow. Then not slow at all.
