He made a sound. The low old sound from the night he came back from the twelve days. Only this time it didn’t stop. It broke in the middle. He bent forward in the seat with his face in her hands and his whole body shaking, and he wept.

Not one tear, contained and filed. Nothing like that. He sobbed. Great dragging ugly sobs that hurt to listen to. Like something rusted shut for ten years being forced open with a bar.

She climbed over the gearstick. Banged her knee on the handbrake. Didn’t swear. Into the passenger seat with him, half in his lap, half on the door. She pulled his head down onto her shoulder and held it there with both arms.

“I’ve got you. I’ve got you, I’ve got you…”

A train went over. Then another. She counted without meaning to. Three. Four.

“I can’t—” Wrecked, into her neck. “Sera. I can’t do it again.”

“Rule four.” Into his hair.

He went still in her arms.

“Not yet. If I say it now, they’ll know before I’ve got anything. They’ll know by Thursday.” A breath that shook all the way down. “There’s something. I saw something. In a book I wasn’t supposed to read. I need to think.”

“Then think. I’ll be here.” She held on tighter. “I’ll have the car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept just after dawn.

All at once, from the bottom up, like a building coming down. One second he was breathing torn and fast against her neck. The next, his whole weight went into her. His head went heavy on her shoulder. His breathing went long. Slow. Down.

She didn’t move. Squashed against Nonna’s door, a grown man asleep in her arms, her knee throbbing, grey light under the shutter. Six hours.

Big Wu came in with the doughnuts, and stopped, and looked. Then he went out again and pulled the shutter all the way down behind him from outside. Slowly. So it wouldn’t make a sound.

When he finally woke it was nearly noon. The first thing he looked for was the clementine. It had rolled into the footwell. He picked it up and peeled it in one long spiral without breaking it once. He gave her half.

“Eat.”

“You eat.”

He ate his half. Then he pulled her back into him in the cramped seat, both arms, tight, his face in her hair. He kissed her temple. Then her mouth. Slow. Salt and clementine. Like he was coming back into himself one piece at a time and wanted her to be the first thing he found there.

“You stayed.”

“Where was I going to go?” She was crying again. Stupid. “It’s my car.”

chapters.title: The Song Family Opposes the Match
chapters.desc: Her mother writes for the first time in seven years: bring him. The house on the Peak has lot numbers on everything, and her mother asks him nine questions.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody keeps her, madam. I’d like to be wherever she is. That’s all I’m asking for.” — Qin Haozhen
chapters.content:
The letter came on the Wednesday. Cream envelope. Her mother’s handwriting.

Seven years since Serafina had seen that handwriting on anything addressed to her. It came to the garage under the railway bridge, which her mother had never once admitted existed. Big Wu put it on the bench and stood back from it like it might go off.

One card. One line.

Saturday. Four o’clock. Bring him. Before there is no house to bring him to. — V.

She turned it over. Nothing on the back.

“How does she KNOW?”

“The hill climb.” Mouse, from the end of the bench. “You held your hand up to the camera. With the ring. It was in the papers on Monday. Racer shows off ring on mountain.” A pause. “It was quite a big picture.”

“She’d have known before the papers.”

Haozhen was at the kettle. Two weeks he’d been coming in through the side door again, at normal hours, picking up his mug and staying. He looked better. Not well. Better. Four hours a night in the loft. Two more in Nonna’s passenger seat in the afternoons. Big Wu’s mother sent soup every day and nobody said a word about it.

“She’s had someone on you since you left. The first one stopped. She’ll have found another.” He looked at the card. “Someone at the circuit. Someone in the series office. She’ll know roughly what I earn. Where I live. She’ll think she knows what I am.”

“And what does she think you are?”

“A security guard.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t want to go. She said so for two days, loudly, to everyone, including the transporter.

Friday night, coast road, he said, “Your father will be there.”

She didn’t answer.

“You didn’t go in July. When your sister rang. Because of me.” He was looking at the sea. “It’s being sold. All of it. The rooms you grew up in. After this they won’t exist.”

“Good.”

“Sera.”

“GOOD, I said.”

“I’ve walked a lot of people out of a lot of rooms they were never going back to.” Quiet. “I’d like you to walk out of this one yourself. On your own feet. Not see it in a newspaper.”

She drove a long way without saying anything. Then:

“If she’s cruel to you, I’ll put her through a window.”

“She’ll be cruel to me.” He sounded completely calm about it. “Please don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house on the Peak was yellow and huge, at the top of a drive that curved up through old trees with the whole harbour falling away below. The last time Serafina walked that drive, she was nineteen and going the other way. Evening dress. Shoes in her hand.

This time it was black jeans, boots, the leather jacket. She was NOT dressing for her mother.

He walked beside her in the forgettable suit. Halfway up, without looking, he took her left hand. The ring hand. He didn’t let go.

The front door was open. There was nobody to open it. Eleven staff, when she was fifteen.

They went in.

There were stickers on everything.

Little white ovals with black numbers. On the hall table. On the Venetian mirror at the foot of the stairs. On the grandfather clock that came from Milan in a crate in 2011. On a painting of a harbour she’d stared at every breakfast for five years. Through the music-room door, on the piano. Lot 212. Lot 213. Lot 214.

She couldn’t move.

“Sera.”

“I’m fine. I’m absolutely fine. I just didn’t think there’d be numbers—”

His hand tightened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was in the morning room.

Yellow too. The yellow of the old house in Milan, copied exactly when they moved. Tall windows on the harbour. A walnut writing desk with brass shell handles, with a sticker. Two sofas facing each other. A silver coffee pot on the low table between them, with a sticker.

Vittoria Song on the left-hand sofa. Black. Back straight.

Fifty-four. Still the most beautiful woman Serafina had ever seen, and the coldest. Exactly how she’d looked at the bottom of the stairs the night Serafina left. Perfect. Still. Waiting. Small diamonds at her ears.

Nothing on her hands. No rings.

That was new.

Across from her, in a grey cardigan with leather buttons that was much too big for him, sat Song Weiren.

Seven years. At three in the morning, sometimes, she’d imagined it. Papà the same as always. Big, warm, loud, his hand on everybody’s shoulder.

He wasn’t. He’d gone old. He’d gone small. He sat with his hands between his knees and looked up at her. His eyes filled. He didn’t say a word. Was this what seven years did? To Papà?

“Papà…”

Her voice cracked. She couldn’t stop it.

“Sit down.” Italian. Her mother. “Both of you. There’s coffee. The last of the good coffee. Everything else has gone to a valuer called Mr. Szeto, who wears brown shoes with a grey suit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat at the end of her father’s sofa with his back to the window. He watched the door in the silver coffee pot. Serafina sat beside him and didn’t let go of his hand.

Her mother looked at him. Not at her. At him.

The look Serafina grew up under. It went over him like a valuer’s eye over a sideboard, hunting for the sticker. Suit. Shoes. Hands. Face. His face gave her nothing. It slid off her like rain off a windscreen.

Then it stopped on their hands.

“Show me.”

Serafina didn’t move.

“The ring, Serafina. I saw it in the newspaper. I’d like to see it in my house while I still have one.”

She held out her hand. She didn’t let go of his to do it.

Her mother leaned forward. Looked. Didn’t touch.

“Burmese. Thirties. Handmade.” Flat. “The shank’s been opened at the back. Your sister.”

“Nonna’s gold.”

Something moved in her mother’s face. Gone before Serafina could name it.

“A pawnshop ring.” Vittoria sat back. “For my daughter.”

Then, in English, to him: “What do you do?”

“I’m in security, madam.”

“What kind?”

“Close protection. Events. Embassies, sometimes.”

“A security guard.”

The way she used to say second place.

“Yes.”

“What do you earn?”

He told her. A figure. Exact. Serafina knew it was exact, because she’d read it off a bank statement in Da Gianni. Her mother’s face didn’t move. She didn’t ask what he’d saved. He kept that to himself.

“Where is your family from?”

“A mining town in the north. You won’t have heard of it.”

“Your father?”

“He died in a roof fall when I was nine.”

“Your mother?”

“A seamstress. She still works. She’s sixty-one.”

“Brothers? Sisters?”

“None.”

“Where do you live?”

“Two rooms. Above a laundry. In the old harbour streets.”

“Do you own anything?”

He thought about it. Properly. Like the wine on Harbour Road.

“A notebook. Some shirts. And half a clementine, which I’m told I owe someone.”

Serafina made a noise and turned it into a cough.

Her mother didn’t smile.

Nine questions. Serafina counted. Every answer short. Every answer true. Not one flicker of anything in his voice. And every true answer was a perfect lie. Her mother sat in the yellow room with stickers on everything and looked at a man who had read the Song family’s file before the banks had. And saw a security guard who lived above a laundry.

They had no idea. Not one of them.

He wasn’t going to tell them.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You walked out of an engagement dinner.” Italian, to her daughter. At last. “At the Harbour Hotel. Two hundred people. Between the soup and the fish.”

“Mamma—”

“On a boy whose father owned the third-biggest construction company in the province. Who would have made you comfortable for life. Who would have made us comfortable.”

“He was an IDIOT, Mamma!”

“He was an idiot with a construction company. Do you know what Li Zhenhua bought in June?”

“I don’t care what—”

“Two of your father’s sites up the river. For a third of what they were worth.” She glanced at her husband. Away. “You said you’d rather marry a carburettor. And now you bring me your fidanzato.” She didn’t look at him. “A man who stands by doors.”

“He doesn’t stand by doors!”

“I’ve had someone watching you for seven years, Serafina.” Her voice never went up. Not once. “I know where you sleep. Over a garage.”

“Congratulations.”

“I know where you go on Saturday nights, to a woman in a folding chair, and what they’d give you for it if anybody bothered to write it down. I know he drives you there.” For the first time something crossed her face. A twist at the corner of her mouth. “I know he sleeps in your car.”

“You don’t know ANYTHING about him.”

“I know what he is. I can see it from here.” Calm. Almost kind. “He’s nothing. He’s a pair of shoes at the edge of a room. You could have had anything. You chose an engine. Now you’ve chosen a man who’ll still be standing at a door at sixty, waiting for someone important to come out of it.”

Serafina’s hand had gone white in his.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Madam.”

Low. English.

Her mother turned her head. First time she’d looked at his face properly. Serafina watched her look. Watched her find nothing.

“You’re right. I’m not important. I don’t own anything.” He paused. “I’ll probably stand at doors.”

“Then—”

“But I’m not asking you to let me keep her.” He looked at Serafina. Once. Then back. “Nobody keeps her, madam. I’ve watched her for ten months. Nobody’s ever going to keep her.”

“Then what are you asking for?”

“I’d like to be wherever she is. That’s all I’m asking for.” A beat. “And I’m not really asking you.”

The yellow room went completely quiet.

On the other sofa, her father put his hand over his eyes.

Vittoria Song had made a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman cry without raising her voice. She had stood at the bottom of those stairs while her younger daughter walked out. She’d raised a glass at a birthday party in front of two hundred guests and shut her older daughter’s shop.

She looked at the man on her sofa.

Then she turned to Serafina. Italian. Almost tender. The voice she used right before the worst thing.

“I had two daughters, Serafina. One of them was the best thing I ever made.” She folded her empty hands. “And the other one was a mistake I made in August.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember standing up.

She remembered the coffee pot. Her knee caught the table, and the coffee went over the sticker, Lot 31. Her father saying “Vittoria—” in a voice she’d never heard, broken right down the middle.

She remembered her hand was still in Haozhen’s. When she stood, he stood. No sound. Half a second before her, like he’d known.

Through his hand she felt something go through him. A jolt. Like a live wire. The wish to hurt somebody, held down by main force. He didn’t look at her mother. He stepped half a pace forward, his shoulder in front of hers, between her and the sofa. He stayed there. His thumb went once over her knuckles. Over the ring.

Walk. I’ve got you.

She looked down at her mother.

She’d had a hundred things to say. Seven years of them, saved up at three in the morning on the coast road. She didn’t need any of them. There was her mother. In black. Nothing on her hands. Every chair round her numbered for a man in brown shoes.

You’re scared. You’re so scared you can’t even see.

She didn’t say that either.

She turned round and walked out.

Morning-room door. The hall. The Venetian mirror, Lot 7. The clock from Milan. The great staircase, where Aurelia had stood at twenty and watched her go. The front door, open, because there was nobody left to close it.

She didn’t run. That was the bit she was proudest of, after. She walked. On her own feet. Down the drive, through the old trees, the harbour falling away below, his hand in hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway down, someone behind them.

She didn’t stop. He did. Then she did.

Her father. Coming down the gravel in his too-big cardigan and house slippers, one hand out like he was reaching for a rail that wasn’t there. Out of breath. He stopped three metres away under the trees.

“Sera.”

She couldn’t answer.

“The hill climb. In June. I watched it.” He was panting. “On the computer. In the office. I don’t know how to work it, the girl from accounts had to show me. But I watched it.” His face crumpled. “You waved. At the top. And for one second I thought—”

He stopped. He didn’t finish.

Oh.

For one second, in a tower that was about to belong to a bank, he’d thought she was waving at him.

She let go of Haozhen’s hand.

Three metres back up the gravel. She stood in front of her father. He was shorter than her now. When did that happen? He’d always been taller. She put her arms round him, oily leather jacket and all. He made a sound into her shoulder like something snapping. He held on.

“It was a very good climb, Papà.”

“It was. It was.” Muffled. “You took the hundred and twelfth on the outside. Lau never does that.”

She laughed into his cardigan. Wet.

“How do you know about LAU?”

“I asked the girl from accounts to find me everything.” He pulled back and held her face in both hands, the way he had when she was small. He looked at it. Then down at the hand on his arm. The ring.

“Is it a good one?”

“It’s the best one.”

He looked past her. Down the drive at the man in the forgettable suit, standing on the gravel with his hands at his sides where people could see them.

He didn’t say anything to him.

He nodded. Once.

Haozhen nodded back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the bottom of the hill she had the engine running and her face wet and her hands on the wheel. She hadn’t put it in gear.

“She’s frightened.”

“Of WHAT?”

“Of ending up with nothing. Nothing in her hands. Nobody in the room.” He was looking at the gates. “I’ve seen it. A lot of rooms. People who’ve had everything, the week before it goes. They say the worst thing they can think of. To the person they’re most scared of losing.” He paused. “So it’s their choice.”

“That doesn’t make it okay.”

“No. It doesn’t make it anything. It’s just what it is.” He turned his head. “I’m sorry I made you go.”

“Don’t be.” She put it in first. Her hands were shaking. “He watched the hill climb. On a computer. The girl from accounts had to show him…”

“I heard.”

Then, fast, like it got out before he could stop it:

“She’s wrong.”

She looked at him.

“You’re the best thing anybody ever made. I’d have said it in there.” His jaw went tight. “You were walking. I wasn’t going to stop you walking.”

She took it out of gear again.

He reached across before she could say a thing. Took her face in both hands. Turned it to him. Kissed her wet eyes, one, then the other. Then her mouth. Slow. Deliberate. At the bottom of her mother’s drive with the engine running and the gates open. Like he was putting back what had been taken out of her in the yellow room, one piece at a time.

She was shaking. He kept going until she wasn’t. Her hands found his shirt under the jacket and grabbed.

“Do that again.”

He did it again. Harder. Fingers in her short hair. Until a car came up behind them and flashed its lights. She laughed into his mouth. Wet. Wobbly. Real. First time since the hall.

She pulled out onto the road down the Peak. The house went away behind them in the trees. Yellow. Enormous. Numbers on everything.

After the first bend he put his hand on the back of her neck.

“Don’t move it,” she said.

He didn’t, the whole way down the hill.

chapters.title: Jinx Builds the Getaway Car
chapters.desc: Rule four, at the kettle: he wants out. That means a car nobody knows, so they go to Jinx.
chapters.epigraph: “One order. No questions. And you never bring it back here with a hole in it.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
“Sera. I want out.”

Tuesday. Early. He was at the kettle with the plain mug in his hand and steam coming off it.

No build-up. No plan. Just turned round and said it across the garage, the way she’d told him to in January. Before you’ve worked it out. Tell me first.

She was on the bottom stair pulling her boots on. She stopped with a lace in each hand.

“…What?”

“I want out.”

Nobody else in yet but Mouse, a shape at the end of the bench with her headphones on. Her hands went still on the keyboard.

“Rule four.”

He nodded.

She tied her boots. Double knots. Both. Then she stood up.

“Okay. I’ll have the car.”

“Not your car.”

“What do you mean, not my—”

“They know your car.” He put the mug down. “They know all of them. Nonna. Gilded. The transporter. Mine, obviously, they gave it to me. Big Wu’s van. Mr. Kwok’s old taxi. The scooter Mouse rides to the night market.” No drama at all. Shopping list. “They’ve got every plate. When they come, the first thing they look for is a red Lancia. If we’re in it, it’s over before the bridge.”

“When they COME?”

“They’ll come.”

She stared at him. Her heart was going like a piston, and he was standing there with his hot water.

“So what do we need?”

“A car nobody knows. Nobody’s seen. That doesn’t look like anything.” A pause. “That’ll do two hundred and sixty on the coast road with four people shooting at it.”

“Two hundred and sixty. In something that looks like NOTHING.”

“If possible.”

She picked her jacket off the stair rail. Then she put it down again. Crossed the garage. Grabbed his face, mug and all, and kissed him so hard the hot water slopped on both of them.

“Ow.”

“Why now?” She was still holding his face. “Tell me why now.”

He looked at the notebook on the bench. Open at the page that said WEDDING. The line for the date. Still empty.

“Because I want to fill that in.”

She let go of him. She had to. Her eyes had gone.

“…Then we need Jinx.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina: need a car built. not a bike. dont say it

Jinx: cars are bikes for cowards

Serafina: i said dont say it

Jinx: saturday. bring cash. bring whoever it is

Serafina: how do u know theres a whoever

Jinx: u used a full stop last week. ur in love. come saturday

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx’s garage was near the Iron Docks, in an old sailmaker’s on a street of chandlers and rope shops and a noodle place that only fed men off the container ships. The part of the city where people said Zhao Zhendong’s name under their breath, or not at all. Black roll-up door. No sign. Inside, motorbikes in every stage of being born.

The third Saturday in September. Serafina kicked the door three times. You had to.

Jinx rolled out on a creeper. Tall, fierce, twenty-seven. Hair shaved up one side. Black nails. Tattoos from wrists to shoulders on both arms, a whole garden of them, peonies and gears and a carp swimming up the inside of her left forearm toward a spark plug. She grinned up at Serafina.

Then she looked past her. At the quiet man in the doorway.

The grin went.

“No.”

“You haven’t heard what it is!”

“I know what it is. It’s standing in my doorway.” She sat up. She’d grown up round the kind of men who used to stand outside her father’s shop. She could pick one out across a street. “Bureau.”

“I can’t tell you that.”

Jinx looked at him.

Then she laughed. Short. Surprised. She got up and wiped her hands.

“Elowen says that. About Zhao. Word for word.”

“It’s going round.” Serafina shrugged.

“Still no. I build bikes.”

“I’m not asking you to build a car. I’m asking you to help ME build one. Here. Where nobody’s looking.” Serafina stuck her hands in her pockets. “You owe me for the gearbox.”

“I paid you for that gearbox.”

“You paid me in a BIKE. Which I love. Which I ride every day. Which is not money.” She tilted her head. “And he wants out, Jinx.”

Jinx went still.

She looked at Haozhen again. Different this time. The way she looked at an engine making a noise she’d never heard.

“Out. Of the…” She didn’t say the word. “Out of that.”

“Yes.”

Jinx’s eyes dropped to Serafina’s hand. The ruby.

“That’s new.”

“Engaged.”

“To him?”

“To him.”

Jinx was quiet. Then she turned and walked to the back wall, where drawings hung on a line with clothes pegs. She stood in front of one with her arms folded. A motorbike, in pencil. Every bolt and spoke. Underneath, in neat architect’s letters: J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021.

“One order. No questions.” Still facing the drawing. “I don’t want to know where. Or who’s chasing. Or your name.” She turned round. “And you never bring it back here with a hole in it.”

“Agreed.”

“You.” A black nail at Serafina. “Wash my floor. Every night. Good soap.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They found it that afternoon in a breaker’s yard at the end of the Docks road.

A grey 2006 Toyota Crown estate. A taxi company’s, then a funeral company’s, then nobody’s. Two hundred and ninety thousand kilometres. A dent in the rear door. A cracked dash. Wooden-bead seat covers, the kind taxi drivers put on for their backs.

The dullest, most invisible car Serafina had ever seen. Jammed between a burnt-out van and a pile of tyres. She put her hand over her mouth.

“Oh. Oh, it’s PERFECT.”

He looked at it a while. The corner of his mouth moved.

“It looks like me.”

“It looks EXACTLY like you!”

She paid the breaker four hundred and twenty in cash. They pushed it onto Jinx’s trailer by hand. Serafina sat on the bonnet the whole way back and refused to get off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five weeks. Nights.

Every night after dinner Jinx went downstairs, pulled the roll-up door down and put the lights on. Upstairs she’d told Raiden she had a big job on. A customer’s car. True. Serafina came. The quiet man came. After the first week, Mouse came too, with a rucksack, two laptops and a soldering iron. Nobody had asked her. She sat in the gutted passenger seat and started doing things to the wiring that she would not explain to anybody.

“What’s she doing?” Jinx, under the bonnet.

“No idea. Don’t touch it.”

Haozhen held lamps. Passed spanners. Fetched noodles from the place for the container-ship men. They looked at him the first night, and never again.

“Does he ever sit down?” Jinx, at two in the morning.

“Only in my car.”

“Weird.”

“Very.”

They took the engine out. It was tired and honest and had carried a lot of people to a lot of funerals. Serafina patted it before they lifted it.

Jinx snorted. “Don’t get attached.”

“I’m not attached!”

“You patted it.”

“It was a GOOD engine, Jinx…”

The new one took Jinx three phone calls and a favour from somebody in the Walled City she wouldn’t name. It had never been meant to share a road with a family estate. It sat in the Crown’s engine bay like a tiger in a dog kennel.

He paid. All of it. Engine, brakes, everything after, in cash, in a plain envelope he left on Jinx’s bench the first night without a word. Jinx counted it twice and pushed half back across the bench.

“Too much.”

In the morning the half was in her toolbox, under the socket tray. He was holding a lamp for Serafina like he’d never seen an envelope in his life.

Jinx looked at the toolbox. At him. Let it go. So did Serafina. An envelope on a bench in front of everybody. That was nearly his name on something. She’d take it.

Brakes. Suspension, set so the car still sat at exactly the height of a tired old estate and wallowed a bit at walking pace, until you asked it not to. A different tank. Tyres that kept going when they shouldn’t. The dent stayed. The cracked dash stayed. The beads stayed.

“Beads stay. Nobody looks under the bonnet of a car with beads.”

On the second Saturday there was no work. Jinx put on a dress and went to a wedding in a flower shop.

“Whose?”

“My boyfriend’s sister’s.” Jinx was trying to do her eyeliner in a wing mirror. “Thirty people and a tulip floor. Don’t ask.”

Serafina didn’t ask. She went home and sat on the loft mattress and looked at her ring for an hour. A flower shop. Thirty people. When? Whose door would he be watching that night? Would there ever be a date on that page?

He came up the stairs at midnight and lay down beside her with his shoes still on.

“Soon,” he said. Like he’d heard every word she hadn’t said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fourth Saturday, in the middle of the night, footsteps on the stairs.

Jinx looked up from under the bonnet. Serafina froze with a lamp in her hand. Mouse stopped soldering. The quiet man didn’t move at all. Which was worse.

Raiden Lin came down the back stairs in shorts and a paint-spattered jumper, with his sketchbook under his arm and a flask in his other hand. He looked at the car. At Serafina. At the quiet man. At the girl with the laptops in the passenger seat.

“Darling, I’ve brought soup.”

Nobody breathed.

He didn’t say anything else. Not one word. He put the flask on the bench. He sat down on the bottom stair and opened the sketchbook and drew.

Forty minutes. The only sound was his pencil and Mouse, very slowly, starting to solder again.

Then he tore the page out. Got up. Gave it to the quiet man. And went back upstairs to bed. Serafina came round the car to look.

It was the Crown. Grey, dented, beaded, every crease and chip exactly how it looked from outside. Except he’d drawn the outside like glass. And through the glass, everything underneath. The engine like a tiger. The brakes. The tank. Mouse’s wiring, a fine silver web. Every bolt and spring.

In the bottom corner, tiny, a ring with a square stone. He’d seen it in the half-second on the stairs.

Underneath, in the careful letters: Nobody’s car, as it really is. R. 2023.

“Nobody.”

Haozhen looked at the drawing for a long time.

“Nobody,” she said again. “That’s her name. Obviously.” Her voice wobbled. “What else would she be called?”

Jinx came out from under the bonnet, wiping her hands. She looked at the drawing. At the stairs.

“He won’t mention it,” she said. “Ever. Don’t you mention it either.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They took Nobody out for the first time on the last Saturday in October. Three in the morning, the Docks road.

Serafina drove. He sat beside her on the beads. The grey Crown rolled out into the street of chandlers at walking pace, wallowing a bit, a tired old estate going home off a night shift. Onto the Docks road. Four kilometres, dead straight, empty except for the cranes.

“Ready?”

“Yes.”

“Really ready? Hold on to something.”

“I’m holding on.”

She put her foot down.

It was like falling. That was the only way she could ever explain it to Jinx. Nobody sat down on its back wheels. The beads dug into her spine. The engine made a noise no taxi had ever made, a long rising scream from somewhere deep in the grey bodywork. The cranes went past like fence posts. The needle went round the cracked dial to a hundred and eighty, where the taxi company’s numbers ran out, and lay there.

Mouse’s little screen under the dash kept counting. Two hundred and sixty-four. In a grey Toyota with wooden beads on the seats and a dent in the back door.

She braked at the end and the car stopped dead straight, like it had hit a wall of feathers. She sat with both hands on the wheel and started laughing and couldn’t stop.

He was laughing too. Out loud. Braced on the cracked dashboard, head back.

She grabbed his shirt across the gearstick and hauled him over and kissed him. Hard. Fast. Teeth. The engine ticking. The cranes standing over them in the dark.

“Two hundred and sixty-four,” he said, into her mouth.

“Four extra. You’re welcome.”

He kissed her back. Properly. His hand on her jaw. The windows fogged. Her elbow hit the horn, which was the original taxi horn and sounded like a goose. Neither of them stopped until someone banged on the roof with a spanner.

Jinx. She’d ridden down after them on her bike. Visor up, spanner in her hand, standing at Nobody’s door.

“Not in my car. I’ve only just done the seats.”

“They’re beads, Jinx!”

“They’re MY beads.”

She got back on the bike and rode away up the Docks road. At the far end, under the last crane, they saw her stop. Turn round. Sit there in the dark, watching them. Making sure.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody went under a cover at the back of the sailmaker’s, beside the dyno, where nobody looked. Serafina came once a week to start it. She sat in it and listened to it and went away again.

The next morning there was a sheet by the kettle under the railway bridge. Torn out of the black notebook along the perforations. One line in his small square letters, neat as a run sheet.

Way out: built.

She read it twice. Then she uncapped the red marker. Underneath, big and messy, right off the edge of the paper, she wrote:

DRIVER: ME.

When he came in, he read it. He didn’t say anything. He folded it once and put it in his inside pocket. Left side. Where the gauge used to be.

chapters.title: The Mission He Didn’t Take
chapters.desc: A grey building in the capital that isn’t on any map. A seventh-floor office with a radiator that knocks. A thin folder about a journalist in Singapore. For the first time in eleven years, he says one word to the state, and it’s the wrong one.
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know what happens to people who say no, Haozhen?” “Yes, Director. I’ve driven them.”
chapters.content:
“Sit STILL.”

“I am sitting still.”

“You’re sitting still like a man about to jump out of a window.” Serafina snipped. A bit of black hair fell on the towel round his shoulders. “Which you can’t, by the way. It’s a loft. You’d land on Gilded and Big Wu would kill you.”

Monday night. The mattress. A towel, the kitchen scissors, a mug of water to wet the comb. The same scissors she did her own hair with, over the sink, every six weeks, badly.

He’d said it at dinner. Rule three, exactly how she’d asked for it in January, over egg sandwiches on Nonna’s bonnet.

I’ll be gone. The capital. Two days, maybe three.

And then, because it was him, the rest of it. Without her asking.

They’re giving me something. I’m going to say no.

So now she was cutting his hair. Why? No idea. Her hands had wanted something to do, and his hair was there.

“You don’t say no to the state with a fringe,” she said. “It’s a rule.”

“Whose rule?”

“Mine. Number five.” Snip. “Head down.”

He put his head down. She did the back of his neck, short, the way he wore it, and blew the cut ends off his skin. He shivered. A man who’d once stood forty-one minutes at a service door without moving a finger, and he shivered.

She did it again. On purpose.

“Sera.”

“What? It’s hair. I’m being thorough.”

The ruby caught the lamp every time she moved the scissors. He watched it in the black window like it was a bird he was waiting to fly off.

“If I nick your ear it’s the ring’s fault,” she said. “It’s heavy. Your fault, really. You bought it.”

“I’ll take the blame.”

“Good.” She combed. Snipped. Combed. Then her hands stopped in his hair. “Hao. What do they do. When you say it.”

“Nothing. The first time.” He didn’t lift his head. “They give you time to change your mind.”

“And the second time?”

He didn’t answer. She hadn’t really expected him to.

She put the scissors down on the mattress. She pulled the towel off his shoulders and shook it out over the floor. Then she climbed round in front of him on her knees, took his face in both hands, and turned it to the lamp.

Crooked. A bit. Over the left ear.

“Is it straight?”

“It’s perfect.” She kissed him. Fast. Hard. Her knee on the scissors. “Ow. It’s perfect, Hao. Nobody in the capital will be able to take their eyes off it.”

“That’s the opposite of what I want.”

“I know,” she said, and kissed him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The building had no name.

Seven floors. A wall. A gate. A guard box with a chilli plant in the window. Taxi drivers who were asked to go there took you to the bus stop opposite and let you walk.

He had been walking it since he was eighteen.

Old Tsui came out of the box with his bad hip and looked at him. Looked at his hair. Said nothing. Lifted the barrier.

The lift stuck between four and five. He kicked it. Same spot as always, low on the left. It went on.

The radiator on the seventh floor knocked three times. Nobody had fixed it since 2009. It always sounded like somebody wanting to be let in.

He knew what he was going to say. That was new. Eleven years of this corridor and he had never once walked down it knowing what he’d say. He’d just said yes. Yes was easy. Yes didn’t need a shape.

This had a shape. He’d had it since a hotel lobby in Lisbon at dawn. Since a boy on a step with a ball under his arm. Since the third night in the passenger seat, with her arms round his head.

He ran the other thing too. The thing he always ran in a building. Exits. The stairs at the east end. The fire door on three that didn’t lock. The archive on two, which was paper, all of it. If they put a hand on her, he’d start there. He’d worked that out on the plane, between the meal and the landing. It hadn’t taken long.

Then he put it away.

In his inside pocket, left side, there was a page torn out of his own notebook. Way out: built. Under it, in red marker, right off the edge of the paper, in letters three times the size of his: DRIVER: ME.

He knocked once on the door at the end.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Come.”

Small office. Warm. A desk, two chairs, a window that looked at a wall. A kettle. A photograph on the desk turned away from the visitor, which nobody had ever seen. Director Duan behind it in her grey cardigan with the darned elbow, knitting the red scarf.

“Sit. Hot water’s in the flask.”

He sat. He didn’t pour.

“How is she?”

“Well, Director.”

“Won her class at the endurance round in October. Six hours. Second overall, with the one with the beard.” The needles clicked. “And the house on the Peak goes under the hammer on the twenty-eighth. I’m sorry. I saw the brochure. Lovely staircase.”

He didn’t say anything.

“You’ve had your hair cut.”

“Yes.”

“At home, I think.” She didn’t look up. “It’s a bit short over one ear. Sleeping?”

“Yes.”

“Liar.” Kindly. Still on the wool. “Mr. Gong is being very cooperative, by the way. In case you wondered. He’s told us everything.” A row. “Which is nothing. He never showed anyone. Upstairs are thrilled.”

The radiator knocked.

“His wife has written to the embassy in Lisbon. Eleven times. The boy wrote once. Crayon. Portuguese. I had it translated.” She looked at him over her glasses. “Would you like to know what it said?”

“No.”

“No. I didn’t think so.” A folder came out of the drawer. Thin. Grey. She laid it on the desk between them. “Singapore.”

He didn’t open it.

“A journalist. Thirty-four. She writes for a magazine there about money. Where it goes. Lately she’s been writing about some of ours, and she’s good, which is the trouble. She was born here. Mother’s still here.” Click. Click. “We’d like her home.”

“In what condition?”

The needles stopped.

Half a second. The row left hanging on the bamboo. She looked at him over the top of her glasses, the same look she’d given him in the tea house in May. A farmer looking at a dog she’d raised, who’d just looked at the gate.

“Alive. Of course. We’re not animals.” She started again. “December. Two weeks, perhaps three. You’ll have Tianyi. He loves Singapore. The chilli crab.”

He looked at the folder.

Thin. Grey. A woman of thirty-four was inside it. He could feel her in there, already in the back seat. Hands on her knees.

His hand was flat on his chest. When had he put it there?

DRIVER: ME.

“No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing happened.

That was the part he’d remember. On the plane he’d run it a hundred times and something always happened. A door. A hand on a phone. Her face.

She went on knitting. Exact same speed. Finished the row. Turned the scarf. Started the next.

“No,” she said, after a while. Trying it out. A word from somebody else’s language.

“No, Director.”

“You don’t want Singapore. All right.” In, round, through, off. “There’s a man in Prague nobody else wants. It snows in Prague in December. You like snow.”

“Not Prague. Not anywhere.”

“Eleven years.” Click. “You’ve never said no to me. Not once. Not I’d rather not. Not can someone else.”

He waited.

“You went to that hotel at eighteen and came back and filled in the form. Best I ever had. Best I’ve got.” She didn’t look up. “And now you sit there and say no like a child with his greens. Because of a girl who fixes cars.”

“Not because of her.”

“Then what?”

He thought about it. Properly. She’d taught him that.

“A boy with a football.” He looked at the folder. “He looked at me.”

The needles stopped again. This time they stayed stopped.

She put the knitting down.

She never put it down. Not in the commandant’s office. Not in the tea house. Not once in a hotel room with a man on the carpet. She laid the needles and the long red ribbed scarf on the desk and folded her hands on top. Took her glasses off.

Without them her eyes were small. Tired. Older than he’d let himself see.

“Do you know what happens to people who say no, Haozhen?”

“Yes, Director. I’ve driven them.”

The radiator knocked three times. Like someone wanting in.

She put her glasses back on. Picked up the needles. Found her place.

“Go home.” Click. “Think about it. You have until the New Year.” Click. “Think about your mother in her little flat with her machine. Think about Miss Song and her car with the number on the door.”

She turned the scarf.

“You don’t have a name without us, Haozhen. No file. Not one thing you didn’t get from this building.”

He stood up.

“Come back after the New Year and tell me you’ve changed your mind. I’ll give you Prague. We’ll never mention it.” Click. “I’ll put it down to the strain of the engagement.”

“Thank you, Director.”

“Leave the folder.”

He left it. At the door he turned round.

“The scarf. Who’s it for?”

The needles didn’t even slow down.

“Go home, Haozhen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi was in the corridor.

Leaning on the wall by the radiator. Hands in his pockets. Cinnamon gum going. He took one look at Haozhen’s face and stopped chewing.

“She gave you Singapore.”

Nothing.

“And you said—” He blew out through his nose. “Oh, Haozhen… you idiot.”

“Don’t take it.”

“I’ll take it. I like Singapore.” He pushed off the wall. “She’ll call me in this afternoon and watch my face the whole time I’m holding it. Checking if it’s catching.”

He laughed. It came out wrong.

“It’s not catching! I haven’t got a racing driver. I’ve got a fish tank and an ex-wife who sends me pictures of her new dog.”

“Tianyi.”

“What happened to you? Honestly. Before Lisbon, even.”

Haozhen thought about the east service door. A woman in a borrowed black dress and boots, walking straight across a ballroom at him, not one bit scared.

“Someone told me I wasn’t a guard.”

“And you believed her?”

“It took a year.”

Tianyi looked at him. Then at the floor. Down below them, the lift stuck between four and five, and somebody kicked it.

“You know what they do. If you keep saying it.” He wasn’t chewing at all now. “They don’t send a stranger. They never do. It’s in the training. They send the friend.”

“I know.”

“So it’ll be me.”

“I know. I’m sorry.”

For a second Tianyi was sixteen again. The boy in the next bed in a dormitory of forty, under a roof that leaked, who laughed with his whole face and wouldn’t give the window seat to anyone but the quiet one from the mining town.

Then he grinned the old grin and put a fresh stick in his mouth.

“Don’t be sorry. Be faster.” He was at the director’s door. He stopped with his knuckles up. “Still no date? For the wedding?”

“Not yet.”

“Get one.” He knocked. “I’ve never been invited to anything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang her from a payphone at the airport. The phone in his pocket belonged to the building.

First ring.

“If that’s the tyre people, I already paid—”

“It’s me.”

“Hao!” A clatter. Something metal going into the bucket. The radio on. “Okay. Okay. Did you know Jinx is MARRIED?”

He closed his eyes.

“To Raiden! Since 2021! Two whole years! I was holding a sump plug and she just said it. My husband says hi. Like it was the oil grade. His whole family found out at that flower-shop wedding and she never told ME, and I let her put her hands in my engine bay…” A breath. “Why aren’t you surprised?”

“I checked her.”

“You checked—”

“Before Nobody. I check everyone who touches your car.”

“You CHECKED Jinx!”

“The registry’s in the old town. Thursday. Ten in the morning.”

“Oh my God.” A laugh, half outraged. Then it went. “Hao. Why are you ringing me from a payphone. What happened?”

He leaned his forehead on the glass of the booth. Cold. Somebody’s fingerprints on it. Down the line he heard a train start, far off, coming up to the bridge.

“I said no.”

She didn’t say anything.

The train came. He heard it get onto the bridge. Heard the whole garage shake, the shelf rattle, the spanner in the bucket jump. Eleven hundred kilometres away. The most ordinary noise in the world. He listened to it go all the way over.

“How did it feel?”

He thought about it.

“Like the fourth lamp post.”

A sound came down the line. A laugh with something broken in the middle of it. He heard her put her hand over her mouth.

“When do you land?”

“Morning.”

“I’ll be there. Arrivals. In Nonna.”

“Sera, they’ll be watching the—”

“Good! Let them!” She was crying now. He could hear it. She didn’t care. “Red car, dent in the door, NO WAITING lane, engine running, for as long as I like. I want every one of them to see who’s picking you up.”

He stood there with his head on the glass.

“I love you.”

“I know. You said it through a window. I’m still cross about that.” A sniff. A big one. “Get on the plane.”

“Sera.”

“What?”

“When I get in that car, I’m going to kiss you before you’ve got it out of first. Then I’m going to keep going until the warden blows his whistle.” A pause. “Then a bit longer.”

Nothing on the line. Just her breathing. Then the train, the next one, a long way off.

“Get on the plane, Hao.”

Her voice had gone completely to pieces.
